lsj_entry_text: λῆμμα, ατος, τό, (λαμβάνω) anything received, opp. δόμα, Antig. ap. Plu. 2.182e ; λ. καὶ ἀνάλωμα receipt and expense, Lys. 32.20 , Pl. greek_sentence: Ἐῶ γὰρ λέγειν ὅτι οὐδὲ ἐπιστημονικοῖς ἐν ἅπασι τοῖς τοιούτοις λόγοις οἱ σοφισταὶ χρῶνται [470] πρὸς τὴν τῶν λημμάτων εὕρεσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς, καὶ τὸ χεῖρον ἁπάντων, ὅτι μηδ’ ἐπισκεψάμενοί ποτε περὶ φύσεως ἐπαγωγῆς, μηδ’ ἄν τις αὐτοὺς εἰς τοῦτο προκαλῆται, τολμῶντες ἀκολουθεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς ὑπὲρ ἀποδείξεώς τι πραγματευομένοις ἐπιτιμῶντες.
english_sentence_A: For I pass over saying that in all such arguments the sophists do not even employ scientific [methods] [470] for the discovery of the premises, but [argue] from induction; and, what is worst of all, that they have never even inquired into the nature of induction, nor, should anyone challenge them to this, do they dare to follow, but they even censure those who occupy themselves at all with demonstration.
english_sentence_B: For I pass over the fact that in all such matters the sophists do not even use scientific arguments [470] for finding the lemmas, but argue from induction. Worst of all, they have never once examined the nature of induction, and they do not dare to follow even if someone challenges them to it; they even censure those who devote some labour to demonstration.

greek_sentence: ἔτι δὲ χεῖρον ὅτι μηδ’ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς μόνον, ἀλλ’ ἐκ παραδειγμάτων ἐνίοτε συλλογίζονται, καθάπερ οἱ ῥήτορες.
english_sentence_A: And still worse, that they sometimes reason not even from induction alone, but from examples, just as the orators do.
english_sentence_B: Still worse, they draw their conclusions not from induction alone but sometimes from examples, as the rhetors do. For the man who says that oil is cold because it is viscous, as phlegm also is, reasons through an example.

greek_sentence: ὅ τε γὰρ φάσκων ψυχρὸν εἶναι τοὔλαιον, ὅτι καὶ γλίσχρον, ὥσπερ καὶ τὸ φλέγμα, διὰ παραδείγματος συλλογίζεται, τὴν ἴσην ἰσχὺν τῆς ἀποδείξεως παρέχων ὁμοίως τῷ λέγοντι θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν αὐτὸ, διότι γλίσχρον ἐστὶν, ὡς ὁ ἰξός· ὅ τε φάσκων θερμὸν εἶναι, ὅτι ῥᾳδίως ἐκφλογοῦται καθάπερ ἄσφαλτος, τῷ λέγοντι ψυχρὸν εἶναι, διότι ῥᾳδίως πήγνυται, καθάπερ ὕδωρ.
english_sentence_A: For the one who asserts that oil is cold because it is also viscous, just as phlegm is, reasons by means of an example, furnishing an equal strength of demonstration, in the same way as the one who says that it is hot because it is viscous, like birdlime; and the one who asserts that it is hot because it readily bursts into flame, like asphalt, [furnishes a demonstration of equal strength] to the one who says that it is cold because it readily congeals, like water.
english_sentence_B: He offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is hot because it is viscous, like birdlime. Likewise, the man who says it is hot because it easily bursts into flame, like bitumen, offers a demonstration of equal force with that of the man who says it is cold because it easily congeals, like water.

greek_sentence: τὸ γὰρ ἐκ παραδείγματος ἢ ἐκ παραδειγμάτων πιστοῦσθαί τι διαφέρει τοῦ δι’ ἐπαγωγῆς πιστουμένου τῷ τὸν μὲν ἐκ παραδειγμάτων πιστούμενον ἓν μὲν ἢ δύο τῶν ὁμογενῶν λέγειν, ἢ πάντως γε ὀλίγα τὰ πλείω παραλείποντα, τὸν δ’ ἐξ ἐπαγωγῆς ἅπαντα περιλαμβάνειν πειρᾶσθαι τὰ διὰ τῆς ἐμπειρίας ἐγνωσμένα, καὶ [471] μηδὲν ὡς οἷόν τε παραλιπεῖν ὃ προφανές τε καὶ δῆλον τοῖς πολλοῖς, ἀλλὰ ἀποκεκρυμμένον τε καὶ ὀλίγοις γνωστόν.
english_sentence_A: For establishing something from an example or from examples differs from what is established through induction in this respect: the one who establishes from examples mentions one or two of the things of the same kind, or at any rate few, omitting the majority, whereas the one who proceeds from induction attempts to encompass everything that is known through experience, and [471] to omit, so far as possible, nothing that is obvious and clear to the many, but also what is hidden and known to few.
english_sentence_B: For establishing something from an example, or from examples, differs from establishing it through induction in this: the one who establishes from examples cites one or two of the things of the same kind, or in any case a few, leaving out the greater number, whereas the one who argues from induction tries to take in all the things known through experience, and [471] to leave out, so far as possible, nothing: not [only] what is evident and plain to the many, but [also] what is hidden and known to few.

english_sentence_A: For I have resolved to go through, under heads, everything that has been said by physicians about the power of oil, plausibly in appearance, but not truly.
english_sentence_B: For I have resolved to go through, under main headings, everything that has been said by the physicians about the power of oil, plausibly in appearance, but certainly not truly.

greek_sentence: συνεκπυροῦσθαί τε γὰρ, φησὶ, καὶ ἐπικαίειν τὸ ἔλαιον ὑπὸ τῆς τρίψεως θερμαινόμενον [472] ἐνόμιζεν καὶ κατὰ τοῦτο ἐξικμάζειν καὶ ξηραίνειν ἱκανῶς, ὥσπερ τῶν ὀπτωμένων τὰ χριόμενα.
english_sentence_A: For he thought, he says, that the oil, being heated by the rubbing, [472] is set ablaze together with the skin and burns it, and that in this way it draws out the moisture and dries it considerably, just as, among things that are roasted, those that have been anointed.

english_sentence_A: For first he thought that such rubbing becomes uneven, because the hands slip and cannot take hold of the flesh in the same way on account of the grease.
english_sentence_B: For in the first place he thought that such rubbing turns out uneven, because the hands slip and cannot take hold of the flesh evenly on account of the fat.

greek_sentence: τούτου δὲ γιγνομένου [473] πολλὰ τῶν εἰθισμένων διὰ τῆς σαρκὸς μετὰ τοῦ πνεύματος ῥεῖν καὶ ἔξω διαπίπτειν ἀποστέγεσθαι, ὥσπερ καὶ διὰ τῶν ἠθμῶν καὶ τῶν ὀθονίων καὶ ἐρίων καὶ πάντων δι’ ὧν ἠθεῖταί τι ἐγχεόμενον καὶ χριόμενον, οὐ δύνασθαι τὰ ὑγρὰ ῥεῖν ὁμοίως.
english_sentence_A: And when this happens, [473] many of the things that are accustomed to flow through the flesh together with the pneuma and to pass out are held back, just as also through strainers and linen cloths and wools and all the things through which something is strained, when oil is poured on and smeared over them, the liquids cannot flow in the same way.
english_sentence_B: And when this happens, [473] many of the things that are accustomed to flow through the flesh together with the pneuma and to pass out are, he thought, shut in; just as through strainers and linen cloths and wool, and through all the things through which something poured on or smeared on is strained, liquids cannot flow in the same way.

lsj_entry_text: ἔκ-κρισις, εως, ἡ, separation, Arist. Mete. 342a15 , Onos. 9.1 (pl.). secretion, of the animal functions, Arist. PA 689a16 , GA 727a2 ; τῶν ὑγρῶν Eun. Hist. p.263 D. = ἔκκριμα , of excrement, Hp. Aph. 2.15 ; of the menses, Arist. HA 583a2 , etc.
greek_sentence: ἀπολαμβανομένης δὲ τῆς τοιαύτης ἐκκρίσεως τὰ μὲν παλιῤῥοεῖν εἴσω, συμπληροῦν ἀθροιζόμενα τοὺς πόρους ἀλλήλοις πλεκόμενα καὶ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐλαίου περιλαμβανόμενα διὰ τὸ ἔχειν τι ἰξῶδες τὸ ἔλαιον, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων φαίνεται τὸ λιπαρὸν τοὺς κονιορτοὺς καὶ τὰ κάρφη καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τὰ τοιαῦτα συνθηρεύειν.
english_sentence_A: And when such excretion is intercepted, some of them flow back inward, and, gathering together, fill up the pores, being entangled with one another and enclosed by the oil because the oil has something glutinous in it, just as in other cases the oily substance is seen to catch up dust and chaff and other such things.
english_sentence_B: And when such excretion is intercepted, some of it flows back inward, and, collecting, fills up the pores, being interwoven with one another and enveloped by the oil, because the oil has something viscid about it, just as in other cases the oily is seen to catch up dust, bits of chaff and other such things.

greek_sentence: ἄνευ μὲν οὖν τρίψεως ἀλειφομένους οὐδὲν λυπεῖν· ἀσθενεστέραν γὰρ εἶναι τὴν δῆξιν ἢ ὥστε ποιεῖν τινα αἴσθησιν· μετὰ δὲ τῆς τρίψεως ﻿ [474] εἰσδυόμενον εἰς τὴν σάρκα, κακουργεῖν μᾶλλον τῇ δήξει καθάπερ πολλὰ τῶν φαρμάκων, οὕτω μὲν ἐπιχρισθέντα ἧττον ἰσχύειν, προσπιεζόμενα δὲ καὶ εἰσδυόμενα εἴσω μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖν.
english_sentence_A: Those, then, who anoint themselves without rubbing it does not trouble at all; for the biting is too weak to produce any sensation; but with rubbing, [474] as it penetrates into the flesh, it does more harm by its biting, just as many drugs, when merely smeared on in this way, are less strong, but when pressed in and penetrating inward act more powerfully.

english_sentence_A: For it is possible to give an empirical cause for each of such problems: the cooks would say that they smear the fish and the meat for this reason, that their outer parts become dry and scorched round about when they are roasted without fat; the gymnastic trainers would say that they rub the athletes in oil because this both dissolves the fatigues already present and mitigates those to come, and makes the rubbing itself perfectly even and gentle, and prepares the body for the movements to come.
english_sentence_B: For it is possible to give an empirical cause for each of such problems: the cooks would say that they anoint the fish and the meat for this reason, that their outer parts become dry and scorched all round when they are roasted without the fat; the trainers would say that they rub the athletes in oil because it both dissolves the fatigues already present and soothes those that are to come, and renders the rubbing itself even and perfectly gentle, and prepares the body for the movements that are to follow.

greek_sentence: οὐδὲ γὰρ διὰ τί λευκὸς μὲν ἐλλέβορος ἄνω καθαίρει, μέλας δὲ κάτω γινώσκοντες, [477] οὐδὲ διὰ τί κνίκος μὲν φλέγματος ἀγωγόν ἐστιν, ἐπίθυμον δὲ μελάνων οὐκ εἰδότες, ὅμως χρῶνται τοῖς φαρμάκοις εἰς ἅπερ ἐδίδαξεν ἡ πεῖρα καὶ θεραπεύουσι τοὺς δεομένους καὶ πιστεύουσι τοῖς ἐναργῶς φαινομένοις καὶ καταγελῶσι τῶν τῷ λόγῳ τἀναντία κατασκευαζόντων.
english_sentence_A: For not even knowing why white hellebore purges upward and black downward, [477] nor knowing why cnecus is evacuative of phlegm and epithymum of black humours, they nevertheless use the drugs for those purposes which experience has taught, and they treat those in need, and they trust what is evidently apparent, and they laugh at those who establish the contrary by reasoning.

english_sentence_A: For he says that dry rubbing is better than that with oil, because it renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas it becomes softer in those who are rubbed dry.
english_sentence_B: For he says that dry rubbing is better than rubbing with oil, because [oil] renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas in those who are rubbed dry it becomes softer.

greek_sentence: λέγει μὲν γὰρ ἀμείνω τὴν ξηρὰν τρίψιν εἶναι τῆς μετ’ ἐλαίου, διότι τὸ σῶμα σκληρότερόν τε καὶ ξηρότερον τοῖς ἀλειφομένοις ἐργάζεται, μαλακώτερον δὲ τοῖς ξηροῖς τριβομένοις γίγνεται.
english_sentence_A: For he says that dry rubbing is better than that with oil, because it renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas it becomes softer in those who are rubbed dry.
english_sentence_B: For he says that dry rubbing is better than rubbing with oil, because [oil] renders the body harder and drier in those who are anointed, whereas in those who are rubbed dry it becomes softer.

greek_sentence: λέγει δ’ οὐδὲν ἧττον ἐν αὐτῷ τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ προελθὼν βραχὺ καὶ τὰ ξύλα καὶ τὰ δέρματα καὶ τὰ ἄλλα τὰ μετ’ ἐλαίου τριβόμενα διαδιδόναι μέχρι τοῦ βάθους αὐτοῦ καὶ τοῦτο εἶναι μέγιστον μαρτύριον ὅτι κᾀν τοῖς ἡμετέροις σώμασιν εἴσω χωροῦν ἐμπλάττει τε τοὺς πόρους καὶ κωλύει τὰς τῶν ὑγρῶν ἐκροάς.
english_sentence_A: Yet no less, in this same discourse, after proceeding a little further, he says that wood and hides and the other things that are rubbed with oil let it pass through as far as their depth, and that this is the greatest testimony that in our bodies too, passing inward, it plasters up the pores and prevents the outflows of the moist humours.
english_sentence_B: Yet, going on a little further in this very argument, he no less says that pieces of wood and hides and the other things rubbed with oil let it pass through to their very depth, and that this is the greatest testimony that in our bodies too it passes inwards, blocks up the pores, and prevents the outflows of the fluids.

english_sentence_A: For if oil prevents the outflows of the fluids, it would surely not be said to dry, so that [478] it is in vain that it is guarded against, as something drying, in the rubbings.
english_sentence_B: For if oil prevents the outflows of the fluids, it could surely not be said to dry; so that [478] it is in vain that it is avoided in rubbings as something drying.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ταῦτά γέ φησι ποιεῖν θερμὸν, ἢ ψυχρὸν, ἢ εὔκρατον, ἢ χλιαρὸν, ἢ ζέον ἔλαιον, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τὸ ὕδωρ αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: For he surely does not say that hot, or cold, or well-tempered, or lukewarm, or boiling oil does the same things, just as water itself does not either.
english_sentence_B: For surely, he says (?), hot, or cold, or well-tempered, or lukewarm, or boiling oil does not produce these same effects, just as water itself does not either.

english_sentence_A: But if it is neither markedly cold nor hot, but such as what is called by most people spring-water, then it does none of the things mentioned, but displays its own proper power.

english_sentence_A: So too, then, if anyone wishes to examine oil, let him first render it free of all acquired coldness and heat, and in this way make the test.
english_sentence_B: So, then, if anyone wishes to examine oil as well, let him first make it free of all acquired cooling and heat, and in that state carry out the test.

english_sentence_A: So that when someone is rubbed with oil in the customary way, as all those devoted to gymnastics are, he is rubbed in oil alone, with every quality from without kept away from the outset.

lsj_entry_text: πίστις, ἡ, gen. εως, Ion. ιος Parm. 8.12 , Emp. 114 ; dat. πίστει, Ion. πίστι Hdt. 3.74 , 9.106 : Ion. nom. and acc. pl. πίστις v.l. in Id. 3.8 ; dat. πίστισι Id. 4.172 : (πείθομαι):—trust in others, faith, first in Hes. , πίστιες καὶ ἀπιστίαι ὤλεσαν ἄνδρας Op. 372 ; πίστει χρήματ' ὄλεσσα, ἀπιστίῃ δ' ἐσάωσα Thgn. 831 ; π. ἴσχειν τινί S. OC 950 ; τῷ θεῷ πίστιν φέροις Id. OT 1445 , etc.: generally, persuasion of a thing, confidence, assurance, Pi. N. 8.44 (πιστόν Sch.), etc.; ἡ βεβαιοτάτη π., ἀταραξία καὶ π. βέβαιος, Epicur. Ep. 1p.19 , 2p.36U. ; σωφροσύνης π. ἔχειν περί τινος to be persuaded of his probity, D. 18.215 ; π. περὶ θεῶν ἔχειν Plu. 2.1101c . in subjective sense, good faith, trustworthiness, honesty, Thgn. 1137 , A. Pers. 443 , Hdt. 8.105 ; θνῄσκει δὲ π., βλαστάνει δ' ἀπιστία S. OC 611 . of things, credence, credit, τὰν π. σμικρὰν παρ' ἔμοιγ' ἔχει E. El. 737 (lyr.); πίστιν τὰ τοιαῦτα ἔχει τινά Arist. EN 1179a17 ; π. λαβεῖν Plb. 1.35.4 . καλῇ π., = Lat.bona fide, PGnom. 180 (ii A.D.), etc.; αἱ κατὰ πίστιν γεινόμεναι κληρονομίαι, = Lat. hereditates fideicommissariae, ib. 56 . in a commercial sense, credit, π. τοσούτων χρημάτων ἐστί τινι παρά τισι he has credit for so much money with them, D. 36.57 , cf. 44 ; εἰς πίστιν διδόναι [τί τινι] Id. 32.16 ; εἰ ἕξω ἐλπίδα πίστεως Astramps. Orac. 68p.6H. position of trust or trusteeship, ἐν πίστει κληρονόμος ἀπολειφθείς left in trust, as guardian, Plu. Cic. 41 , cf. 2c supr.; ἐν πίστει ὤν τῷ βασιλεῖ IG 22.646.11 . Theol., faith, opp. sight and knowledge, 1 Ep.Cor. 13.13 , etc. that which gives confidence : hence, assurance, pledge of good faith, guarantee, οὐκ ἀνδρὸς ὅρκοι π. ἀλλ' ὅρκων ἀνήρ A. Fr. 394 , cf. S. El. 887 , E. Hipp. 1055 ; ὅρκοις καὶ πίστεσιν ἀναγκάξειν Antipho 6.25 : distd. from ὅρκοι and δεξιαί, Arist. Rh. 1375a10 , cf. E. Med. 22 ; ἔμβαλλε χειρὸς πίστιν S. Ph. 813 ; δός μοι χερὸς σῆς π. HG 1.3.12 ; πίστιν δοῦναι to give assurances, Hdt. 9.91 , cf. Th. 4.86 , 5.45 ; ὅρκους καὶ πίστιν ἀλλήλοις δότε Ar. Lys. 1185 ; ἔδοσαν πίστιν καὶ ἔλαβον interchanged them, X. Phd. 70b , Isoc. 3.8 , etc.: in Arist. , opp. a demonstrative proof (ἀπόδειξις), π. ἔντεχνοι, ἄτεχνοι, Rh. 1355b35 , 1375a22 : also, generally, π. ἐκ τῆς ἐπαγωγῆς APo. 90b14 , al.; π. ἡ διὰ συλλογισμοῦ Top. 103b7 ; ἡ τῶν λόγων π. english_sentence_A: For above all, as has also been shown before, one must avoid proofs drawn from external things, when one is in a position to apply to each thing its own proper test.

english_sentence_A: But if ever someone should wish to do even this, let him at least try to compare similar things, as he did in the case of the hides and the straps.

english_sentence_A: For no one, having first warmed the oil or [480] first cooled it in snow, but each taking whatever oil comes to hand, rubs down straps and hides, just as, I think, the physical instructors also rub down the boys with whatever oil comes to hand, neither having first warmed it on a fire nor first cooled it on snow.
english_sentence_B: For no one warms the oil beforehand or [480] chills it beforehand in snow; each takes whatever comes to hand and rubs down straps and hides with it. In the same way, I think, the masters of the palaestra (paidotribai) rub down the boys with whatever oil comes to hand, neither warming it beforehand over a fire nor chilling it beforehand on snow.

english_sentence_A: And if, once both have been stated in succession, someone should wish to draw a conclusion, one of two things follows: either, as an empiricist, he will say that he knows the power of each of the drugs from experience in relation to something, but is ignorant of its proper nature in itself; or, as a rationalist, that contrary powers, both biting and soothing, belong to the same drug—and then, I think, he will have the greatest difficulty in rendering the cause of why sometimes the one of them acts perceptibly and sometimes the other, the other being either destroyed or at any rate not clearly apparent.
english_sentence_B: And if, both having been stated one after the other, someone should wish to draw a conclusion, it will be one of two things: either, as an Empiric, he will say that he knows from experience the power of each of the drugs in relation to something, but is ignorant of its proper nature in and of itself; or, as a Rationalist, that opposite powers, biting and soothing, belong to the same drug; and then, I think, he will be in the greatest difficulty when he gives the cause why sometimes the one of them acts perceptibly and sometimes the other, the other having either perished or at any rate not being clearly apparent.

english_sentence_A: The solutions of all such puzzles, if they are posed as physical problems, are exceedingly difficult; but if they are referred to the use of the art, they require much experience [483], and epilogisms not many in number, but accurate and well-defined.

english_sentence_A: Most physicians, then, reason very carelessly and negligently about all these matters, not having said in what condition the person is to whom the oil is given, nor even what sort of oil it is; and then some of them assert that it bites and scrapes the inner parts in every case, while others assert that even if there is some biting already present beforehand, it soothes this too.
english_sentence_B: Most physicians, then, reason about all these matters very carelessly and indolently, not stating in what condition the person is to whom the oil is given, nor even of what kind the oil itself is. english_sentence_A: For surely it makes no small difference whether one introduces into a phlegmatic belly the oil which is called, and really is, entirely without salt, or into a clean one that which partakes of a great deal of salt.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ σμικρὸν δήπου διήνεγκεν ἢ τὸ παντάπασιν ἄναλον ὀνομαζόμενόν τε καὶ ὄντως ὑπάρχον ἔλαιον εἰς φλεγματώδη κοιλίαν ἐμβαλεῖν, ἢ τὸ πλείστων ἁλῶν μετέχον εἰς καθαράν.
english_sentence_A: For surely it makes no small difference whether one introduces into a phlegmatic belly the oil which is called, and really is, entirely without salt, or into a clean one that which partakes of a great deal of salt.
english_sentence_B: For surely it makes no small difference whether one puts oil that is called, and truly is, entirely unsalted into a phlegmatic belly, or oil that has a very large share of salt into a clean one.

Ph. 25 , etc., dat. ἀμφοῖν Aj. 1264 , etc.:—both, of individuals, Il. 1.363 ; of armies or nations, 2.124 :— Hom. uses only nom. and acc.: from Hom. downwards freq. with pl. greek_sentence: ἄμφω μὲν γὰρ λαπάξει τὴν γαστέρα, διαφερούσαις μέντοι ταῖς δυνάμεσιν.
english_sentence_A: For both will empty the belly, but by different powers.
english_sentence_B: For both will loosen the belly, but by different powers.

lsj_entry_text: ἄναλος, ον, (ἅλς A) without salt, not salted, Arist. Pr. 927a35 , Gal. 10.401 . of salt itself, salt which is no salt, Ev. Marc. 9.50 .
greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἄναλον ἐν φλεγματώδει διὰ τὸν ὄλισθον ὁμοίως [488] μαλάχαις τε καὶ βλίτοις καὶ μόροις· τὸ δὲ ἡλισμένον ἐν καθαρᾷ διὰ τὴν δριμύτητα παραπλησίως ἅλμῃ καὶ θαλάττῃ.
english_sentence_A: For the unsalted oil in a phlegmatic belly works through its slipperiness, in the same way as [488] mallows, blites and mulberries; whereas the salted oil in a clean belly works through its pungency, much as brine and sea-water do.
english_sentence_B: For the unsalted [oil] will loosen a phlegmatic [belly] through its slipperiness, in the same way as [488] mallows, blites and mulberries; the salted [oil] will loosen a clean [belly] through its pungency, similarly to brine and sea-water.

lsj_entry_text: αἱματ-ώδης, ες, looking like blood, διαχωρήματα Hp. Prog. 11 ; φάρυγξ Th. 2.49 , cf. Arist. Mete. 342a36 , Thphr. HP 6.4.6 , etc. of the nature of blood, bloody, ὑγρότης Arist. GA 726b32 , cf. PA 665b7 ( Comp. ), al.; διαχώρησις Diocl. Fr. 147 .
greek_sentence: μὴ τοίνυν μήτε ξύειν ἁπλῶς λέγομεν τοὔλαιον πάντως τἀντὸς, ἢ διαχωρήματα ποιεῖν αἱματώδη, μήτε πραΰνειν δήξεις, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν ἁλῶδες ἐν καθαρᾷ ξύειν, τὸ δ’ ἄναλον ἐν φλεγματώδει μὴ ξύειν.
english_sentence_A: Let us therefore say neither, simply, that oil in every case scrapes the inside, or produces bloody stools, nor that it soothes bitings, but rather that the salty oil scrapes in a clean belly, while the unsalted oil in a phlegmatic belly does not scrape.
english_sentence_B: Let us therefore say neither that oil simply scrapes the inner parts in every case, or produces bloody evacuations, nor that it soothes bitings. Let us say rather that the salty [oil] scrapes in a clean [belly], and that the unsalted [oil] in a phlegmatic [belly] does not scrape.

lsj_entry_text: δῆξις, εως, ἡ, (δάκνω) bite, biting, Arist. HA 623a1 ; δήξιες σπλάγχνων gnawings, Hp. VM 19 : metaph., of mental anguish, pangs, Zeno Stoic. 1.51 (pl.), Chrysipp.ib. 3.119 , Phld. D. 3 . Fr. 22 ; also, biting jokes, Plu. Lyc. 14 .
greek_sentence: συνεξάγονται γὰρ σὺν αὐτοῖς ἐνίοτε ταῦτα τὸν τὴν δῆξιν ἐργαζόμενον χυμὸν, ἰάματά τε γίγνεται δήξεως ὁμοίως τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασιν, τοῖς ἀποπλύνουσί τε καὶ ῥύπτουσιν.
english_sentence_A: For these sometimes carry out together with themselves the humour that produces the biting, and they become remedies for biting in the same way as all the other things that wash away and cleanse.
english_sentence_B: For these sometimes carry out along with themselves the humour that produces the biting, and so become remedies for biting, like all the other things that wash away and cleanse.

lsj_entry_text: ἐπίκρασις, εως, ἡ, (ἐπικεράννυμι( mixing of wine, Διοσκούροις IG 11 ( 2 ). 159 A 7 (iii B.C.), al.; tempering, Diph.Siph. ap. Ath. 3.91f ; of humours, Herod.Med. ap. Orib. 5.30.3 , Gal. 10.640 ; φαυλοτήτων Dsc. 2.49 .
greek_sentence: τῷ γὰρ τῆς κενώσεως λόγῳ τὴν ἴασιν, οὐ τῷ τῆς ἐπικράσεως ἐργάζεται.
english_sentence_A: For they bring about the cure by reason of evacuation, not by reason of tempering.
english_sentence_B: For they effect the cure by way of evacuation, not by way of tempering.

lsj_entry_text: ῥόδινος, η, ον, (ῥόδον) made of or from roses, στέφανος Anacr. 83 ; ἄλειφα Hippon. 58 ; μύρον Cephisod. 3 ; μύρον is understood in Thphr. greek_sentence: κηρωτὴ μέντοι πολλάκις ἐνεθεῖσα διὰ ῥοδίνου καὶ στέατος ἢ πιμελῆς, ἐν τῷ παραχρῆμα τὰς δήξεις ἰάσατο τῷ τῆς ἐπικράσεως λόγῳ.
english_sentence_A: A cerate, however, injected many times, made with rose oil and suet or soft fat, has at once cured the bitings by reason of tempering.
english_sentence_B: A cerate made with rose oil and suet or fat, however, when injected, has often healed bitings on the spot by way of tempering.

Ph. 883 ; -ώτερος γίγνεσθαι suffer less pain, Hp. Prorrh. 2.7 ; τὸ ἀνώδυνον, = ἀνωδυνία , Plu. 2.102d . Adv. ἀνωδύνως, τίκτεσθαι Hp. Coac. 527 , cf. Plu. Cic. 2 ; ἰᾶσθαι D.Chr. 41.9 : Sup. -ώτατα Hp. Acut. 4 . causing no pain, harmless, τὸ μὴ φρονεῖν γὰρ κάρτ' ἀ. κακόν S. Aj. 554b ; ἁμάρτημα ἢ αἶσχος ἀ., definition of τὸ γελοῖον, Arist. Po. 1449a35 . Adv. -ως, ἰάσασθαι τὴν πατρίδα Plu. Cleom. 10 . Act. , allaying pain, Hp. Aph. 5.22 , Dsc. 4.68 ( Comp. and Sup. ); φάρμακον ἀ. anodyne, Plu. 2.614c :—the epitaph of a physician in IG 14.1879 combines both signfs., πολλούς τε σώσας φαρμάκοις ἀνωδύνοις, ἀνώδυνον τὸ σῶμα νῦν ἔχει θανών.
greek_sentence: ἡμεῖς δὲ καὶ τοῖς διά τινα ψύξιν ἀλγοῦσι τἀντὸς ἐνιέντες ἐλαίου θερμοῦ παραχρῆμα πολλάκις ἀνωδύνους εἰργασάμεθα.
english_sentence_A: We ourselves, too, by injecting warm oil into those who have pain in the internal parts because of some chilling, have often rendered them free of pain immediately.
english_sentence_B: We, moreover, by injecting hot oil into those who suffer pain internally through some chilling, have often made them free of pain at once.

HP 1.11.2 , Alex. 127.5 , Theoc. 15.119 , Ev.Matt. 23.23 , Dsc. 3.58 , SIG 1170.26 (ii A. D.), Bilabel Ὀψαρτ. p.10 . (ἀνν- in Ar.ll.cc. Not to be confused with ἄννησον, q.v.)
greek_sentence: καὶ εἰ μείζονα δὲ τὴν ψύξιν εἶναι στοχαζόμεθα, προσεπιβάλλομεν ἄνηθον, θερμαίνοντες τοὔλαιον, εἰ δ’ ἔτι μείζονα, καὶ πήγανον καὶ ἄσφαλτον.
english_sentence_A: And if we conjecture the chilling to be greater, we add dill as well, heating the oil; and if greater still, rue and bitumen too.

english_sentence_A: [491] Thus, then, milk too often, as soon as it has been taken, turns sour in some people and nidorous in others, before, having been well concocted, it can temper the corruption.
english_sentence_B: [491] In the same way, then, milk too often, as soon as it has been administered, turns sour in some people and becomes nidorous in others, before, having been well concocted, it can temper the corruption. In these cases one must first evacuate the bulk of the bad humours, and only then administer groats and ptisan and milk and the other things which, when well concocted, contribute to good humours.

greek_sentence: καὶ χρὴ τούτων πρότερον ἐκκενώσαντας τὸ πολὺ τῆς κακοχυμίας οὕτω προσφέρειν καὶ χόνδρον καὶ πτισάνην καὶ γάλα καὶ τἄλλα ὅσα καλῶς πεφθέντα πρὸς εὐχυμίαν συντελεῖ, μὴ μέντοι μήτε τὰς χείρους μήτε τὰς ἐναντίας ἔχειν δυνάμεις ὅσον ἐπὶ τούτῳ νομίζειν ἅπαντα μήτε παραλιπεῖν ἐν τοῖς λόγοις ἑκόντα τῶν γιγνομένων θάτερα, καθάπερ Ἀρχίδαμος ἐπ’ ἐλαίου τῶν μὲν δακνομένων ὀφθαλμῶν ἐμνημόνευσεν καὶ τῆς κερχνώδους φάρυγγος καὶ τῆς ξυομένης γαστρὸς, ὅτι δὲ πολλάκις καὶ στόμαχον ἰσχυρῶς δακνόμενον ἔλαιον γλυκὺ ποθὲν ἰάσατο παραχρῆμα καὶ τὰς καθ’ ὅλην τὴν γαστέρα δήξεις ἐνεθὲν ἐπράϋνε καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ θαψίας τε καὶ ἀκαλήφης καὶ σκίλλης κατὰ τὸ δέρμα γιγνομένας ἐπαλειφθὲν ἔπαυσεν, οὐκ ἔτ’ ἐμνημόνευσεν.
english_sentence_A: And in these people one must first evacuate the greater part of the cacochymia and only then administer both groats and ptisane and milk and all the other things which, when well concocted, contribute to euchymia; one must not, however, suppose, so far as this is concerned, that all of them possess either worse or contrary powers, nor deliberately pass over in one's discussions one of the two things that happen, just as Archidamus, in the case of oil, mentioned the eyes that are bitten and the rasping throat and the belly that is scraped, but that sweet oil, when drunk, has often at once cured even a stomach that was being strongly bitten, and when injected has soothed the bitings throughout the whole belly, and when smeared on has stopped those arising on the skin from thapsia and nettle and squill—this he no longer mentioned.
english_sentence_B: One must not, however, suppose that all these, so far as depends on themselves, possess either the worse or the contrary powers, nor in one's account deliberately pass over one of the two sets of things that happen, as Archidamus did in the case of oil. He mentioned the eyes that are bitten, the rasping throat and the scraped belly, but he no longer mentioned that sweet oil, when drunk, has often at once healed even a stomach that was strongly bitten, that when injected it has soothed the bitings throughout the whole belly, and that when smeared on it has stopped those arising on the skin from thapsia, nettle and squill.

greek_sentence: θέασαι γὰρ ὡδί πως ἑκάτερον ἐπὶ παραδειγμάτων, ὑπόδειγμα θέμενος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ δύο τινὰς ἀνθρώπους δακνομένους μὲν ὁμοίως τὸ τῆς γαστρὸς στόμα, προσφερομένους δὲ χυλὸν πτισάνης ἢ χόνδρον ἢ ἄρτον πλυτὸν, εἶτα τῷ μὲν ἑτέρῳ παυομένην τὴν δῆξιν, αὐξανομένην δὲ θατέρῳ, πότερον οὖν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ δακνώδης ἐστὶν ὁ χυλὸς τῆς πτισάνης, ἢ ὁ χόνδρος, ἢ ὁ ἄρτος, κατὰ δέ τι συμβεβηκὸς ἐπὶ θατέρου τῶν ἀνθρώπων οὐχ ὅπως ηὔξησεν, ἀλλὰ παρηγόρησεν τὴν δῆξιν;

greek_sentence: θέασαι γὰρ ὡδί πως ἑκάτερον ἐπὶ παραδειγμάτων, ὑπόδειγμα θέμενος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ δύο τινὰς ἀνθρώπους δακνομένους μὲν ὁμοίως τὸ τῆς γαστρὸς στόμα, προσφερομένους δὲ χυλὸν πτισάνης ἢ χόνδρον ἢ ἄρτον πλυτὸν, εἶτα τῷ μὲν ἑτέρῳ παυομένην τὴν δῆξιν, αὐξανομένην δὲ θατέρῳ, πότερον οὖν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ δακνώδης ἐστὶν ὁ χυλὸς τῆς πτισάνης, ἢ ὁ χόνδρος, ἢ ὁ ἄρτος, κατὰ δέ τι συμβεβηκὸς ἐπὶ θατέρου τῶν ἀνθρώπων οὐχ ὅπως ηὔξησεν, ἀλλὰ παρηγόρησεν τὴν δῆξιν;

lsj_entry_text: ἐπικεραστικός, ή όν, tempering the humours, Gal. 6.260 ; ἀγωγή Alex.Trall. 7.7 .
greek_sentence: ἐγὼ μὲν ἐπικεραστικὸν ὑπάρχοντα κατά γε τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φύσιν φημὶ τὸν χυλὸν τῆς πτισάνης, ἢ τὸν χόνδρον, ἢ τὸν ἄρτον, ἢ νὴ Δία τὸ γάλα, παροξύνεσθαι δὲ θατέρῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὴν δῆξιν, τῷ φθάσαι νικηθῆναι πρὸς τῆς διαφθορᾶς.
english_sentence_A: For my part, I say that the juice of ptisane, or the spelt-groats, or the bread, or, by Zeus, milk, being tempering in its own nature, the biting is exacerbated in the other of the two men because it has first been overcome by the corruption.
english_sentence_B: I for my part say that the juice of ptisane, or the groats, or the bread, or, by Zeus, the milk, is tempering by its own nature, and that the biting is exacerbated in the other of the two men because the food has first been overcome by the corruption.

greek_sentence: πρῶτον μὲν τὸ παραχρῆμα πραΰνειν, ἢ μὴ, καὶ δεύτερον τὸ συνεκκενοῦσθαι τὰ λυποῦντα, ἢ μὴ, καὶ [495] τρίτον τὸ καταλιπεῖν τινα τραχύτητα περὶ τοῖς σώμασιν, ἢ μὴ, καὶ τέταρτον, εἰ μὴ τοῖς οὕτως ἔχουσι χρηστὸν φαίνοιτο.
english_sentence_A: First, whether it soothes immediately or not; second, whether the distressing matters are evacuated along with it or not; [495] third, whether it leaves behind some roughness in the bodies or not; and fourth, whether it would not appear beneficial to those who are in such a condition.
english_sentence_B: First, whether it soothes at once or not; second, whether the troublesome matters are evacuated together with it or not; [495] third, whether it leaves behind some roughness about the bodies or not; and fourth, whether it should fail to appear wholesome to those who are in this condition.

lsj_entry_text: δῆξις, εως, ἡ, (δάκνω) bite, biting, Arist. HA 623a1 ; δήξιες σπλάγχνων gnawings, Hp. VM 19 : metaph., of mental anguish, pangs, Zeno Stoic. 1.51 (pl.), Chrysipp.ib. 3.119 , Phld. D. 3 . Fr. 22 ; also, biting jokes, Plu. Lyc. 14 .
greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν γὰρ μήτε ἐν τῷ παραχρῆμα πραΰνειν τὰς δήξεις, ἀλλὰ μετὰ πλείονός γε σφοδρότητος ἐκκρινόμενον μήτε μένειν ἔνδον ἰώμενον, ἀπολεῖπόν τέ τινα περὶ τοῖς σώμασιν ἀνιαρὰν τραχύτητα, παροξῦνόν τε ταύτην εἰ προσαχθείη δεύτερον, ἀναβρωτικὸν μέν ἐστιν καὶ δακνῶδες τῇ φύσει, κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς δέ ποτε δήξεις ἰᾶται, τὸ δὲ κᾀν τῷ παραχρῆμα πραϋντικὸν ἔκκρισίν τε μηδεμίαν ἐρεθίζον, ἀλλὰ μηδὲ τραχῦνον ἐν τῷ μένειν, ἴαμά τε τῶν τετραχυμένων γιγνόμενον αὐτὸ μὲν φύσει χρηστόν ἐστι, δακνῶδες δ’ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀλλοιούσης αὐτὸ καὶ διαφθειρούσης κακοχυμίας ἔστιν ὅτε γίγνεται.
english_sentence_A: For that which neither soothes the bitings immediately, but is rather excreted with greater vehemence, nor remains within and heals, and which leaves behind some painful roughness in the bodies and exacerbates this if it is applied a second time, is erosive and biting by nature, though it sometimes heals bitings by accident; whereas that which is soothing even immediately and provokes no excretion, nor roughens while it remains, and becomes a remedy for the parts that have been roughened, is itself beneficial by nature, but there are times when it becomes biting through the cacochymia which alters and corrupts it.
english_sentence_B: For that which neither soothes the bitings at once, but is excreted with greater violence, nor heals by remaining within, and which leaves behind about the bodies a distressing roughness and aggravates it if it is applied a second time, is erosive and biting by nature, but by accident sometimes heals bitings. That which is soothing at once and provokes no excretion, does not roughen while it remains, and becomes a remedy for what has been roughened, is itself wholesome by nature, but sometimes becomes biting through the bad humours that alter and corrupt it.

english_sentence_A: But if something is stony and hard, like cadmia and scale of copper and burnt copper, one should break those down thoroughly into fine pieces and grind them for a very long time in spring water that is as pure as possible, pouring off the previous water many times, until nothing settles on top when the water stands still and it becomes without any quality of the drug being ground; but so long as either something of its quality is perceptible to those tasting, or something settles on top, up to that point one should continue both grinding and pouring off.
english_sentence_B: But if something is stony and hard, such as cadmia, flake of copper and burnt copper, one should break these up thoroughly into fine pieces and grind them for a very long time in spring water that is as pure as possible, often pouring off the earlier water, until nothing any longer forms on the surface when the water has settled, and the water becomes without quality from the drug being ground. As long as either something of its quality is apparent to those who taste it, or something forms on the surface, for so long one should keep grinding and pouring off.

greek_sentence: μόνως γὰρ ἂν εἴπερ ὡμολόγητο, πᾶν τὸ κερχνῶδες δακνῶδες ὑπάρχειν, ἀληθῶς ἂν εὑρέθη τὸ τοιοῦτον συνημμένον, εἰ κερχνῶδές ἐστι τὸ ἔλαιον, καὶ δακνῶδές ἐστιν, ἵνα ἕπηται τούτῳ τῷ λόγῳ προσλήψεως τοιᾶσδε γενομένης· ἀλλὰ μὴν κερχνῶδές ἐστι τὸ ἔλαιον, ἕπεται τὸ συμπέρασμα κατὰ τὸν πρῶτον ἀναπόδεικτον τοιοῦτον, δακνῶδες ἄρα ἐστὶ τὸ ἔλαιον.
english_sentence_A: For only if it had been agreed that everything throat-roughening is biting would such a conditional have been found true—'if oil is throat-roughening, it is also biting'—so that, when a co-assumption of the following kind has been added to this argument, 'but indeed oil is throat-roughening', the conclusion follows, according to the first indemonstrable, as follows: 'therefore oil is biting'.
english_sentence_B: For only if it had been agreed that everything roughening is biting would a conditional of this sort have been found true, 'if oil is roughening, it is also biting'. Then, when an additional assumption (πρόσληψις) of this kind is made to this statement, 'but oil is roughening', the conclusion follows, according to the first undemonstrated [argument], as follows: 'therefore oil is biting'.

greek_sentence: ἢ γὰρ ἐν ἡλίῳ θερμῷ θέντες ἀγγεῖον εὐρύστομον ἐλαίου μεστὸν, αἴροντες κόγχαις ἐξ αὐτοῦ πολλάκις ἄνωθεν καταράττουσιν, ἢ θερμὴν ὑποτιθέασιν τέφραν τοῖς περιέχουσιν ἀγγείοις τοὔλαιον, ἡλιοειδῆ θερμασίαν ὡς ἔνι μάλιστα μιμούμενοι.
english_sentence_A: For either, having set a wide-mouthed vessel full of oil in the hot sun, they repeatedly lift it out of it with shells and dash it down from above, or they place hot ash beneath the vessels that contain the oil, imitating as far as possible a sun-like warmth.
english_sentence_B: Either they set a wide-mouthed vessel full of oil in the hot sun, take it up with shells and repeatedly dash it down from above, or they put hot ash under the vessels containing the oil, imitating as closely as possible the sun-like warmth.

lsj_entry_text: ποιότης, ητος, ἡ, quality, Pl. Tht. 182a (where he apologizes for the use of the word as ἀλλόκοτον ὄνομα), Arist. Cat. 8b26 , EN 1173a15 (pl.), Gal. Nat.Fac. 1.2 , POxy. 2113.16 (iv A.D.), etc.; of size, Babr. 28.10 , Aesop. 84 .
greek_sentence: [505] φυλάττονται γὰρ τὴν πλείονα, μεταβάλλουσαν αὐτὸ κατὰ ποιότητα καὶ κνισσοῦσαν ἑτοίμως, ἢ πυρῆνας ἐλαιῶν, ἢ σῖτον ἐν κύκλῳ περιτιθέασιν, ἢ ἐπεμβάλλουσί τινα φάρμακα τοῖς ἀγγείοις αὐτοῖς, ἑνὶ δὲ λόγῳ τὸ μὲν ὑδατῶδες ἐξάγουσι καὶ δαπανῶσι, τὸ λοιπὸν δὲ φυλάττουσιν.
english_sentence_A: [505] For they guard against the greater heat, which alters it in quality and readily gives it a burnt, greasy smell; or they set olive-stones or grain around it in a circle, or they add certain drugs to the vessels themselves; in a word, they draw out and consume the watery part and preserve what remains.
english_sentence_B: [505] For they guard against the greater heat, which alters it in quality and readily makes it smell burnt; or they set olive stones or grain in a circle around it, or they also throw certain drugs into the vessels themselves. In a word, they draw off and consume the watery part, and preserve the rest.

english_sentence_A: If, then, you take oil that is sweet and white in this way, which from the beginning had no share of salt at all, and in addition also wash it, as was said before, this is for you the least biting of all drugs.
english_sentence_B: If, then, you take oil made sweet and white in this way, oil which from the beginning did not contain salt, and further also wash it, as was said earlier, this is for you the least biting of all drugs.

Supp. 8.5 , 25.10 :—a stronger form of τοῖος, bearing the same relation to τοιόσδε as οὗτος to ὅδε, such as this, in Hom. not so common as τοῖος, but in Att. the most common of the three forms; anteced. to οἷος, Od. 4.269 , Pl. Smp. 199d , etc.; to ὡς, Il. 21.428 ; to ὅς, ὅς, ὅσπερ, S. Ant. 691 , Th. 1.21 , Lys. 13.1 , 30.14 , X. Lac. 7.5 , Pl. R. 349d , etc.; to οἷόσπερ, v. l. in X. O. 6.16 , Hdt. 2.2 , etc.; freq. with implications, so good, so noble, so bad, etc., Il. 7.242 , etc.; τοιοῦτον . . ἐστὶ τὸ . . τέλειον ἄνδρα εἶναι so great a thing is it . . , Pl. Ph. 1271 : τ. ἕτερος such another, Hdt. 3.47 ; ἕτερα τοιαῦτα, ἕτερον τοιοῦτον, Id. 1.120 , 2.5 ; referring to what precedes, Id. 3.82 , Pl. Id. 3.37 ; ἐν τῷ τ. in such a case, ib. 81 , etc. (but also ἐν τῷ τ. in such a place, X. Ages. 6.7 ; ἐν τ. τῆς οἰκίας Id. Eq. 4.1 ); also ἐν τ. εἶναι τοῦ κινδύνου to be in such a state of peril, Id. An. 1.7.5 . in narrative, τοιαῦτα prop. refers to what goes before, τοιαῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα A. Pr. 500 ; καὶ ταῦτα μὲν τ. S. El. 696 , cf. X. An. 2.5.12 , etc.; cf. τοιόσδε fin. after a question, τοιαῦτα affirms like ταῦτα (v. οὗτος c. VII. 1 ), just so, even so, E. Hec. 776 , El. 645 . τοιαῦτα abs., τἂ πλοῖα, τὰ τοιαῦτα ships and suchlike, D. 8.25 . τοιαῦτα as Adv., in such wise, S. OT 1327 : regul. Adv. τοιούτως only late, EM 650.42 .—Cf. τοσοῦτος. greek_sentence: καὶ ἡμεῖς τοι πολλάκις τοιοῦτόν τισιν ἔλαιον ἐδώκαμεν πιεῖν καὶ αὐτοί τε προσηνεγκάμεθα πείρας ἕνεκα καὶ ἦν ἄδηκτόν τε κατ’ ἔντερον ἀκριβῶς καὶ τῆς φάρυγγος ἥκιστα κερχνῶδες, ἐγχεόμενόν τε τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς βραχεῖαν αἴσθησιν ἔφερεν αὐτῷ μόνῳ τῷ ξένῳ καὶ ἀήθει μᾶλλον ἢ τῇ δριμύτητι διοχλοῦν.
english_sentence_A: And indeed we have often given oil of this kind to certain people to drink, and have ourselves taken it for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least roughening to the throat, and when poured into the eyes it brought on a slight sensation, troubling them by its strangeness and unfamiliarity alone rather than by its pungency.
english_sentence_B: And indeed we have often given such oil to certain persons to drink, and have taken it ourselves for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least of all roughening to the throat; and when poured into the eyes it produced only a slight sensation, troubling them by its mere strangeness and unfamiliarity rather than by any pungency.

english_sentence_A: And indeed we have often given oil of this kind to certain people to drink, and have ourselves taken it for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least roughening to the throat, and when poured into the eyes it brought on a slight sensation, troubling them by its strangeness and unfamiliarity alone rather than by its pungency.
english_sentence_B: And indeed we have often given such oil to certain persons to drink, and have taken it ourselves for the sake of trial, and it was entirely non-biting in the intestine and least of all roughening to the throat; and when poured into the eyes it produced only a slight sensation, troubling them by its mere strangeness and unfamiliarity rather than by any pungency.

lsj_entry_text: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο, gen. τούτου, ταύτης, τούτου, etc.: the dual fem. never in Att. , v. ὁ, ἡ, τό, init.:—demonstr. Pron., this, common from Hom. downwds. ORIGIN and FORMS: οὗτος, αὕτη, τοῦτο prob. arose from a reduplication of the demonstr. ὁ, ἡ , τό with insertion of -υ- (= Skt. Particle u), e.g. ταῦτα fr. τα-υ-τα: Dor. gen. sg. fem. τούτας Philol. 11 ; nom. pl. τοῦτοι, ταῦται A.D. Synt. 111.23 : the former occurs Sophr. 24 , GDI 3045 B 6 (Selinus), SIG 339.16 (Rhodes, iii B. C.), etc., the latter is dub. in Sophr. 97 , certain in SIG 241 B 117 (Delph., iv B. C.): in Boeot. all forms begin with οὑτ-, as gen. sg. neut. οὕτω Supp.Epigr. 3.359.11 (iii B. C.); acc. sg. fem. οὕταν Corinn. Supp. 2.80 ; acc. pl. neut. οὗτα SIG 1185.20 (Tanagra, iii B. C.), etc.: gen. pl. fem. Att. τούτων, Cret. ταυτᾶν Leg.Gort. 5.19 ; neut. ταύτων Michel 1334.10 (Elis, iv B. C.).—In Ion. sts. written ταότην, ταο ͂τα, SIG 283.19 (Chios, iv B. C.), 46.7 (Halic., v B. C.), al.—In Att. οὗτος was freq. strengthd. by the demonstr. -ί, οὑτοσί, αὑτηί, τουτί, gen. τουτουί, dat. τουτῳί, acc. τουτονί; pl. nom. οὑτοιί, neut. ταυτί, etc., this man here: sts. a Particle is inserted between the Pron. and -ί, as αὑτηγί for αὑτηί γε, Ar. Ach. 784 ; τουτογί for τουτί γε, Id. V. 781 , Av. 894 , al.; ταυταγί for ταυτί γε, Id. Eq. 492 , Pax 1057 , al.; τουτοδί for τουτὶ δέ, Id. Pl. 227 ; τουτουμενί for τουτουὶ μέν, Id. Ra. 965 .—In codd. the ν ἐφελκυστικόν is sts. added in the forms οὑτοσίν, οὑτωσίν, and οὑτοσίν is said to be Att. by A.D. Pron. 59.24 , 82.11 . [This ι is always long, and a long vowel or diphthong before it becomes short, as αὑτηί, τουτῳί, οὑτοιί, Ar. Nu. 201 , Pl. 44 , Ach. 40 , etc.] USAGE in regard to CONCOR D. οὗτος is freq. used as a Pron. Subst.: hence neut. is folld. by gen., κατὰ τοῦτο τῆς ἀκροπόλιος Hdt. 1.84 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ὕβρεως ἐλήλυθεν D. 4.37 ; εἰς τοῦθ' ἥκεις μανίας Id. 36.48 ; ταῦτα τῶν μαθημάτων Pl. Euthd. 278b : but quite as freq. as Adj., in which case its Subst. commonly takes the Art., οὗτος ὁ ἀνήρ or ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος.—But the Art. is absent, always in Ep. Poets (exc. Od. 18.114 ), οὗτος ἀνήρ Il. 14.471 , Od. 1.406 , etc.: sts. also in Trag., A. Pers. 122 (lyr.), 495 , S. Ph. 406 , OC 471 , 1177 : once in an Inscr., τοπεῖα: τούτων τὰ ἡμίσεα τοπείων IG 22.1622.135 (iv B. C.). sts. when the Noun is so specified that the Art. is not needed, ἐς γῆν ταύτην . . , ἥντινα νῦν Σκύθαι νέμονται Hdt. 4.8 ; ταύτας ἃς οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν μελέτας Th. 1.85 , cf. Pl. R. 449d , etc.; πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος, ὃν θρηνεῖς ἀεί S. El. 530 . when οὗτος is used in local sense, here, v. infr. c. 1.5 . when the Noun with which οὗτος agrees stands as its Predicate, αὕτη γὰρ ἦν σοι πρόφασις S. Ph. 1034 ; δικαστοῦ αὕτη ἀρετή [ἐστι] Pl. Ap. 18a : this exception extends to cases in which the Predicate is not so distinctly separated from the Subject, αἰτίαι μὲν αὗται προυγεγένηντο these were the grievances which already existed, Th. 1.66 ; ταύτην φήμην παρέδοσαν this was the report which . . , Pl. Phlb. 16c : freq. with a Sup. , κίνησις αὕτη μεγίστη δὴ . . ἐγένετο this was notably the greatest movement which . . , Th. 1.1 , cf. 3.113 : with πρῶτος Id. 1.55 , 98 , 6.31 , Ev.Luc. 2.2 . when 3rd pers. is used for 2nd to express contempt, οὗτος ἀνήρ, οὑτοσὶ ἀνήρ, Pl. Grg. 467b , 489b , etc. though οὗτος usu. agrees with the Noun that serves as Predicate, it is not rare to find it in the neut., μανία δὲ καὶ τοῦτ' ἐστί E. Ba. 305 ; τοῦτο γάρ εἰσι . . εὔθυναι D. 19.82 , etc.: and in pl., οὐκ ἔστι ταῦτα ἀρχή Aeschin. 3.13 ; ταῦτ' ἐστὶν ὁ προδότης Id. 2.166 : so with an explanatory clause added, τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν ὁ συκοφάντης, αἰτιᾶσθαι μὲν πάντα ἐξελέγξαι δὲ μηδέν D. 57.34 . so also with a Noun in apposition, τούτοισιν μὲν ταῦτα μέλει, κίθαρις καὶ ἀοιδή Od. 1.159 ; τούτου τιμῶμαι, ἐν πρυτανείῳ σιτήσεως Pl. Ap. 36e , cf. E. Fr. 323.3 , etc. the neut. also may refer to a masc. or fem. Noun, καρπὸν φορέει κυάμῳ ἴσον: τοῦτο ἐπεὰν γένηται πέπον κτλ. Hdt. 4.23 , cf. X. An. 1.5.10 , etc. the neut. is also used of classes of persons, μελιτοπῶλαι καὶ τυροπῶλαι: τοῦτο δ' εἰς ἕν ἐστι συγκεκυφός Ar. Eq. 854 , cf. Pl. Lg. 711a ; or of an abstract fact, οὐκ Ἰοφῶν ζῇ;—τοῦτο γάρ τοι καὶ μόνον ἔτ' ἐστὶ λοιπὸν ἀγαθόν Ar. Ra. 73 . with Prons., personal, οὗτος σύ, in local sense, v. infr. c. 1.5 . interrog., τί τοῦτ' ἔλεξας; what is this that . . ? S. Ph. 1173 (lyr.), cf. Ant. 7 ; ποίοισι τούτοις; for ποῖά ἐστι ταῦτα οἷς [ἔχεις ἐλπίδα]; Id. OC 388 , cf. Ant. 1049 ; Νέστορ' ἔρειο ὅν τινα τοῦτον ἄγει whom he brings here, Il. 11.612 . with οἷος, Od. 20.377 , Pl. Phd. 61c . possess., πατὴρ σὸς οὗτος this father of thine, S. El. 530 , cf. X. An. 7.3.30 . demonstr., οὗτος ἐκεῖνος, τὸν σὺ ζητέεις, where ἐκεῖνος is the Predicate, Hdt. 1.32 ; τοῦτ' ἔστ' ἐκεῖνο E. Hel. 622 , cf. Or. 804 ; αὐτὸ τοῦτο, v. αὐτός 1.7; τοῦτον τὸν αὐτὸν ἄνδρα this same man, S. Ph. 128 . exceptionally, Διφίλου οὗτος ὅδ' ἐστὶ τύπος IG 12(5).300 (Paros). ἄλλος τις οὗτος ἀνέστη another man here, Od. 20.380 . with Numerals, τέθνηκε ταῦτα τρία ἔτη these three years, Lys. 7.10c odd.; [στρατείαν] ἑνδέκατον μῆνα τουτονὶ ποιεῖται for these eleven months, D. 8.2 , cf. 3.4 ; τριακοστὴν ταύτην ἡμέραν Men. Epit. 27 ; ταύτας τριάκοντα μνᾶς D. 27.23 , cf. Pl. Grg. 463b , etc. SIGNIFICATION AND SPECIAL IDIOMS: this, to designate the nearer, opp. ἐκεῖνος, that, the more remote, ταῦτα, like τὰ ἐνταῦθα , things round and about us, earthly things, Pl. Phd. 75e (v. l.); cf. ὅδε init.: but οὗτος sts. indicates that which is not really nearest, but most important, δεῖ . . τὸ βέλτιστον ἀεί, μὴ τὸ ῥᾷστον λέγειν: ἐπὶ ἐκεῖνο μὲν γὰρ ἡ φύσις αὐτὴ βαδιεῖται, ἐπὶ τοῦτο δὲ κτλ. D. 8.72 , cf. 51.3 and 18 . when, of two things, one precedes and the other follows, ὅδε prop. refers to what follows, οὗτος to what precedes, οὐκ ἔστι σοι ταῦτ', ἀλλά σοι τάδ' ἔστι S. OC 787 , cf. ὅδε III. 2 : freq., however, where there are not two things, οὗτος refers to what follows, Il. 13.377 , Od. 2.306 , etc.; οὔκουν . . τοῦτο γιγνώσκεις, ὅτι . . ; A. Pr. 379 , etc. οὗτος is used emphat., generally in contempt, while ἐκεῖνος denotes praise, ὁ πάντ' ἄναλκις οὗτος, i.e. Aegisthus, S. El. 301 ; τούτους τοὺς συκοφάντας Pl. Cri. 45a ; so D. de Coron. uses οὗτος of Aeschines, ἐκεῖνος of Philip; but οὗτος is used of Philip, D. 2.15 , 4.3 . of what is familiar, τούτους τοὺς πολυτελεῖς χιτῶνας, of the Persians, X. An. 1.5.8 ; οἱ τὰς τελετὰς . . οὗτοι καταστήσαντες Pl. Phd. 69c , cf. Men. 80a ; τὸ θυλακῶδες τοῦτο the familiar bag-like thing, Thphr. HP 3.7.3 , cf. 3.18.11 , 4.7.1 ; οἱ τὰς κόρας ταύτας ὠνούμενοι τοῖς παισίν D.Chr. 31.153 . in Att. law-language, οὗτος is commonly applied to the opponent, whether plaintiff (as in Aeschin. 2.130 ) or defendant (as in Id. 1.1 ); so, in the political speeches of D. , οὗτοι are the opposite party, 4.1 , 8.7 , etc.; but in the forensic speeches, οὗτοι freq. means the judges, the court, 21.134 , 36.47 . much like an Adv., in local sense (cf. ὅδε init.), τίς δ' οὗτος κατὰ νῆας . . ἔρχεαι; who art thou here that comest . . ? Il. 10.82 ; freq. in Att. , τίς οὑτοσί; who's this here? Ar. Ach. 1048 ; πολλὰ ὁρῶ ταῦτα πρόβατα I see many sheep here, X. An. 3.5.9 (as v.l.): with Pron. of 2 pers., οὗτος σύ ho you! you there! S. OT 532 , 1121 , E. Hec. 1280 , etc.: and then οὗτος alone like a voc., οὗτος, τί ποιεῖς; A. Supp. 911 ,cf. S. Aj. 71 , E. Alc. 773 , Ar. Eq. 240 , Nu. 220 , al.: with a pr. n., ὦ οὗτος, Αἴας S. Aj. 89 ; ὦ οὗτος οὗτος, Οἰδίπους Id. OC 1627 , cf. Ar. V. 1364 : with voc., βέντισθ' οὗτος Theoc. 5.76 :—the fem. is rarer, αὕτη E. Med. 922 ; αὕτη σύ Ar. Th. 610 .—This phrase mostly implies anger, impatience, or scorn. simply as antec. to ὅς, Od. 2.40 , S. OT 1180 , etc.: freq. following relat. clause, ἅ γ' ἔλαβες, . . μεθεῖναι ταῦτα Id. Ph. 1247 , cf. 1319 , Ant. 183 , 203 , Pl. Grg. 469c . = τοιοῦτος, οὗτος ἐγὼ ταχυτᾶτι Pi. O. 4.26 ; σὺ τοίνυν οὗτος εὑρέθης D. 18.282 , cf. 173 . after a parenthesis, the Subject, though already named, is freq. emphat. repeated by οὗτος, οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ Ἀριστέης . . , οὐδὲ οὗτος προσωτέρω . . ἔφησε ἀπικέσθαι Hdt. 4.16 , cf. 81 (s. v. l.), 1.146 , Pl. Phd. 107d , etc. καὶ οὗτος is added to heighten the force of a previous word, ξυνεστῶτες . . ναυτικῷ ἀγῶνι, καὶ τούτῳ πρὸς Ἀθηναίους Th. 4.55 , cf. Hdt. 1.147 , 6.11 , etc.; so οὐδὲ τούτου Aeschin. 2.100 ; v. infr. VIII. 2 . repeated, where for the second we should merely say he or it, τοῖσιν τούτου τοῦτον μέλεσιν . . κελαδοῦντες Ar. Ra. 1526 , cf. Pl. La. 200d . ταῦτα is used in some special phrases, ταῦτ', ὦ δέσποτα yes Sir (i. e. ἔστι ταῦτα, ταῦτα δράσω, etc.), Ar. V. 142 , Pax 275 , cf. Eq.III; so ταῦτα δή Id. Ach. 815 ; ταῦτά νυν Id. V. 1008 ; so also ἦν ταῦτα even so, true, E. Ph. 417 . ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ὑπάρξει so it shall be, Pl. Phd. 78a . καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα so much for that, freq. in Att. , as Pl. Smp. 220c . ταῦτα at end of a formula in epitaphs, etc., prob. short for ταῦτα οὕτως ἔχει or ὁ βίος ταῦτά ἐστιν, e.g. οὐδὶς ( = -εὶς ) ἀθάνατος: ταῦτα IG 14.420 ; Προκόπι ταῦτα ib. 1824 ; χαίρεται ( = -τε ) ταῦτα ib. 1479 , etc.: similarly perh. in a letter, ἂμ μὴ πέμψῃς, οὐ μὴ φάγω, οὐ μὴ πείνω. ταῦτα POxy. 119.15 (ii/iii A. D.). Adverbial usages: ταῦταabs., therefore, that is why . . , Il. 11.694 ; ταῦτ' ἄρα Ar. Ach. 90 , Nu. 319 , 335 , 394 , al., X. Smp. 4.55 ; ταῦτα δή A. Pers. 159 , Pl. Smp. 174a ; ταῦτ' οὖν S. Tr. 550 , Ar. V. 1358 , etc.; αὐτὰ ταῦτα ἥκω, ἵνα . . Pl. Prt. 310e : τοῦτο is rare in this sense, τοῦτ' ἀφικόμην, ὅπως . . εὖ πράξαιμί τι S. OT 1005 ; αὐτὸ γὰρ τοῦτο just because of this, Pl. Smp. 204a . πρὸς ταῦτα so then, therefore, prop. used in indignant defiance, A. Pr. 992 , 1043 , S. Aj. 971 , 1115 , 1313 , OT 426 , OC 455 , etc. καὶ ταῦτα, adding a circumstance heightening the force of what has been said, and that, ἄνδρα γενναῖον θανεῖν, καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς γυναικός A. Eu. 627 : but mostly with a part., ὅς γ' ἐξέλυσας ἄστυ . . , καὶ ταῦθ' ὑφ' ἡμῶν οὐδὲν ἐξειδὼς πλέον S. OT 37 , cf. Ar. Ra. 704 , Pl. Phdr. 241e , etc.; or with a part. omitted, ἥτις . . τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὕβρισεν, καὶ ταῦτα τηλικοῦτος (sc. οὖσα) S. El. 614 ; so καὶ ταῦτα μέντοι Pl. Erx. 400b . καὶ ταῦτα anyhow, no matter what happens (or happened), ἐπεχείρησας, οὐδὲν ὢν καὶ ταῦτα you tried, but were no good anyhow, i.e. try as you might, Id. R. 341c , cf. Diod.Com. 3.5 . τοῦτο μέν . . , τοῦτο δέ . . on the one hand . . , on the other . . , partly . . , partly . . , very freq. in Hdt. , as 1.161 , al.; τοῦτο μέν is sts. answered by δέ only, 4.76 , S. Aj. 670 , OC 440 ; by δὲ αὖ, Hdt. 7.176 ; by ἔπειτα δέ, S. Ant. 61 ; by ἀλλά, D. 22.13 ; by εἶτα, S. Ph. 1345 ; by τοῦτ' αὖθις, Id. Ant. 165 . dat. fem. ταύτῃ, on this spot, here, ταύτῃ μὲν . . , τῇδε δ' αὖ . . Id. Ph. 1331 ; ἀλλ' ἐὰν ταύτῃ γε νικᾷ, ταυτῃὶ πεπλήξεται Ar. Eq. 271 , cf. Th. 1221 . in this point, herein, μηδὲν ταύτῃ γε κομήσῃς Id. Pl. 572 , cf. X. Hier. 7.12 , etc. in this way, thus, A. Pr. 191 , S. OC 1300 , etc.; οὐ . . ταῦτ' ἐστί πω ταύτῃ Ar. Eq. 843 ; ἀλλ' οὔτι ταύτῃ ταῦτα E. Med. 365 , cf. A. Pr. 511 : antec. to ὥσπερ, Pl. R. 330c ; to ὅπῃ, X. Cyr. 8.3.2 ; οὕτω τε καὶ ταύτῃ γίγνοιτο Pl. Lg. 681d ; καὶ οὕτω καὶ ταύτῃ ἂν ἔχοι ib. 714d ; ταύτῃ καλεῖσθαι, etc., like οὕτω κ. , Sch. Pl. Smp. 215b . ἐκ τούτου or τούτων thereupon, X. HG 3.1.6 , Oec. 2.1 ; therefore, Id. An. 3.3.5 . ἐν τούτῳ in that case, Pl. R. 440c . in the meantime, Hdt. 1.126 , Th. 3.72 , X. Mem. 2.1.27 . πρὸς τούτοις (-οισι) besides, Hdt. 2.51 , Pl. Prt. 326a , X. Mem. 2.4.4 , Ar. Pl. 540 .
greek_sentence: εἶθ’ ὅταν μηκέτι τὸ πρότερον οἷον ἐνδίπλωμα παραπτομέναις ταῖς χερσὶν ἕπεσθαι δύνηται, τουτὶ μὲν ἀνατρέχει καὶ ἀνασπᾶται πρὸς τὸ συνεχὲς, αἱ χεῖρες δ’ ἀθρόως ἐφ’ ἕτερον τοῦ δέρματος μετέρχονται μόριον, ὑπερβαίνουσαι τὸ κάτωθεν μέρος τῆς ἐνδιπλώσεως καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ σκληρᾶς καὶ ἀνωμάλου καὶ κοπώδους τῆς τοιαύτης τρίψεως αἰσθανόμεθα· σκηρᾶς μὲν, ὅτι τε τείνεται βιαίως καὶ θλᾶται τὸ δέρμα, διὰ δὲ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ κοπώδους, ἀνωμάλου μὲν διότι μὴ παντὶ μορίῳ τοῦ δέρματος αἱ τρίβουσαι χεῖρες ἐπιπίπτουσιν, ἀλλ’ ὑπερβαίνουσιν ἀεὶ τὸ κάτωθεν μέρος τῆς ἐνδιπλώσεως.
english_sentence_A: Then, when the former fold, so to speak, can no longer follow the hands as they pass over it, this fold runs back and is drawn back toward the continuous part, while the hands pass all at once to another part of the skin, skipping over the under part of the fold; and for this reason we perceive such rubbing as hard, uneven, and fatiguing: hard, because the skin is forcibly stretched and bruised, and for the same reasons also fatiguing; uneven, because the rubbing hands do not fall upon every part of the skin, but always skip over the under part of the fold.
english_sentence_B: Then, when the earlier doubling, as one may call it, can no longer follow the hands as they glide along past it, this doubling runs back and is drawn back to the continuous skin, while the hands pass all at once to another part of the skin, passing over the lower part of the doubling. For this reason we perceive such rubbing as hard, uneven and fatiguing: hard because the skin is forcibly stretched and bruised, and fatiguing for the same reasons; uneven because the rubbing hands do not fall upon every part of the skin but always pass over the lower part of the doubling.

greek_sentence: καὶ γίνεται τοῦτο διά τε τὰς φυσικὰς τοῦ δέρματος τραχύτητας, καὶ μάλιστα ἐν τοῖς παρηβῶσι σώμασιν, καὶ ὅτι χαλαρόν ἐστι τοῖς ἄλλοις σχεδὸν ἅπασι, τοῖς τε ἰσχνοῖς καὶ πρεσβύταις μάλιστα.
english_sentence_A: And this happens both because of the natural roughnesses of the skin, especially in bodies past their prime, and because it is slack in almost all other people, and most of all in the lean and in old men.

greek_sentence: ἐπεὶ δὲ χαλαρόν τέ ἐστιν καὶ τραχὺ, δεῖταί τινος ἔξωθεν φαρμάκου τάς τε ῥυτίδας ἀναπληρώσοντος αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸν ὄλισθον ταῖς τριβούσαις χερσὶν παρέξοντος, εἰς ταῦτα δὲ οὐδὲν ἂν εὕροις ἐπιτηδειότερον ἐλαίου.

Prose fem. τρηχέα, acc. τρηχέαν, gen. τρηχέης, dat. τρηχέῃ (imperfectly preserved in codd.; in Hdt. 4.23 , 9.122 , codd. ABCP have τρηχέη, -έην, -έης, RSV have -εῖα, -εῖαν, -είης; for codd. Hp. v. Kühleweinip. lxxxvi); τρηχείην (before conson.) Simon. 89 codd., A.R. 2.375 codd.; τρηχείης (as pr. n.) Hippon. 47 ; gen. pl. neut. ἐρίων . . τρηχείων GDI 5633.14 (Teos); dual in Trag. τραχεῖ, Ion Trag. 67 :—jagged, λίθος Il. 5.308 ; χαλινοί, opp. λεῖοι, X. Eq. 9.9 , cf. 10.6 ; τ. καὶ γωνιοειδής Thphr. Sens. 65 ; prickly, ἄκανθαι, ἄκανθα, Plu. 2.32e , 138d (both Sup. ); rugged, ἀκτή, ἀταρπός, Od. 5.425 , 14.1 ; as epith. of Ithaca, 9.27 , 10.417 ; so γῆ λιθώδης καὶ τρηχέα Hdt. 4.23 ; Χερσονήσου τῆς Τρηχέης καλεομένης, of the Crimea, ib. 99 ; and freq. in Trag. and Att. of rocky districts, A. Pr. 726 , E. Fr. 1083 ; τὰ τραχέα, τὰ τραχύτατα, X. Cyn. 4.10 , Plu. Flam. 4 ; τ. καὶ χαλεπὴ ὁδός Pl. R. 328e ; also, rough, γλῶσσα Hp. Morb. 2.63 ; ἔρια GDI l. c., PCair.Zen. 287.2 (iii B. C.); σφόγγοι ib. 12.56 (iii B. C.); χῆμαι ib. 82.12 (iii B. C.); σινδόνες (towels, opp. μαλακαί) Gal. 6.418 ; χερσὶ μὴ πάνυ μαλακαῖς, ὥσπερ αὖ μηδὲ τραχείαις, ἀνατρίβειν τὸ σῶμα ib. 417 ; τὰ τ. κατὰ τὰς ἀνωμαλίας ἀλλήλοις ἐμπλεκόμενα ἑνοῦται, τὰ δὲ λεῖα κτλ. Diocl.Fr. 26 ; βλέφαρα Sor. 2.16 , PTeb. 273 intr. (ii/iii A. D.); shaggy, τὰ κάτωθεν τ. καὶ τραγοειδής, of Pan, Pl. Cra. 408d , cf. 420e ; λάσιον καὶ τ. [τὸ κέαρ] . . ἔχοντες Id. Tht. 194e ; τ. σώματα, opp. λεῖα, X. Mem. 3.10.1 ; of the voice, harsh, Pl. Ti. 67c , etc.; esp. of the voice of boys, when it breaks, μεταβάλλειν ἐπὶ τὸ -ύτερον Arist. HA 581a18 ; τὸ τ. τῆς φωνῆς Plu. Mar. 14 ; and of a person, τῇ φωνῇ τ. X. An. 2.6.9 ; also τραχυτάτη γλῶσσα (cf. τραχύστομος) Str. 14.2.28 ; of sounds and their combinations, harsh, opp. λεῖος, σύνθεσις, διάλεκτος, Phld. Simon. 89 ; φάλαγγες Tyrt. 12.22 . of natural forces, ῥόθιον A. Pr. 1048 (anap.); -ύτερα τὰ νοσήματα ἀπεργάζεσθαι Pl. Ti. 84c ; of a river, Plu. Alex. 60 , etc.; ἄελλαι A.R. 1.1078 . of persons, their acts, feelings, or conditions, rough, harsh, savage, τ. ἔφεδρος Pi. N. 4.96 ; οὐ τ. εἰμι καταθέμεν I am not niggardly in paying, ib. 7.76 ; Ἡσυχία Id. P. 8.10 ; ἅπας δὲ τ. ὅστις ἂν νέον κρατῇ A. Pr. 35 , cf. 188 (anap.), 326 ; δικαστὴς τ. εἶ Id. english_sentence_A: So when the philosophers say that olive oil is [510] hot, and set down as no small evidence of this, as they think, the speed of its change into flame, some people object and say that this indeed belongs to it because it is thin and airy, but that from its congealing quickly in winter it clearly displays its coldness; for it is more readily overcome by the cold not only than wine and vinegar, but even than water itself.
english_sentence_B: So, when the philosophers say that oil is hot [510] and put forward as no small proof of this, as they think, the speed of its change into flame, some, contradicting them, say that this does indeed belong to it, but because it is fine and airy; whereas from its congealing quickly in winter it clearly indicates its coldness.

english_sentence_A: [511] For they say that what happens in its case is not even congealing at all, if we examine the matter precisely, but a kind of setting and thickening, and they say that this comes about because it is thick and viscous, not because it is cold; so that here too the argument from either side again arrives at an impasse, the one party establishing opposite conclusions from the fact that oil is overcome by cooling sooner than water, the other from the fact that water congeals more than oil. In addition, then, to disputing about these matters, not even all agree that it is airy.
english_sentence_B: [511] For they say that what happens in its case is not even congelation at all, if we examine it precisely, but a sort of consolidation and thickening; and they say this occurs because it is thick and viscous, not because it is cold. So here too, once again, the argument arrives at an impasse from both sides: the one party establishes the contrary from the fact that oil is overcome by cooling more quickly than water, the other from the fact that water congeals more than oil.

greek_sentence: ὑδατώδεις γὰρ ὄντας τὰ πρώτα καὶ λεπτοὺς ταῖς συστάσεσιν καὶ διαῤῥέοντας, ἐπειδὰν ἑψηθῶσιν, παχεῖς καὶ γλίσχρους γίνεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: For being at first watery and thin in their consistency and running, once they have been boiled they become thick and viscous.
english_sentence_B: For being watery at first, thin in their consistency and running freely, once they are boiled they become thick and viscous.

lsj_entry_text: παχύς, εῖα ( Ion. -έα Hp. Superf. 21 ), ύ, thick, stout, χειρὶ παχείῃ Il. 5.309 , etc. ; παχέος παρὰ μηροῦ 16.473 ; παχὺν αὐχένα Od. 9.372 ; π. πούς Hes. Op. 497 ; of trees, ib. 509 ; ῥίζα Thphr. HP 6.3.1 ; later of persons, περὶ σφυρὸν παχεῖα, μισήτη γυνή thick-ankled, Archil. 184 ; fat, οἱ παχύτατοι τῶν παίδων Hp. Aph. 3.25 ; π. γυνή Id.Superf. l.c.; χοῖρος π., ὗς π., Ar. Ach. 766 , Men. 21 : metaph., of soil, rich, fertile, X. Oec. 17.8 ( Comp. ) ; π. τράπεζα a well-spread table, Philostr. VA 3.26 . Adv., παχέως διαιτᾶσθαι ibid. of inorganic things, thick, massive, π. λᾶας Il. 12.446 ; σκῆπτρον 18.416 ; αὐλὸς αἵματος Od. 22.18 ; θρυαλλίδες Ar. Nu. 59 ; πέδαι Id. V. 435 ; π. δραχμή a thick drachma, i. e. the Aeginetan, which weighed more than the Attic, Poll. 9.76 , or ( Hsch. ), = δίδραχμον ; thick, coarse, opp. λεπτός, ἱμάτιον Pl. Cra. 389b , cf. Poll. 7.57 , 61 , etc.; χλαῖναν . . παχεῖαν ἐπιβαλῶ Λακωνικήν Theopomp. Com. 10 ; of hair, Arist. HA 502a26 ; π. τὴν σάρκα, of the pig, Jul. Or. 5.177c . Adv. coarsely, roughly, of stating or arguing, παχέως ὁρίζεσθαι, prob. for ταχέως, Arist. Pol. 1275b25 ; παχύτερον or -έρως, Pl. Plt. 294e , 295a . of liquids, thick, curdled, clotted, αἷμα Il. 23.697 ; ἀπορρέει . . παχὺ καὶ μέλαν Hdt. 4.23 ; of marshwater, Hp. Aër. 7 ; of urine, Id. Prog. 12 ; τὸ παχύτερον τῶν γαλάκτων Arist. HA 521b28 ; τὸ παχὺ τῆς δυνάμεως [τῶν οἴνων] Ath. 1.33b . τὰ παχέα καλούμενα νοσήματα, of certain diseases supposed to be due to thickened phlegm, Hp. Int. 47 ,al. in Com., fat, great, π. πρᾶγμα, χάρις, Ar. Lys. 23 , Ec. 1048 . of timbre, thick, opp. λεπτός, Arist. Aud. 803b29 , cf. 804a10 ( Comp. ). Adv., κορώνη παχέα κρώζουσα Arat. 953 . of speech, coarse, heavy, διάλεκτος παχυτέρα D.H. Pomp. 2 ; παχύτερος τὴν λέξιν Id. Is. 19 ; παχύτερον ποιεῖν τὸν λόγον Hermog. Id. 1.6 . ample, of periphrasis, Longin. 29.1 ( Sup. ). of flame, dull, Thphr. HP 5.9.3 . οἱ παχέες men of substance, the wealthy, Hdt. 5.30 , 77 , 6.91 ; τοὺς π. καὶ πλουσίους Ar. Pax 639 ; ὃς ἂν ᾖ π. Id. Eq. 1139 ; ἀνὴρ π. Id. V. 287 ; cf. πάχης. Com. and Prose, thick-witted, gross, stupid, ἀμαθὴς καὶ π. Id. Nu. 842 ; τὸ τῶν παχυτέρων πλῆθος Phld. Rh. 1.202 S. ; π. καὶ ἠλίθιοι, π. καὶ ἀπαίδευτοι, Luc. Alex. 9 , 17 ; ἐς τὰς τέχνας π. καὶ οὐ λεπτοὶ οὐδὲ ὀξέες Hp. Aër. 24 ; π. τὴν μνήμην Philostr. VS 2.1.10 ; π. λόγος Gal. 8.606 . Adv., παχύτερον ἔχειν τῆς ἀκοῆς Hld. 5.18 . prov., πηλοῦ παχύτερος, of a dullard, Eun. Hist. p.265 D. Adv. -έως, v. supr. Comp. πάσσων, ον , Od. 6.230 , 8.20 , 24.369 ; παχίων, ον , Arat. 785 : Sup. πάχιστος Il. 16.314 , Call. Aet.Oxy. 2079.23 : regul. forms παχύτερος, παχύτατος (v. supr.). (I.- E. bhṇĝhú-, cf. Skt. bahús, Lett. biezs 'thick'.)

lsj_entry_text: γλίσχρος, α, ον, sticky, Hp. VC 14 ; γῆ Thphr. 6.5.4 ; joined with λιπαρός, Pl. Ti. 82d , 84a ; γ. τὸ σίαλον Pherecr. 69.3 ; of oil, Arist. greek_sentence: καὶ μὲν δὴ κᾀκ τῶν κατὰ μέρος παραδειγμάτων ἑκάτεροι τἀναντία πιθανῶς κατασκευάζουσιν, οἱ μὲν ἰξὸν καὶ μέλι καὶ πίτταν ὑγρὰν καὶ ῥητίνην, ἕτερά τε τοιαῦτα τῶν ὁμολογουμένων γλίσχρων τε ἅμα καὶ θερμῶν προτείνοντες.
english_sentence_A: And indeed from particular examples too each side plausibly establishes the opposite conclusions: the one proposing bird-lime and honey and liquid pitch and resin and other such things among those agreed to be at once both viscous and hot; the other mentioning the juice of hemlock and fleawort and orach and blite, and in addition to these bringing forward phlegm as a kind of colophon to their argument, for this clearly seems to them to be both viscous and cold.
english_sentence_B: And indeed, from particular examples as well, each side plausibly establishes the opposite conclusion: the one side putting forward birdlime, honey, liquid pitch and resin, and other such things that are agreed to be at once viscous and hot; the other side mentioning the juice of hemlock, fleawort, orache and blite, and, in addition to these, bringing forward phlegm as a kind of finishing stroke to the argument; for this seems to them plainly to be both viscous and cold.

english_sentence_A: For the one party say that it produces the free flow by diffusing [the blood] through its heat, the other that it does so by furnishing slipperiness through its coldness, [513] like ice.
english_sentence_B: For the one party say that it produces the free flow as liquefying [the blood] by its heat, the others as [513] furnishing slipperiness by its coldness, in the manner of ice.

greek_sentence: κᾄπειτ’ ἐντεῦθεν ἐκτραπόμενοι περὶ τῆς τῶν ὀλισθηρῶν ἁπάντων φύσεως διαλέγονται, μέχρι τῆς ἐσχάτης φιλολογίας ἀνιόντες τῷ λόγῳ.
english_sentence_A: And then, turning aside from this point, they discourse about the nature of all slippery things, ascending in their argument to the furthest extremity of learned disquisition.
english_sentence_B: And then, turning aside from this point, they hold discourse about the nature of all slippery things, ascending in their argument to the very extremity of learned disputation.

lsj_entry_text: πιμελ-ή, ἡ, (πίων, πῖαρ) soft fat, lard, Hdt. 2.40 , 47 , Hp. Aër. 19 , S. Ant. 1011 , Democr. ap. Ael. NA 12.18 , Alex. 83 : distd. from στέαρ as being χυτὸν καὶ ἄπηκτον, Arist. HA 520a8 , cf. PA 651a20 ; ἡ ἐπιπολάζουσα [γάλακτι] π., of cream, Philostr. Im. 1.31 .
greek_sentence: καταγινώσκοντες δὲ τῆς τούτων ἄλης, ὥς φασιν, ἕτεροι τὴν πιμελὴν τῷ λόγῳ προχειρίζονται, πλησιαίτατα μὲν ἐλαίῳ τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχουσαν, ἐναργῶς δ’ εὑρεθῆναι δυναμένην ὁποία τίς ἐστι τὴν κρᾶσιν, ἐν αὐτοῖς γὰρ ἡμῖν συνισταμένην οὐκ ἂν δύνασθαι λαθεῖν.
english_sentence_A: But others, condemning the wandering of these men, as they call it, bring forward soft fat for the argument, which is closest to olive oil in its nature but can be clearly discovered as to what sort it is in its mixture; for since it is formed within ourselves it could not escape notice.
english_sentence_B: Others, condemning the wandering of these men, as they say, put forward fat for the argument, since it is very close to oil in nature, yet can be clearly discovered as to what sort it is in its mixture; for since it is formed within us ourselves, it could not escape notice.

lsj_entry_text: εὐτραφ-ής, ές, (τρέφω) well-fed, thriving, fat, Hp. Aër. 12 , E. Med. 920 , IT 304 , Arist. HA 546a15 , etc.; large, well-grown, of peppercorns, Gal. 6.270 ( Sup. ); luxuriant, of hair-growth, Id. 1.326 ( Sup. ); τὸ εὐτραφές, = εὐτροφία , Polyaen. 7.36 . Adv. -φῶς, Ion. -φέως, ἔχειν to be fat, Hp. Septim. 8 , cf. Philostr. VS 2.1.7 . Act. , nourishing, ὕδωρ A. Th. 308 ( Sup. , lyr.); γάλα Id. Ch. 898 , Philostr. VA 3.9 ; v.l. in Thphr. CP 1.18.1 .
greek_sentence: αὐτίκα γέ τοί φασιν ἐν τοῖς ὑγιεινοῖς καὶ εὐτραφέσι σώμασιν γεννᾶσθαι πιμελὴν πολλὴν, ἃ μηδὲ μανέντα τινὰ φάναι ψυχρά.
english_sentence_A: To begin with, at any rate, they say that in healthy and well-nourished bodies much soft fat is generated, bodies which no one, not even if mad, would call cold; for such bodies come about when nature is strong, and nature all the natural philosophers have agreed to be a hot thing.
english_sentence_B: For instance, they say that much fat is generated in healthy and well-nourished bodies, which not even a madman would call cold.

lsj_entry_text: χρῆμα, ατος , τό: (χράομαι):— need, in the phrase παρὰ χ. or παραχρῆμα (q. v.); a thing that one needs or uses, cf. X. Oec. 1.9 sq. (pl.): hence in pl., goods, property ( χρήματα λέγομεν πάντα ὅσων ἡ ἀξία νομίσματι μετρεῖται Arist. EN 1119b26 ), Od. 2.78 , 203 , al. (never in Il. ), Hes. Op. 320 , 407 , etc.; of temple-treasures, heirlooms, etc., Mnemos. 57.208 (Argos, vi B. C.); τὰ ἱρὰ χ. τῆς Ἀθηναίης Hdt. 2.28 , cf. 9.81 ; θησαυρούς . . ἄλλα τε χρύσεα ἄφατα χ. Id. 7.190 ; πολλῶν χ. ἐξαίρετον ἄνθος A. Ag. 954 ; πειρῶ τὸν πλοῦτον χρήματακαὶ κτήματα κατασκευάζειν· ἔστι δὲ χ. μὲν τοῖς ἀπολαύειν ἐπισταμένοις, κ. δὲ τοῖς κτᾶσθαι δυναμένοις Isoc. 1.28 ; τοῖς σκεύεσι καὶ τοῖς χρήμασιν ἀποθήκη Th. 6.97 ; πρόβατα καὶ ἄλλα χ. X. An. 5.2.4 ; τὰ ἀνδράποδα . . καὶ χρήματα τὰ πλεῖστα ἀπέδρα αὐτούς ib. 7.8.12 : prov., χρήματα ψυχὴ πέλεται . . βροτοῖσι a man's money is his life, Hes. Op. 686 ; χρήματ' ἄνηρ 'money makes the man', Alc. 49 , Pi. I. 2.11 ; ἐν χρήμασιν οἰκεῖ πατρώοις A. Eu. 757 , cf. Ch. 135 ; also χρημάτων πένητες E. El. 37 ; τὰ χρήματ' ἐνεχυράζομαι Ar. Nu. 241 ; χρήματα πορίζειν Id. Ec. 236 ; ἄτιμοι ἦσαν τὰ σώματα, τὰ δὲ χ. εἶχον And. 1.74 ; χρημάτων ἥσσων Democr. 50 ; χρημάτων κρείσσων Th. 2.60 ; χρήμασι νικώμενος ibid.; χρημάτων ἀδωρότατος ib. 65 ; ἐλπίδα χρήμασιν ὠνητήν Id. 3.40 ; μήτε χρημάτων φειδομένους μήτε πόνων Pl. Phd. 78a ; ζημιοῦσθαι χρήμασιν Id. Lg. 721b ; even of debts, διαλῦσαι τὰ χ. D. 20.12 ; δεθέντ' ἐπὶ χρήμασιν ἐν τῷ δεσμωτηρίῳ Id. 24.168 .—Acc. to Poll. 9.87 the Ion. used also the sg. in this sense, and so we find, ἐπὶ κόσῳ ἂν χρήματι . . ; for how much money . . ? Answ. ἐπ' οὐδενί, Hdt. 3.38 ; ταύτην (sc. τὴν χλανίδα)πωλέω μὲν οὐδενὸς χ. δίδωμι δὲ ἄλλως ib. 139 ; also in Thgn. 197 , χ. δ' ὃ μὲν Διόθεν καὶ σὺν δίκῃ ἀνδρὶ γένηται; in Att. , οὐδενὸς ἂν χ. δεξάμενοι at no price, And. 2.4 ; and in later Prose, fund, sum of money, Arch. f. Religionswiss. 10.211 (Cos, ii B. C.); τὸ πλῆθος τοῦ χ. D.S. 13.106 , cf. Act.Ap. 4.37 , Luc. VH 1.20 ; χρήματα merchandise, Heraclit. 90 , X. HG 1.6.37 , Th. 3.74 ; property, substance, Berl.Sitzb. 1927.161 (Cyrene). generally, thing, matter, affair, esp. in Ep. and Ion. , h.Merc. 332 , Hes. Op. 344 , 402 ; χρημάτων ἄελπτον οὐδέν Archil. 74 ; πάντων χ. δικαιότατον Mimn. 8 ; πρῶτον χρημάτων πάντων Hdt. 7.145 ; ἀντὶ πάντων χ. on every account, And. 2.21 ; δεινότατον ἁπάντων χρημάτων ib. 1 ; πᾶν χ. ἐκίνεε 'left no stone unturned', Hdt. 5.96 ; τεκμαίρει χρῆμ' ἕκαστον 'deeds show the man', Pi. O. 6.74 ; πάντων χ. μέτρον ἄνθρωπος Protag. 1 ; περαίνεται τὸ χ. the issue is being decided, Plu. Caes. 47 : pl., simply, things, ὁμοῦ πάντα χ. ἦν Anaxag. 1 , cf. Pl. Cra. 440a , Euthd. 294d , Plot. 4.2.1 . χρῆμα is freq. expressed where it might be omitted, δεινὸν χ. ἐποιεῦντο Hdt. 8.16 ; οἷόν τι χ. ποιήσειε ib. 138 ; ἐς ἀφανὲς χ. ἀποστέλλειν ἀποικίην to send out a colony without any certain destination, Id. 4.150 ; freq. in Trag., τί χρῆμα; = τί; what? τί χ. λεύσσω; A. Pr. 300 , Ch. 10 ; or why? E. Alc. 512 ; so in gen., τοῦ χ. (sc. ἕνεκα); Ar. Nu. 1223 ; τί χ. δρᾷς; S. Aj. 288 , cf. Ph. 1231 ; τί χ. πάσχει; E. Hipp. 909 ; τί δ' ἐστὶ χρῆμα; what is the matter? A. Ch. 885 ; πικρόν τί μοι δοκεῖ χ. εἶναι Pl. Grg. 485b ; ἡδύ Id. Tht. 209e , al.; μάλιστα χρημάτων most of anything, i. e. certainly, Anon. Oxy. 1611.68 (iii A. D.); cf. χρέος 11.2 . used in periphrases to express something strange or extraordinary of its kind, ὑὸς χ. μέγα a huge monster of a boar, Hdt. 1.36 ; ἦν τοῦ χειμῶνος χ. ἀφόρητον Id. 7.188 ; τὸ χ. τῶν νυκτῶν ὅσον what a business the nights are! Ar. Nu. 2 ; λιπαρὸν τὸ χ. τῆς πόλεως what a grand city! Id. Av. 826 , cf. Lys. 83 ; κλέπτον τὸ χ. τἀνδρός a thievish sort of fellow, Id. V. 933 ; τὸ χ. τοῦ νοσήματος Id. Lys. 1085 ; μακάριον . . λέγεις τυράννου χ. your tyrant-creature, Pl. R. 567e ; χ. θαυμαστὸν γυναικός Plu. Ant. 31 : without a gen., ἔλαφον, καλόν τι χ. καὶ μέγα X. Cyr. 1.4.8 ; σοφόν τοι χρῆμ' ἄνθρωπος truly a clever creature is he! Theoc. 15.83 ; κοῦφον χ. ποιητής ἐστιν καὶ πτηνὸν καὶ ἱερόν, of the poet, Pl. Ion 534b ; χ. καλόν τι such a fine thing! Theoc. 15.23 ; also in a periphrastic use, οὐδὲν χ. τοῦ ἀγκῶνος κάμψαι δύνανται cannot bend the elbow at all, Hp. Fract. 42 . so, to express a great number or mass, as we say, a deal, a heap of . . , πολλόν τι χ. τῶν τέκνων, χ. πολλὸν ἀρδίων, νεῶν, Hdt. 3.109 , 4.81 , 6.43 ; χ. πολλόν τι χρυσοῦ Id. 3.130 ; σμικρὸν τὸ χ. τοῦ βίου E. Supp. 953 ; ὅσον τὸ χ. παρνόπων what a lot of locusts! Ar. Ach. 150 ; ὅσον τὸ χ. τοῦ πλακοῦντος Id. Eq. 1219 ; πολὺ χ. τεμαχῶν Id. Pl. 894 ; τὸ χ. τῶν κόπων ὅσον what a lot of them! Id. Ra. 1278 ; τῶν λαμπάδων ὅσον τὸ χ. Id. Th. 281 ; also of persons, χ. θηλειῶν womankind, E. Ph. 198 ; σφενδονητῶν πάμπολύ τι χ. X. Cyr. 2.1.5 ; μέγα χ. Λακαινᾶν Theoc. 18.4 : without a gen., ὅσον τὸ χ. ἐπὶ δεῖπνον ἦλθε what a crowd . . ! Ar. Pax 1192 . (χράω (B) A) oracle, Emp. 115.1 .
greek_sentence: γίνεσθαι γὰρ τοιαῦτα τῆς φύσεως ἐῤῥωμένης, ἣν δὴ θερμόν τι χρῆμα πάντες ὡμολογήκασιν οἱ φυσικοὶ φιλόσοφοι.
english_sentence_A: To begin with, at any rate, they say that in healthy and well-nourished bodies much soft fat is generated, bodies which no one, not even if mad, would call cold; for such bodies come about when nature is strong, and nature all the natural philosophers have agreed to be a hot thing.
english_sentence_B: For such things come about when nature is strong, and nature all the natural philosophers have agreed to be a hot thing.

lsj_entry_text: ψυχρός, ά, όν, cold, χάλαζα, νιφάδες, χιών, Il. 15.171 , 19.358 , 22.152 ; ψ. χαλκός (as we say 'cold steel') 5.75 : freq. of water, ψ. ὕδωρ Od. 9.392 , Th. 2.49 ; ψυχρόν (without ὕδωρ) Thgn. 263 ; λοῦνται ψυχρῷ Hdt. 2.37 ; ἀναγαργαρίζεσθαι ψυχρῷ IG 42(1).126.30 (Epid., ii A. Fr. 123.5 ; οὔτε ψ. εἶ οὔτε ζεστός Apoc. 3.15 . of flat, lifeless, insipid productions, τὸν Παλαμήδην (the play so named) ψυχρὸν ὄντ' αἰσχύνεται Ar. Th. 848 ; σκῶμμα . . σφόδρα ψ. lsj_entry_text: ἔθνος, εος , τό: (vέθνος, cf. Il. 2.87 , 7.115 , al.): - number of people living together, company, body of men, ἑτάρων ἔ., ἔ. ἑταίρων, band of comrades, Il. 3.32 , 7.115 , etc.; ἔθνος λαῶν host of men, 13.495 ; of particular tribes, Αυκίων μέγα ἔ. 12.330 ; Ἀχαιῶν ἔ. 17.552 : pl., ἔθνεα πεζῶν 11.724 , cf. 2.91 ; ἔ. νεκρῶν Od. 10.526 ; of animals, ἔ. μελισσάων, ὀρνίθων, μυιάων, swarms, flocks, etc., Il. 2.87 , 459 , 469 ; ἔθνη θηρῶν S. Ph. 1147 (lyr.), Ant. 344 ; ἔ. ἀνέρων, γυναικῶν, Pi. O. 1.66 , P. 4.252 ; ἔ. βρότεον, θνατόν, Id. N. 3.74 , 11.42 ; ἔ. τόδε, of the Erinyes, A. Eu. 366 (lyr.). after Hom. , nation, people, τὸ Μηδικὸν ἔ. (γένος being a subdivision of ἔθνος) Hdt. 1.101 ; ἔ. ἠπειρογενές, μαχαιροφόρον, A. Pers. 43 , 56 (anap.), etc.; τῶν μηδισάντων ἐθνέων τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν Hdt. 9.106 . later, τὰ ἔ. foreign, barbarous nations, opp. Ἕλληνες, Arist. Act.Ap. 7.45 ; Gentiles, τῶν ἐθνῶν τε καὶ Ἰουδαίων ib. 14.5 , etc.; used of Gentile Christians, Ep. Rom. 15.27 . at Rome, = provinciae, App. BC 2.13 , Hdn. 1.2.1 , PStrassb. 22.19 (iii A. Ath. 3 ; ἔ. βραχμάνων D.S. 17.102 ; τὰ ἱερὰ ἔ. the orders of priests, OGI 90.17 (ii B. C.); trade-associations or guilds, ἔθνη καὶ ἐργαστήρια PPetr. 3p.67 (iii B. greek_sentence: ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν ἐθνῶν, ἔνθα μὲν τὸ ψυχρὸν κρατεῖ, πιμελώδεις, ἔνθα δὲ τὸ θερμὸν, ἰσχνούς φασι γίνεσθαι τοὺς ἀνθρώπους καὶ προχειρίζονται παράδειγμα τῷ λόγῳ, Κελτοὺς μὲν καὶ Θρᾷκας καὶ ﻿ [514] Βιθυνοὺς καὶ Ποντικοὺς καὶ Γαλάτας, ἅμα μὲν ψυχρᾶς χώρας οἰκήτορας, εὐθὺς δὲ καὶ πιμελώδεις τοὐπίπαν· Ἄραβας δὲ καὶ Λίβυας Αἰγυπτίους τε καὶ Αἰθίοπας, ὅσοι τ’ ἄλλοι θερμὴν ἐποικοῦσι γῆν ἰσχνοὺς καὶ ξηροὺς ἅπαντας.
english_sentence_A: And further, among the nations too, they say that where cold prevails men become fatty, and where heat prevails, lean; and they put forward as an example for their argument the Celts, Thracians, [514] Bithynians, Pontics and Galatians, who are at once inhabitants of a cold country and straightway also fatty for the most part; whereas the Arabs, Libyans, Egyptians and Ethiopians, and all others who dwell in a hot land, are all lean and dry.
english_sentence_B: Further, regarding peoples, they say that where cold prevails men become fat, but where heat prevails, lean; and they put forward as an example for the argument the Celts, Thracians, [514] Bithynians, Pontians and Galatians, who are at once inhabitants of a cold country and also, as a rule, fat; and the Arabs, Libyans, Egyptians and Ethiopians, and all others who inhabit a hot land, all lean and dry.

greek_sentence: εἰσὶ δ’ οἳ καὶ χωρὶς κατὰ μέρος παραδειγμάτων αὐτῷ τῷ καθόλου λόγῳ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀμφισβητοῦσιν, οἱ μὲν μηδ’ ἂν γενέσθαι τὸν λιπαρὸν ἐν ἡμῖν χυμὸν, εἰ μὴ καλῶς ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως αἱ τροφαὶ κατεργασθεῖεν, οἱ δὲ τοῦτον μὲν ἐν ταῖς τροφαῖς περιέχεσθαι, καταναλίσκεσθαι δ’ ὑπὸ τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν θερμασίας, ὥσπερ τοὔλαιον ὑπὸ τῆς φλογὸς, ἧς ἀῤῥώστου γινομένης ἀθροίζεσθαι κατὰ τὸ σῶμα.
english_sentence_A: There are also some who, even apart from particular examples, dispute with one another by means of the general argument itself: the one side holding that the oily humour would not even come to be in us unless the nutriments were well worked up by nature, the other that this humour is contained in the nutriments but is consumed by the warmth in us, just as oil is by the flame, and that when this warmth becomes weak it is accumulated throughout the body.
english_sentence_B: There are also those who, even apart from particular examples, dispute with one another over the general argument itself: some say that the oily humour would not even come into being in us unless the foods were properly worked up by nature; others say that it is contained in the foods, but is consumed by the warmth in us, as oil is by the flame, and that when this warmth becomes weak, it collects in the body.

english_sentence_A: Further, then, from the fact that bees, flies, wasps and ants are destroyed when wetted with oil, some try to demonstrate that oil is cold, others that it is hot, and some that it is moist, others that it is dry.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, from the fact that bees, flies, wasps and ants are destroyed when wetted with oil, some try to show that oil is cold, others that it is hot, and some that it is moist, others that it is dry.

english_sentence_A: For since the animals mentioned are bloodless and for this reason cold, [515] some say that they are readily chilled by the oil and die on that account; others, that, being thoroughly heated, they do not endure the change to the opposite.

lsj_entry_text: ἀμετρ-ία, ἡ, excess, disproportion, opp. συμμετρία, Pl. Ti. 87d , cf. R. 486d , Heraclit. All. 8 , Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.112 , etc. want of moderation, Arist. VV 1251b15 . infinity, countless number, κακῶν Pl. Ax. 367a (in pl.).
greek_sentence: καὶ δὴ καὶ ξηραινόμενα ἀμέτρως ἕτεροι διὰ τὸ φύσει προεξηράνθαι τῷ τῆς ἀμετρίας βλάπτεσθαι λόγῳ.
english_sentence_A: And further, others say that they are dried immoderately, because they have already been dried out by nature, and are harmed by reason of the excess; while yet others say that they are moistened, by the contrariety to their nature.
english_sentence_B: And indeed others say that, being dried immoderately, they are harmed by reason of the immoderation, because they have already been dried beforehand by nature; and still others that, being moistened, they are harmed by the contrariety to their nature.

greek_sentence: ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἐρυσιπελάτων ὅπως ἂν ᾖ ψυχρὸν οὐδὲν ὀνίνησιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ βλάπτειν πέφυκε, τὰ μὲν ἐκ χολώδους ῥεύματος ἀκριβῶς ἅπαντα μεγίστας βλάβας, τὰ δ’ ἐξ αἵματος αὐτῷ μεμιγμένου μικροτέρας μὲν, οὐ μὴν τὰς ἐπιτυχούσας γε οὐδὲ ταύτας.
english_sentence_A: But in cases of erysipelas, however cold it may be, it benefits nothing, but is even of a nature to harm: those that arise purely from a bilious flux, all of them, with the greatest harms, and those from blood mixed with it, with smaller ones, though not even these are trivial.
english_sentence_B: For in cases of scorching, if it is without salt and has moreover been whitened, it gives some relief when poured over cold; but in erysipelata, however cold it may be, it does no good, but is even apt to do harm: to all those that arise purely from a bilious flux, very great harm; to those from a flux with blood mixed in it, smaller harm, though not ordinary harm either.
