english_sentence_A: So as long as they lack such heat, they delay and are slow, being held up in the large pores and, as it were, swimming about in the veins and arteries, and presumably also, in the course of time and amid their long wandering, being themselves affected in turn by the humors contained in these vessels.

english_sentence_A: Accordingly, all bodies that are cold in their mixtures both have the attraction of the arteries weaker than hot ones—for this too was shown—and are unable quickly to break down the substances of the drugs into small parts.

english_sentence_A: Fittingly, then, for those whose harm comes from cooling, the speed of their action contributes to destruction; for being warmed in time they lose the power by which they had their action.

lsj_entry_text: δυσ-κρασία, ἡ, bad temperament, of the air, Str. 6.4.1 , Plu. Alex. 58 (pl.); σώματος Stoic. 3.216 ; τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν δυνάμεων Ph. 1.29 . ( δυσκρασίη Man. 4.543 .)
greek_sentence: ἀπολέσθαι μὲν γὰρ ζῶον οὐκ ἐγχωρεῖ οὐδὲν, ἄνευ τοῦ παύσασθαι τὴν καρδίαν ἐνεργοῦσαν, οὐκ ἐνδέχεται δὲ παύσασθαι ταύτην ἄνευ μεγίστης τινὸς δυσκρασίας.
english_sentence_A: For no animal can perish without the heart ceasing its activity, and it is not possible for this to cease without some very great dyscrasia.
english_sentence_B: For no animal can perish without the heart ceasing from its activity, and the heart cannot cease without some very great bad mixture.

greek_sentence: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἁπλῶς θερμοτέρα τοῦ δέοντος εἰς ὅσον ἔτυχεν ἢ ψυχροτέρα γεννηθεῖσα παύσεται κινουμένη.
english_sentence_A: For surely it will not cease moving simply because it has become hotter than is proper, to whatever degree it happens, or colder.
english_sentence_B: For it will certainly not stop moving simply by becoming hotter than it should to some chance degree, or colder.

greek_sentence: χεῖρον μὲν γὰρ ἐνεργήσει διὰ τὰς τοιαύτας δυσκρασίας, ἀκίνητος δὲ οὐκ ἔσται, πρὶν ἐξαίσιόν τινα θερμασίαν, ἢ ψύξιν, ἢ τῶν ἄλλων τινὰ τῶν δραστικῶν ποιοτήτων ἀναδέξασθαι.

english_sentence_B: For it will act worse because of such bad mixtures, but it will not be motionless until it has taken on some extraordinary warmth, or cooling, or some other of the active qualities.

english_sentence_A: Something similar happens to the drugs that kill by cooling, whenever they are slow in coming to the heart, to what often happens in the case of moist and green pieces of wood.
english_sentence_B: Something similar happens to the drugs that kill by cooling [600] whenever they are slow in coming to the heart, similar to what often happens with moist and green wood.

lsj_entry_text: κώνει-ον, τό, hemlock, Conium maculatum, Hp. Steril. 224 , Thphr. HP 1.5.3 , 9.8.3 , Nic. Al. 186 , Dsc. 4.78 , etc. = νάρθηξ , Call. Iamb. 1.122 , Hsch. hemlockjuice, poison by which criminals were put to death at Athens, Ar. Ra. 124 ; κώνειον πεπωκώς Pl. Ly. 219e ; τὸ κώνειον ἔπιεν X. HG 2.3.56 , cf. And. 3.10 ; κώνεια πιεῖν Ar. Ra. 1051 .
greek_sentence: οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὸ κώνειον ἄνθρωπον μὲν ἀναιρεῖ, τῇ τε τῶν πόρων εὐρύτητι καὶ τῷ πλήθει τῆς θερμότητος καὶ τῇ ῥώμῃ τῆς τῶν ἀρτηριῶν ὁλκῆς, ἰσχυρὸν ἔτι πρὸς τὴν καρδίαν ἀφικνούμενον.
english_sentence_A: So too, then, hemlock kills a human being, arriving at the heart still strong, because of the width of the pores, the abundance of heat, and the strength of the attraction exerted by the arteries; but it does not kill starlings, since, owing to the opposite causes, it is held back and delayed and, in the course of that time, is first concocted beforehand and prepared beforehand, being warmed in advance by the heart as by a kind of hearth, just as the wood is outside [the fire].
english_sentence_B: In the same way, then, hemlock kills a human being, because of the width of the pores, the abundance of the heat, and the strength of the attraction of the arteries, since it arrives at the heart while still strong.

english_sentence_B: In the same way, then, hemlock kills a human being, because of the width of the pores, the abundance of the heat, and the strength of the attraction of the arteries, since it arrives at the heart while still strong.

english_sentence_A: But if someone should already have drunk the juice of the poppy, which is of such a nature as to kill, and yet still be alive, then reasonably [604] this person too is cured by old wine drunk in quantity, and the more so if it should be one of the noble wines; for it also heats more.
english_sentence_B: But if someone has already drunk juice of the poppy, which is by nature capable of killing, and is still alive, it is reasonable that [604] old wine, drunk in quantity, cures this man too, and the more so if it is one of the noble wines; for these also heat more.

greek_sentence: τοιοῦτος οὖν οἶνος τῇ φύσει καὶ παλαιὸς τὴν ἡλικίαν, ἀκρατέστερος ﻿ [605] κεραννύμενος ἰᾶται καὶ τοὺς ἤδη κατεψυγμένους οὐχ ὑπὸ μήκωνος ὀποῦ μόνον, ἤ τινος ἄλλου τῶν τοιούτων ψυχόντων φαρμάκων, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοὺς ἤτοι στομαχικῶς ἢ καρδιακῶς ἐν νόσοις συγκοπτομένους.
english_sentence_A: Such a wine, then, in its nature, and old in age, when mixed rather strong [605] cures also those who have already been chilled, not only by poppy juice or by some other of such cooling drugs, but also those who in diseases fall into syncope either stomachically or cardiacally.
english_sentence_B: Such a wine, then, of this kind by nature and old in age, when mixed rather undiluted [605], cures not only those already chilled by poppy juice or by some other of the cooling drugs of this kind, but also those who in diseases suffer syncope, whether of the stomachic or of the cardiac sort.

Fr. 7 ; ὅρον πολιτείας ὁλιγαρχικῆς ταξάμενοι πλῆθος χρημάτων Pl. R. 551a ; ἀριστοκρατίας ὅρος ἀρετή, ὀλιγαρχίας πλοῦτος Arist. greek_sentence: πάλιν γὰρ τῶν αὐτῶν ἀναμνησθῶμεν, ὡς ἐν τῷ βαλανείῳ ψυχρὸν ἡμῖν φαίνεται τὸ οὖρον.
english_sentence_A: For let us again recall the same things, that in the bath urine appears cold to us.
english_sentence_B: Let us again recall the same examples: in the bath our urine appears cold to us.

lsj_entry_text: δεξαμενή, ἡ, (aor. 1 part. of δέχομαι, with different accent) receptacle for water, tank, cistern, Hdt. 3.9 , 6.119 , PSI 1.66 (v A.D.); of the veins, Democr. 135 ; vehicle, as matter of form, Pl. Ti. 53a , Aen.Gaz. Thphr. p.66 B. : generally, receptacle, Ph. 1.647 , D.C. 76.1 .
greek_sentence: ἀναμνησθῶμεν δὲ καὶ ὡς εἰς δεξαμενὴν θερμὴν ἐνίοτε καταβῆναι μὴ δυνάμενοι, προκαταβάντες εἰς ἑτέραν ἧττον αὐτῆς θερμὴν, ἀλύπως ἐχρησάμεθα τῇ τέως ἀφορήτῳ φαινομένῃ.
english_sentence_A: And let us recall also that, when sometimes we were unable to go down into a hot pool, having first gone down into another less hot than it, we then used without discomfort the one that had until then seemed unbearable.
english_sentence_B: Let us recall too how, sometimes unable to get down into a hot basin, we first got down into another less hot than it, and then used without distress the one that until then had seemed unbearable.

english_sentence_A: And indeed spring water too in winter appears lukewarm to those who have cold hands, but to the others it does not appear so.
english_sentence_B: And spring water in winter appears lukewarm to those whose hands are cold, but to others it does not appear so.

lsj_entry_text: μίσυ, υος and εως, τό, a copper ore found in Cyprus, Hp. Mul. 1.103 , Gal. 12.241 , 15.32 , Dsc. 5.100 , cf. 74 . truffle, Tuber aestivum, growing near Cyrene, Thphr. Fr. 167 .
greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ καὶ μίσυ καὶ χαλκῖτις, ἰός τε καὶ τίτανος καὶ ἕτερα μυρία τῶν τοιούτων, εἰ σεσωρευμένοις αὐτοῖς ἐμβάλῃς τὴν χεῖρα, παραχρῆμά σοι φανεῖται θερμά.
english_sentence_A: So too misy and chalcitis, verdigris and lime and countless others of such things, if you plunge your hand into them when they are heaped up, will at once appear hot to you.
english_sentence_B: In the same way misy and chalcitis, verdigris and lime, and countless other such substances will at once appear hot to you if you thrust your hand into them while they lie heaped up.

english_sentence_A: If, however, you take some lump from among them, its outer surface having been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all.
english_sentence_B: If, however, you take some lump of one of them, whose outer [607] surface has been chilled by the external and surrounding air, you will reasonably perceive no heat at all.

lsj_entry_text: οὐδείς, fem. οὐδεμία (never nom. acc. -μίη, -μίην, since οὐδεμιῇ is prob. in Call. Aet.Oxy. 2080.56 , rarely οὐδ' ἴα Sapph. 69 , Mosch. 4.40 ), neut. οὐδέν (declined and accentuated like εἷς, μία, ἕν ), not one, i.e. no one, none, used by Hom. , Hes. , and Pi. (who prefer οὔτις) only in neut. nom. and acc. οὐδέν, exc. in the phrase τὸ ὃν μένος οὐδενὶ εἴκων Il. 22.459 , al.; οὐδείς is found in B. Fr. 28 ; but all genders and cases are common in all other writers, Hdt. 1.32 , 33 , etc.: rare in pl., no set of persons or things, And. 1.23 (dub. cj.), X. Lac. 3.1 ; πρὸς οὐδένας τῶν Ἑλλήνων D. 18.23 (v.l.), cf. 19.31 , 66 , 312 , 24.214 , 27.7 ; οὐδένων εἰσὶ βελτίους, i.e. οὔ τινων ἄλλων, Id. 2.17 (cf. οὐδενὸς βελτίους Pl. Prt. 324d ): dat. pl. οὐδέσιν Paus. 3.24.3 ; for another sense of the pl., v. infr. 11.3 .—In Ion. the pl. is usu. οὐδαμοί. οὐ. ὅστις οὐ every one, Hdt. 3.72 , etc.; οὐδὲν ὅ τι οὐ every, Id. 5.97 ; this came to be regarded as one word, so that οὐδείς passed into the same case as ὅστις, οὐδένα ὅντινα οὐ κατέκλασε Pl. Phd. 117d ; οὐδενὸς ὅτου οὐ πάντων ἂν . . πατὴρ εἴην Id. Prt. 317c , cf. 323b ; οὐδενὶ ὅτῳ οὐκ ἀποκρινόμενος Id. Men. 70c ; so οὐ. ὃς οὐχὶ . . ὀνειδιεῖ S. OT 373 ; οὐδὲν γὰρ . . οὔτ' αἰσχρὸν οὔτ' ἄτιμόν ἐσθ', ὁποῖον οὐ . . οὐκ ὄπωπ' ἐγώ Id. Ant. 4 . later οὐδὲν ὅ τι without οὐ, = nothing, οὐδὲν ὅ τι παρήσω Agath. Praef. p.137 D. , al. ὅστις οὐδείς not one, ἐτεθνήκεσαν δὲ αὐτῶν μὲν ἀμφὶ τοὺς τετρακοσίους, Ρωμαίων δὲ ὅστις οὐδείς Id. 5.20 . naught, good for naught, ὦ νῦν μὲν οὐ. αὔριον δ' ὑπέρμεγας Ar. Eq. 158 , cf. E. Fr. 187.5 ; τὸ μὲν [γένος ἀνδρῶν] οὐδέν Pi. N. 6.3 : freq. in neut., οὐδὲν εἰδώς knowing naught, Thgn. 141 , E. Fr. 391 ; οὐκ ἄρ' ᾔστην οὐδὲν ἄλλο πλὴν δάκνειν knew nothing save how to . . , Ar. Av. 19 ; οὐδὲν λέγειν to say naught, v. λέγω (B) III. 6 ; τὸ οὐδ' οὐδέν the absolute nothing, Pl. Tht. 180a . in neut., of persons, οὐδέν εἰμι S. Ph. 951 , etc.; οὐδὲν εἶ Ar. Ec. 144 ; πρὸς τὸν οὐδέν E. Ph. 598 ; τὸ μηδὲν εἰς οὐδὲν ῥέπει Id. Fr. 532.2 ; ᾧ ἀνεμέσητον . . οὐδενὶ εἶναι Pl. Tht. 175e . in pl., οὐδένες ἐόντες ἐν οὐδαμοῖσι ἐοῦσι Ἕλλησι being nobodies, Hdt. 9.58 ; ὄντες οὐδένες E. Andr. 700 , cf. IA 371 ; ὁ μηδὲν ὢν κἀξ οὐδένων κεκλήσομαι dub. cj. in Id. Ion 594 ; οὐ γὰρ ἠξίου τοὺς μηδένας S. Aj. 1114 . with Preps., παρ' οὐδὲν εἶναι Id. OT 983 , etc.; παρ' οὐδὲν ἄγειν, θέσθαι, Id. Ant. 35 , E. IT 732 ; δι' οὐδενὸς ποιεῖσθαι S. OC 584 ; ἐν οὐδενὸς εἶναι μέρει D. 2.18 . τὸ οὐδέν naught, zero, in Arith., Nicom. Ar. 2.6 ; used by Democritus as a name for Place, Arist. Fr. 208 . neut. οὐδέν as Adv., not at all, naught, ἄριστον Ἀχαιῶν οὐ. ἔτισεν Il. 1.412 , cf. 24.370 , Hdt. 5.34 , Th. 8.22 , etc.; so οὐδέν τι X. Mem. 1.2.42 , etc.; οὐ. τι πάντως Hdt. 5.65 : in answers, nothing, never mind, no matter, E. Med. 64 , IT 781 , Ar. Nu. 694 ; οὐδέν γε not at all, Id. Av. 1360 , etc.; οὐδὲν μᾶλλον, οὐδὲν ἧσσον, οὐδὲν ὕστερος, v. μάλα 11.5 , ἥσσων 111 , ὕστερος A. I. οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἤ, v. ἄλλος III. 2 . REMARKS: the more emphatic and literal sense, not even one, i.e. none whatever, belongs to the full form, οὐδὲ εἷς, οὐδὲ μία, οὐδὲ ἕν, which is never elided, even in Com. (v. Ar. Ra. 927 , Lys. 1045 (lyr.), Pl. 138 , 1115 ), but freq. has a Particle inserted between, cf. οὐδέ B. — Zen. (in EM 639.17 ) and others wrongly assume οὐδείς as a compd. not of οὐδέ and εἷς, but of οὐ and δείς (q. v.). (Later οὐθείς, q. v.)

greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ τῶν κατεψυγμένων αὐτῆς ἅπτῃ μορίων καὶ πρὶν εἰς λεπτὰ καταθραῦσαι.
english_sentence_A: [607] For you are touching its chilled parts, and that before breaking it up into fine pieces.
english_sentence_B: For you are touching those parts of it that have been chilled, and doing so before breaking it up into fine pieces.

HA 517b27 ( Sup. ); τρίχες Id. GA 783a4 ( Comp. ); σάρξ E. Med. 1189 ; χαλκὸς καὶ δόνακες Pi. P. 12.25 , cf. E. greek_sentence: κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ἐν χειμῶνι πολλάκις, ἢ φρεατιαῖον ὕδωρ, ἢ ἄλλως πηγαῖον ἐφάνη θερμὸν τοῖς ἁπτομένοις, ἀλλ’ εἰ προθερμήνας τις τὰς χεῖρας ἅπτοιτο, φανεῖται ψυχρὸν, ἕτερά τε μυρία τοιαῦτα δυνατὸν ἀναμιμνήσκειν ἐστὶν, ἐξ ὧν οὐκ ἄν τις ἀπιστήσειεν, ὡς τὰ δυνάμει θερμὰ τῶν φαρμάκων, ὡς πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἑτέρῳ γένει ζώων ἐστὶν ἐνεργείᾳ θερμά.

english_sentence_A: For the more fine-particled ones might sometimes even be excreted together with the residues; and it is for roughly these two causes that some of those which kill by putrefaction and erosion have on occasion failed to kill: one, which I have just now finished stating, when they happen to be excreted together with the residues before they have harmed the body; the other, when the one who has taken them has somehow had the good fortune to make use of foods, or of things that would otherwise have been of benefit, or of some physician, if it so chanced, in attendance.

english_sentence_B: One is the cause I have just finished stating: when they happen to have been excreted together with the residues before harming the body. The other is when the person who took them is somehow fortunate enough to make use of foods, or of things that would in other ways have benefited him, or of some physician supervising him, if it so happened.

greek_sentence: εἰ δὲ παντελῶς ὀλίγον εἴη τὸ δηλητήριον, ἐνδέχεται καὶ τοῦτο μηδὲν ἀνύσαι τῷ γε μετὰ τῶν περιττωμάτων ἐκκριθῆναι καὶ τῇ δεούσῃ διαίτῃ χρήσασθαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οἷον εἰ κανθαρίδος εἴη μέρος ἑκατοστὸν τῆς δραχμῆς.
english_sentence_A: But if the poison were altogether small in quantity, it is possible that this too accomplishes nothing, by reason of its being excreted along with the residues and the person's using the requisite regimen—as, for example, if it were a hundredth part of a drachm of cantharis.
english_sentence_B: But if the poison should be altogether small in amount, it is possible that this too accomplishes nothing, through its being excreted with the residues and through the person's following the proper regimen; for example, if it were a hundredth part of a drachm of cantharis.

greek_sentence: καὶ τά γε τοιαῦτα τῶν συνθέτων φαρμάκων ὅταν ἐπιτηδείως μιχθῇ, δραστικώτατα γίνεται, καθάπερ καὶ τὸ διὰ τῆς κανθαρίδος οὐρητικόν.
english_sentence_A: And such compound drugs, when they are suitably mixed, become most efficacious, as for instance the diuretic made with cantharis.
english_sentence_B: And such compound drugs, when they are suitably mixed, become most efficacious, as is also the diuretic made with cantharis.

greek_sentence: ἐξ ὧν ἁπάντων εὔδηλον ὡς ὅσα μὲν τῷ ψύχειν ἀναιρεῖ βραχέα ληφθέντα δύναιτ’ ἂν θρέψαι τὸ σῶμα, καθάπερ καὶ ὁ τῆς θριδακίνης χυλὸς, ὅσα δὲ τῷ διαβιβρώσκειν, ἢ σήπειν, οὐχ οἷά τε τρέφειν ἐστὶν οὐδ’ ἂν ὑπὸ σμικρότητος ἀλύπως διεξέλθῃ τὸ σῶμα.
english_sentence_A: From all of which it is quite clear that those things which kill by cooling, when taken in small amounts, would be able to nourish the body, as indeed the juice of lettuce does, whereas those which kill by eroding or putrefying are not able to nourish, not even if on account of their smallness they pass through the body without harm.
english_sentence_B: From all of which it is quite clear that those things which destroy by cooling could, when taken in small quantities, nourish the body, as the juice of lettuce does, whereas those which destroy by corroding or putrefying are not capable of nourishing, even if, owing to their smallness, they should pass through the body without harm.

lsj_entry_text: ποιότης, ητος, ἡ, quality, Pl. Tht. 182a (where he apologizes for the use of the word as ἀλλόκοτον ὄνομα), Arist. Cat. 8b26 , EN 1173a15 (pl.), Gal. Nat.Fac. 1.2 , POxy. 2113.16 (iv A.D.), etc.; of size, Babr. 28.10 , Aesop. 84 .
greek_sentence: Καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν χυλῶν ἔμπροσθεν εἴπομεν, ὡς σχεδὸν οὐδεὶς αὐτῶν ἐστιν ἄμικτος ἀλλοτρίας ποιότητος, ἀλλὰ κᾀν δένδροις κᾀν ταῖς πόαις κᾀν τοῖς καρποῖς ἀναμεμιγμένοι τοῖς ἑτερογενέσιν εἰσὶν, οὕτω χρὴ νοῆσαι κᾀν τοῖς φαρμάκοις ἀναμεμίχθαι πολλῶν ἑτερογενῶν οὐσίας.
english_sentence_A: Just as we said earlier in the case of the juices, that almost none of them is unmixed with a foreign quality, but both in trees and in herbs and in fruits they are mingled with those of a different kind, so one must conceive that in drugs too the substances of many heterogeneous things are mixed in.
english_sentence_B: Just as we said earlier about the juices (χυλῶν), that hardly any of them is unmixed with a foreign quality, but whether in trees, in herbs or in fruits they are mixed with things of other kinds, so one must understand that in drugs too the substances of many things of other kinds are mixed together.

greek_sentence: εὕροις γὰρ ἂν, εἰ λογίζοιο, κόκκον Κνίδιον διαφέροντα κνίκου τῷ πλείστης μετέχειν θερμότητος.
english_sentence_A: For you would find, if you reckoned it out, that the Cnidian berry differs from safflower in partaking of a very great amount of heat.
english_sentence_B: For you would find, if you reasoned it out, that the Cnidian berry differs from cnicus in partaking of a very large share of heat.

greek_sentence: πάντως μὲν γὰρ ὁμοιότητά τινα ἔχει τὸ καθαῖρον φάρμακον ἑνί γέ τῳ τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν χυμῶν, οὐκ ἐξ ἅπαντος δὲ ἐπιμέμικταί τις αὐτῷ δηλητήριος δύναμις, ὥστ’ οὐδ’ ἐξ ἅπαντος ἀδικήσει μὴ καθᾶραν, ἀλλὰ πεφθήσεταί τε καὶ γεννήσει τοιοῦτον χυμὸν οἵου περ ἦν ἑλκτικόν.
english_sentence_A: For in every case the purging drug has some likeness to at least one of the humours in us, but not in every case is some deleterious power mixed into it, so that neither will it in every case do harm when it has not purged, but it will be concocted and will generate such a humour as that of which it was drawing.
english_sentence_B: For the purging drug certainly has some likeness to at least one of the humours in us; but it is not in every case that some deleterious power has been mixed in with it, so that it will not in every case do harm when it has not purged. Rather, it will be digested and will generate a humour of the same kind as the one it was drawing.

greek_sentence: ἕπεται δὲ τῷ δόγματι τούτῳ καὶ τὰ καθαίροντα φάρμακα τοῖς μὲν ἑλκομένοις χυμοῖς ὑπάρχειν οἰκεῖα, δραστικώτερα δέ πως εἶναι τὰ ἕλκοντα, καθάπερ καὶ ἡ Μαγνῆτις λίθος τοῦ σιδήρου.
english_sentence_A: And it follows from this doctrine that the purging drugs too are akin to the humours that are drawn, but that those which draw are in some way more active, just as the Magnesian stone too is more active than iron.
english_sentence_B: And it follows from this doctrine that purgative drugs are akin to the humours that are attracted, but that the things which attract are in some way more active, just as the Magnesian stone is in relation to iron.

english_sentence_A: For it too is iron-like and is found in the iron mines and resembles iron remarkably in appearance, but it is in some way stronger, so that it draws rather than is drawn.
english_sentence_B: For it too is iron-like, is found in iron mines, and closely resembles iron in appearance, but it is somehow stronger, so as to attract rather than be attracted.

greek_sentence: καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ τὸν κνίκον οὐκ ἀπελπιστέον εἶναι φλεγματώδη, ὡς ἐν τῇ χρόᾳ δείκνυσιν, ἀλλ’ ὑπὸ θερμότητος ἰσχυρότερος φλέγματος, ὡς ἕλκειν μᾶλλον ἢ ἕλκεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: And indeed one must not despair of safflower's being phlegmatic, as it shows in its colour, but it is, owing to its heat, stronger than phlegm, so that it draws rather than is drawn.
english_sentence_B: And indeed one should not despair of cnicus being phlegmatic, as it shows in its colour, but through its heat it is stronger than phlegm, so as to attract rather than be attracted.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ ἐπειδὴ καὶ τὰς ὁλκὰς ταῖς τῶν οὐσιῶν ὁμοιότησιν ἐδείξαμεν γίγνεσθαι, δέδεικται γὰρ πολλάκις ὡς ἐν ταῖς καθάρσεσιν ὁλκὴ τῶν οἰκείων τοῖς καθαίρουσι φαρμάκοις ἐστὶν, οὐ πάντων ὁμοῦ τῶν χυμῶν ἀλλοίωσις, ἀναγκαῖον ὁμοιότητά τινα ταῖς οὐσίαις ὑπάρχειν ἀμφοτέραις, τῇ τε τοῦ καθαίροντος καὶ τῇ τοῦ καθαιρομένου.
english_sentence_A: But since we have also shown that attractions come about through the similarities of substances—for it has been demonstrated many times that in purgations there is an attraction of what is akin to the purging drugs, not an alteration of all the humours together—it is necessary that a certain similarity belong to both substances, that of what purges and that of what is purged.
english_sentence_B: But since we have shown that attractions too come about through the similarities of substances (for it has been shown many times that in purgations there is an attraction of what is proper to the purging drugs, not an alteration of all the humours together), it is necessary that some similarity belong to both substances, that of the purging thing and that of the thing purged.

lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. Pi. P. 3.52 ; παιώνια A. Ag. 848 ; χρήσιμον Pl. R. 382c ; θανάσιμα Ph. Bel. 103.31 ; ὀλέθριον Luc. Herm. 62 . healing remedy, medicine, in Hom. mostly of those applied outwardly, ἐπιθήσει φάρμαχ' ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων Il. 4.191 ; ἐπ' ἄρ' ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε ib. 218 ; ὀδυνήφατα φ. πάσσων 5.401 , 900 , cf. 11.515 , 830 , 15.394 ; προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φ. Od. 10.392 ; φ. περιαλείφειν Ar. Eq. 906 ; also of potions, πιὼν φάρμακ' Od. 10.326 ; φ. πεπωκώς Hdt. 4.160 , cf. Pi. l. c.; παρὰ τοῦ ἰατροῦ Pl. R. 406d , cf. Grg. 467c ; φ. χριστόν E. Hipp. 516 ; ἔγχριστον Theoc. 11.1 ; ἐπίχριστον Str. 17.1.10 ; ἐπίπαστον Theoc. l. c.; καταπλαστόν Ar. Pl. 716 ; ποτόν E. Hipp. l.c.; freq. in Medic. writers, Sor. 1.4 , Gal. 6.265 , etc.; of medicines for cattle, PFlor. 222.11 (iii A. D.). c. gen. (v. infr. 11 ), φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, A. Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. HA 612b16 , cf. 624a16 ; μέθης Amphis 37 ; δίψης AP 6.170 ( Thyill. ); but ὑγιείας φ. a medicine to restore or maintain health, Aristid. Or. 37(2).11 . enchanted potion, philtre: hence, charm, spell, Od. 4.220 sq., Ar. Pl. 302 , Theoc. 2.15 , PSI 1.64.20 (i B. C.); φαρμάκοις τὸν ἄνδρ' ἔμηνεν Ar. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. D.). generally, remedy, cure, Hes. Op. 485 , Alc. 35 , etc.; μεῖζον . . τῆς νόσου τὸ φ. the cure too strong for, i. e. worse than, the disease, S. Fr. 589.4 , cf. Com.Adesp. 455 ; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pi. O. 13.85 ; φ. τινι for a thing, Thgn. 1134 (pl.), Archil. 9 ; πρός τι Arist. Pol. 1321a16 ; ποττὸν ἔρωτα Theoc. 11.1 ; but most freq. φ. τινός remedy against . . χλαῖνα . . φ. ῥίγευς Hippon. 19 ; Ζεὺς πάντων φ. μοῦνος ἔχει Simon. 87 ; τὸ σιγᾶν φ. βλάβης ἔχω A. Ag. 548 ; φ. πόνων, λύπης, E. Ba. 283 , Fr. 1079 ; δόλοι . . χρείας ἀνάνδρου φ. ib. 288 ; φόβου Pl. Lg. 647e ; λήθης φάρμακα (of γράμματα) E. Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. Pol. 1273b23 ; φ. μανίας, of the oil applied to wrestlers, D.L. 1.104 . ἐπὶ θανάτῳ φ. ἑᾶς ἀρετᾶς εὑρέσθαι a remedy or consolation in his own virtue, Pi. lsj_entry_text: σίδηρος [ι], Dor. σίδαρος IG 42(1).102.61 (Epid., iv B.C.), etc.: ὁ; also ἡ, Nic. Th. 923 : neut. σίδηρον, τό, Sch.D Il. 4.151 , v.l. in Hdt. 7.65 and Daimachus 4J. (but prob. f.l. for σιδήριον in Gal. 19.72 , cf. Hsch. s.v. Ἀκίς ): pl. σίδηρα Aret. SD 2.12 , EM 26.36 , Tz. (v. infr.): —iron, ς. πολιός Il. 9.366 , Od. 24.168 ; ἰόεις Il. 23.850 ; μέλας Hes. Op. 151 ; αἴθων Il. 4.485 , al.; πολύκμητος 6.48 , al., cf. Od. 9.393 ; as an article of traffic, οἰνίζοντο . . Ἀχαιοί, ἄλλοι μὲν χαλκῷ, ἄλλοι δ' αἴθωνι ς. Il. 7.473 ; πλέων . . μετὰ χαλκόν· ἄγω δ' αἴθωνα σίδηρον Od. 1.184 ; χαλκός τε χρυσός τε πολύκμητός τε ς., of treasures, Il. 11.133 , al.; as a prize, 23.261 , 850 ; Σκύθης ς., because brought from the Euxine, A. Th. 818 ; ὁ πόντιος ξεῖνος . . θηκτὸς ς. ib. 942 (lyr.). freq. as a symbol of hardness (cf. σιδήρεος 1.2 ), or of stubborn force, Il. 20.372 , Od. 19.494 ; ὀφθαλμοὶ ὡσεὶ κέρα ἕστασαν ἠὲ ς. ib. 211 ; οὔ σφι λίθος χρὼς οὐδὲ ς. Il. 4.510 ; ἐκ ς. κεχάλκευται . . καρδίαν Pi. Fr. 123.4 , cf. S. Fr. 658 ; ἦσθα πέτρος ἢ ς. E. Med. 1279 (lyr.), cf. Pl. Lg. 666c ; also of firmness, steadfastness, πέτρης ὅ γ' ἔχων νόον ἠὲ ς. Mosch. 4.44 , cf. Ach.Tat. 5.22 . anything made of iron, iron tool or implement, for husbandry, Il. 4.485 , cf. 23.834 : also of weapons, arrow-head, 4.123 ; sword or knife, 18.34 , 23.30 ; αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα ς. Od. 16.294 , cf. E. Or. 966 (lyr.); axe-head, Od. 19.587 : generally, arms, οἱ Ἀθηναῖοι ς. κατέθεντο Th. 1.6 ; ὅπλοις τε καὶ σιδήρῳ διώξειν OGI 532.25 (Galatia, i B.C.): also, knife, sickle, Hes. Op. 387 : pl., fishing-hooks, Theoc. 21.49 ; irons, fetters, Aret. SD 2.12 , Tz. H. 13.302 ; cf. σιδήριον. place for selling iron, smithy or cutler's shop, ἀγαγόντα εἰς τὸν ς. X. HG 3.3.7 .
greek_sentence: τοὐναντίον γὰρ ἅπαν, οὔτε σίδηρος σίδηρον οὔτε [614] σὰρξ ἕλκει σάρκα, ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν σιδηρῖτις λίθος τὸν σίδηρον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ τὸ αἷμα.
english_sentence_A: For it is entirely the opposite: neither does iron attract iron nor [614] flesh flesh, but the iron-stone attracts iron, and flesh attracts blood.
english_sentence_B: For it is wholly the contrary: neither does iron attract iron nor does [614] flesh attract flesh; rather, the iron-stone (sideritis) attracts iron, and flesh attracts blood.

greek_sentence: φλέγμα μὲν γὰρ φλέγματι ταὐτὸν καὶ κνίκος κνίκῳ, φλέγματι δὲ ὅμοιον κνίκος, οὐ μὴν ταὐτόν γε.
english_sentence_A: For phlegm is the same as phlegm, and safflower as safflower, but safflower is similar to phlegm, yet certainly not the same.
english_sentence_B: Phlegm is the same as phlegm, and cnicus as cnicus, but cnicus is similar to phlegm, not, however, the same.

lsj_entry_text: φλεγματώδης, ες, full of phlegm, κεφαλαί Hp. Aër. 3 . of food, nourishing, Id. Loc.Hom. 41 . inflammatory, Pl. R. 406a . of persons, phlegmatic, Hp. Epid. 3.14 , Arist. Pr. 860b9 . like phlegm, κάθαρσις Id. HA 574b5 , 578b19 ; τὸ αἷμα . . ῥέει -έστερον Hp. Nat.Hom. 6 . apt to produce phlegm, ὕδατα Id.Aër 7 ( Sup. ).
greek_sentence: οὐδὲ γὰρ ὅσα χολώδη τῶν ἐδεσμάτων ἢ φλεγματώδη λέγομεν, ὡς ἤδη χολὴν ἢ φλέγμα περιέχοντα, τοιαῦτα προσαγορεύομεν.
english_sentence_A: For neither, in the case of those foods which we call bilious or phlegmatic, do we so name them on the grounds that they already contain bile or phlegm.
english_sentence_B: Nor, indeed, when we speak of certain foods as bilious or phlegmatic do we give them these names as though they already contained bile or phlegm.

greek_sentence: Ταυτὶ μὲν οὖν καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα πάντα παρετέον, ἐκεῖνο δὲ αὖθις ἀναληπτέον, ὡς αὐτῶν τῶν καθαιρόντων φαρμάκων ἔνια μὲν ἤδη κέκτηται τὴν εἰς ὁλκὴν ἐπιτηδείαν ὁμοιότητα, τινὰ δ’ οὔπω μὲν ἔχει τελέως.
english_sentence_A: These matters, then, and all such things must be set aside; but that point must be taken up again, namely that of the purging drugs themselves some already possess the similarity suitable for attraction, whereas some do not yet have it completely.
english_sentence_B: These matters, then, and all such, must be passed over; but that other point must be taken up again: of the purging drugs themselves, some already possess the similarity suitable for attraction, while some do not yet have it completely,

lsj_entry_text: ὁλκ-ή, ἡ, (ἕλκω) drawing, trailing, dragging, e. g. of the hair, A. Supp. 884 ; ἡ τῆς γνάψεως ὁ. the drawing of the carding instrument in fulling cloth, Pl. english_sentence_A: These, then, come about when the purgative drug, having gained sufficient strength, produces at the mouths of the vessels that extend down to the belly both a biting and at the same time an opening of the mouths that is greater, and, by continuously irritating and tearing the bodies, breaks down the power in the vessels.
english_sentence_B: These, then, occur when the purgative drug, having prevailed sufficiently, produces at the mouths of the vessels that reach down to the stomach both biting and at the same time a greater opening of their mouths, and, continually irritating and tearing their bodies, dissolves the faculty in the vessels.

An. 1.7.5 . in narrative, τοιαῦτα prop. refers to what goes before, τοιαῦτα μὲν δὴ ταῦτα A. Pr. 500 ; καὶ ταῦτα μὲν τ. S. El. 696 , cf. X. greek_sentence: οὔσης δὲ κατ’ ἀρχὰς μὲν ἔτι καὶ τῆς ἀναστομώσεως καὶ τῆς ἀῤῥωστίας μετρίας, τὸ λεπτότατόν τε καὶ ἧττον οἰκεῖον ἐκκρίνεται, ἐπὶ πλέον δὲ προηκόντων ἀμφοτέρων ἤδη καὶ τὰ παχέα καὶ τὰ οἰκειότατα τῷ ζώῳ κενοῦται.
english_sentence_A: While at the beginning both the opening of the mouths (anastomosis) and the weakness are still moderate, what is thinnest and less proper is excreted; but when both have advanced further, now even the thick humours and those most proper to the animal are evacuated.
english_sentence_B: While at the beginning both the opening of the orifices and the weakness are still moderate, what is thinnest and less proper is excreted; but when both have advanced further, then the thick things too, and those most proper to the animal, are evacuated.

greek_sentence: διὰ τοῦτο οὖν ἡ μὲν ξανθὴ χολὴ πρώτη, τὸ δὲ φλέγμα δεύτερον, ἡ δὲ μέλαινα τρίτη, καὶ τούτων ὕστατον ἁπάντων ἐν ταῖς ὑπερκαθάρσεσιν ἐκκρίνεται τὸ αἷμα, τοῦτο μὲν ὡς οἰκειότατος τῇ φύσει χυμὸς, ἔμπροσθεν δὲ αὐτοῦ πρῶτος μὲν ὁ λεπτότατος, ὕστατος δὲ ὁ παχύτατος.
english_sentence_A: For this reason, then, yellow bile is excreted first, phlegm second, black bile third, and last of all these, in the excessive purgations, the blood: this, as the humour most proper to nature; while, before it, the thinnest comes first and the thickest last.
english_sentence_B: For this reason, then, yellow bile is excreted first, phlegm second, black bile third, and last of all these in excessive purgations the blood: this as the humour most proper to the nature, while before it the thinnest is first and the thickest last.

english_sentence_A: And indeed, [617] if it is purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, and after it the yellow, then in the same way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, as though flowing out from vessels that are by now lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have arrived at extreme distension.
english_sentence_B: Moreover [617], if it should be purgative of black bile, it will evacuate that first, after it the yellow, then in this way the phlegm, and last of all the blood will follow, flowing out as if from vessels already lifeless, since great weakness has seized them and their mouths have reached the utmost distension.

english_sentence_A: But since something is also called softening and relaxing, rarefying and condensing, clogging and dispersing, and very many others similar to these, it would be better to go through such things too; and together with them, or even before them, also the [620] substance and at the same time the power of all the flavours, about which something has been said at the end of the first of these commentaries, when I also set out the passage of Plato from the Timaeus; but there it was for the sake of recalling the perceptible affections which the tongue is naturally disposed to undergo in the case of each of them, whereas here my account will be about their substance and power.

greek_sentence: πάσχει μὲν γὰρ δήπου καὶ τἄλλα τοῦ ζώου μόρια τῇ γλώττῃ παραπλησίως, οὐ μὴν ἀκριβῶς αἰσθάνεται τῶν παθῶν, ἡ δέ γε πρὸς τῷ πάσχειν ἔτι καὶ τὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἀκριβὲς κεκτημένη διαγνωστικὴ τῆς φύσεως ἁπάντων τούτων ἐστίν.
english_sentence_A: For surely the other parts of the animal too are affected similarly to the tongue, yet they do not perceive the affections accurately; whereas the tongue, possessing, in addition to being affected, also accuracy of sensation, is capable of discerning the nature of all these.
english_sentence_B: For the other parts of the animal are, of course, also affected in a way similar to the tongue, yet they do not perceive the affections precisely. The tongue, however, besides being affected, also possesses precision of sensation, and so it is capable of discerning the nature of all these things.

english_sentence_A: For indeed it is not the case (οὐ καὶ δὴ τότε) that what is hot or cold or dry or wet is naturally such as either to cool or heat or dry or moisten the tongue, but not also each of the other parts; rather, just as it disposes and alters this one, so too it disposes and alters the others, the difference among them arising in respect of more and less, not in respect of being affected or not being affected.
english_sentence_B: For it is not the case that what is hot, or cold, or dry, or moist is naturally disposed to cool, or heat, or dry, or moisten the tongue, but not each of the other parts as well. Rather, just as it disposes and alters the tongue, so it also disposes and alters the other parts, the difference arising in them according to the more and the less, not according to being affected or not being affected.

greek_sentence: ὅτι μὲν γὰρ καὶ ξηροῦ καὶ ὑγροῦ καὶ θερμοῦ καὶ ψυχροῦ σώματος οὐδὲν ἧττον ἁπάντων τῶν ἄλλων τοῦ ζώου μορίων ἡ γλῶττα πέφυκεν [621] εἶναι διαγνωστικὴ πρόδηλον παντὶ, πικρότητας δὲ καὶ γλυκύτητας, ἁλυκότητάς τε καὶ ὀξύτητας, αὐστηρότητάς τε καὶ στρυφνότητας καὶ δριμύτητας, αὕτη μόνη διακρίνειν πεπίστευται, καίτοι τήν γε ὁμοιότητα τῶν παθῶν ἐστιν εὑρεῖν κᾀν τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασι μέρεσιν, καὶ μάλιστα ἐν τοῖς ἡλκωμένοις.
english_sentence_A: For that the tongue is by nature capable of discerning a dry and a wet and a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal [621] is obvious to everyone; but bitternesses and sweetnesses, saltinesses and sournesses, harshnesses and acerbities and pungencies, it alone is believed to distinguish, although the similarity of the affections can be found in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated.
english_sentence_B: For it is plain to everyone that the tongue is by nature [621] able to discern a dry and a moist, a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal; but bitterness and sweetness, saltiness and sourness, harshness, acerbity and pungency it alone is believed to distinguish, although one can find the similarity of the affections in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated.

english_sentence_A: For that the tongue is by nature capable of discerning a dry and a wet and a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal [621] is obvious to everyone; but bitternesses and sweetnesses, saltinesses and sournesses, harshnesses and acerbities and pungencies, it alone is believed to distinguish, although the similarity of the affections can be found in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated.
english_sentence_B: For it is plain to everyone that the tongue is by nature [621] able to discern a dry and a moist, a hot and a cold body no less than all the other parts of the animal; but bitterness and sweetness, saltiness and sourness, harshness, acerbity and pungency it alone is believed to distinguish, although one can find the similarity of the affections in all the other parts as well, and especially in those that are ulcerated.

english_sentence_A: For when soft bodies are drawn together and compressed, it happens both that their moisture is squeezed out and that their parts are torn apart: the moisture, as in a sponge that is drawn together and compressed by our hands; the being torn apart, as in things that are divided and pulled apart, whether by us dragging with our hands or by something else.
english_sentence_B: For it is not by eating through what is continuous, but by tearing it apart, that the cold is at once painful and biting; hence it does not appear such to hard bodies either. For when soft things are drawn together and compressed, it happens both that their fluid is squeezed out and that their parts are torn apart: the fluid, as in a sponge drawn together and compressed by our hands; the tearing apart, as in things that are divided and torn apart, whether by us pulling with our hands or by something else.

english_sentence_A: But an empty space cannot come into being in continuous bodies while their continuity is preserved.

lsj_entry_text: δακν-ώδης, ες, biting, pungent, Hp. Aph. 5.20 , Gal. 6.237 ; painful, Mich. in EN 499.3 .
greek_sentence: εἴπερ οὖν συνίσταται, δῆλον ὡς φθείρεται μὲν αὕτη, διασπᾶται δὲ τὸ συνεχὲς σῶμα, κᾀν τούτῳ τὸ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἀνιαρόν τε ἅμα καὶ δακνῶδες ὑπαντᾷ πάθος, οὐ μὴν ἥ γε ποιότης ἀμφοῖν ἡ αὐτὴ, τῶν τε διὰ τὸ ψύχειν δακνόντων ἐστὶν καὶ τῶν διὰ τὸ θερμαίνειν, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν προτέρων εὐθέως καὶ τὸ συνάγεσθαί τε καὶ σφίγγεσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν αἴσθησις ἡμῖν ἐστιν, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν δευτέρων ἡ τοῦ διαλύεσθαί τε καὶ χεῖσθαι.
english_sentence_A: If, therefore, one does come into being, it is clear that the continuity is destroyed and the continuous body is torn apart, and in this there arises the affection of sensation that is at once painful and biting. Yet the quality of the two is not the same—of those things that bite by cooling and of those that bite by heating—but in the case of the former we at once also have a sensation of the substance being drawn together and constricted, whereas in the case of the latter one of its being dissolved and diffused.
english_sentence_B: If, then, one does arise, it is clear that this continuity is destroyed and the continuous body is torn apart; and in this the affection of sensation that is at once distressing and biting presents itself. Yet the quality of both is not the same, of the things that bite by cooling and of those that bite by heating.

english_sentence_A: And indeed the speed too is not alike in the two affections; rather, in the case of cooling things the biting is somewhat slower, whereas in the case of heating things it runs through most swiftly.
english_sentence_B: In the former we at once also have a perception of the substance being drawn together and constricted; in the latter, a perception of its being dissolved and diffused. Moreover, the speed is not alike in the two affections: with cooling things the biting is somehow slower, whereas with heating things it passes through most swiftly.

lsj_entry_text: δακν-ώδης, ες, biting, pungent, Hp. Aph. 5.20 , Gal. 6.237 ; painful, Mich. in EN 499.3 .
greek_sentence: ὁπότ’ οὖν αὐτάρκως ἤδη διώρισται καὶ τῇ φύσει τῶν πραγμάτων αὐτῇ καὶ τῇ πρὸς ἡμᾶς αἰσθήσει, καὶ λέλεκται σαφῶς ﻿ [624] ὅπως μὲν τὸ θερμὸν, ὅπως δὲ τὸ ψυχρὸν δακνῶδες φαίνεται.
english_sentence_A: Since, then, it has now been sufficiently distinguished, both by the nature of the things themselves and by our perception of them, and it has been clearly stated [624] in what way the hot and in what way the cold appear biting, one ought surely to reason, even before hearing it from us, that of the biting drugs some must necessarily be hot in their powers, others cold.
english_sentence_B: Since, then, the matter has now been adequately distinguished, both by the very nature of the things and by our perception of them, and it has been stated clearly [624] in what way the hot, and in what way the cold, appears biting, one ought surely to reason out, even before hearing it from us, that of the biting drugs some must be hot in their powers and others cold.

lsj_entry_text: διορ-ισμός, ὁ, division, distinction, Pl. Ti. 38c , Arist. EN 1134b33 , Porph. Abst. 3.20 . logical distinction, Pl. Plt. 282c ; definition, Arist. SE 168a23 , al. Math., particular enunciation of a problem, Procl. in Euc. p.203 F. statement of limits of possibility of a problem, Apollon.Perg. Con.Praef. , Archim. Sph.Cyl. 2.4 , Phld. Acad.Ind. p.17 M.
greek_sentence: καὶ παρ’ ἡμῶν δὲ ἐπιμαθεῖν ἐστι τοὺς διορισμοὺς αὐτῶν ἀκριβῶς, ἀναμνησθέντας πρότερον ὡς καὶ τὸ πόμα καὶ τὸ βαλανεῖον, ὅταν εὐκράτως ἔχῃ, θερμὰ λέγομεν, ἐνίοτε καταχρώμενοι τῇ προσηγορίᾳ.
english_sentence_A: And from us one may further learn the distinctions among them precisely, having first recalled that we call both a drink and a bath, when they are well-tempered, hot, sometimes using the term loosely; for they ought rather to be called well-tempered and moderate than hot.
english_sentence_B: One can also learn from us in addition their precise distinctions, once we have first recalled that we call both a drink and a bath 'hot' when they are well-tempered, sometimes using the term loosely.

greek_sentence: διαχεῖται γὰρ ἡμῶν τὸ συνεστός τε καὶ πεπηγὸς ἐν τοῖς σώμασιν, ἐν ᾧ μάλιστα πάθει τὸ ἥδεσθαι τοῖς ζώοις ἐστίν· χρονίζοντα δὲ καὶ ταῦτα κατ’ ὀλίγον ἀνιαρὰ γίνονται.
english_sentence_A: Things that are hot in this way, then, are gentle and friendly; for what is condensed and congealed in our bodies is diffused, and it is in this affection above all that pleasure lies for living beings.
english_sentence_B: For what is compacted and congealed in our bodies is diffused, and it is chiefly in this affection that pleasure lies for animals. But if prolonged, these too gradually become distressing.

lsj_entry_text: ἀμετρ-ία, ἡ, excess, disproportion, opp. συμμετρία, Pl. Ti. 87d , cf. R. 486d , Heraclit. All. 8 , Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.112 , etc. want of moderation, Arist. VV 1251b15 . infinity, countless number, κακῶν Pl. Ax. 367a (in pl.).
greek_sentence: μεταπίπτει γὰρ εἰς ἀμετρίαν οὕτω γε χύσεως ὡς καὶ διαφορεῖσθαι καὶ διαλύεσθαι καὶ σκεδάννυσθαι τὴν οὐσίαν ἡμῶν.
english_sentence_A: But when they persist for a long time, even these gradually become painful; for it passes over into such an excess of diffusion that our substance is dispersed, dissolved and scattered.
english_sentence_B: For the diffusion passes over into such immoderation that our substance is dispersed, dissolved and scattered.

lsj_entry_text: κατά-πτωσις, εως, ἡ, fall, Hp. Art. 42 ; ἐξ ὀχήματος Gal. 7.560 ; λίθου Simp. in Ph. 261.17 . greek_sentence: ἀλλὰ κᾀν τούτῳ χωρὶς τοῦ δάκνειν ἀνιᾷ, λειποψυχίαν τε ἐμποιοῦντα καὶ κατάπτωσιν δυνάμεως, ὥστε καὶ τὸν θάνατον ἕπεσθαι.
english_sentence_A: But even in this case they cause distress without biting, producing faintness and a collapse of the power, so that death too follows.
english_sentence_B: Yet even in this case they cause distress without biting, producing fainting and collapse of strength, so that even death follows.

lsj_entry_text: δακν-ώδης, ες, biting, pungent, Hp. Aph. 5.20 , Gal. 6.237 ; painful, Mich. in EN 499.3 .
greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον τῶνδε θερμὰ τέμνει καὶ διαιρεῖ καὶ διίστησι τὴν οὐσίαν, ὥστ’ ἐξ ἀνάγκης δακνώδη φαίνεσθαι, καθάπερ [625] καὶ τὸ ζέον ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτό.
english_sentence_A: But those that are still hotter than these cut and divide and separate the substance, so that of necessity they appear biting, just as [625] boiling water does and fire itself.
english_sentence_B: But things still hotter than these cut, divide and separate the substance, so that of necessity they appear biting, as [625] do boiling water and fire itself.

lsj_entry_text: ἄμφω, τώ, τά, τώ, also οἱ, αἱ , τά; gen. ἀμφοῖν S. Ph. 25 , etc., dat. ἀμφοῖν Aj. 1264 , etc.:—both, of individuals, Il. 1.363 ; of armies or nations, 2.124 :— Hom. uses only nom. and acc.: from Hom. downwards freq. with pl. Noun or Verb, Il. 2.767 , 7.255 , etc.; ἐξ ἀμφοῖν, = ἐξ ἀλλήλοιν , S. OC 1425 : sts. indecl., h.Cer. 15 , Arist. Top. 118a28 , Theoc. 17.26 , A.R. 1.165 . (For the root cf. ἀμφί.)
greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν οὖν συνάγειν τε καὶ πηγνύειν τὴν ὑποβεβλημένην ὕλην ἴδιον ἀεὶ τοῦ ψυχροῦ· τὸ δὲ διαχεῖν τε καὶ τήκειν τοῦ θερμοῦ, κοινὸν δ’ ἀμφοῖν ἀμετρότερα αὐξηθέντων τὸ δάκνειν.
english_sentence_A: Now contracting and congealing the underlying matter is always the property of the cold, while diffusing and melting is that of the hot; but common to both, when they have been increased beyond measure, is biting.
english_sentence_B: To draw together and to congeal the underlying matter is therefore always peculiar to the cold, and to diffuse and to melt is peculiar to the hot; but biting is common to both when they have increased beyond measure.

lsj_entry_text: ἀραιός [α], ά, όν, (ἁρ- Hdn.Gr. 2.108 , v.l. in Il. 18.411 , al.) thin, slender, κνῆμαι, χείρ, γλῶσσαι, Il.l.c., 5.425 , 16.161 ; γαστήρ Nic. Col. 797b27 ; ἀκτῖνες ib. 791a27 ; φωναί Id. Aud. 803b28 ; ὀδόντες Poll. 2.94 , etc. ἀραιά (sc. γαστήρ), ἡ, flank, belly, Ruf. Onom. 171 . of the voice, thin, Theoc. 13.59 . (Homeric metre proves vαραιός.)
greek_sentence: ὅσα μὲν οὖν ἀκριβῶς ἐστι ψυχρὰ καὶ θερμὰ, πρὸς τοῖς ἄλλοις ἅπασιν οἷς ἔμπροσθεν εἴπομεν ἀραιοῖς τε καὶ μαλακοῖς μέλεσιν, ἤδη καὶ τοῦ δέρματος ἡμῶν ἅπτεται.
english_sentence_A: Those, then, that are precisely cold and hot, in addition to all the other rare and soft parts of which we spoke earlier, now take hold of our skin as well.
english_sentence_B: Now those things that are cold and hot in the strict sense lay hold even of our skin, in addition to all the other rare and soft members of which we spoke earlier.

lsj_entry_text: μέλος, εος, τό, limb, in early writers always in pl., Il. 7.131 , Pi. N. 1.47 , etc. (κατὰ μέλος is corrupt for κατὰ μέρος in h.Merc. 419 ); μελέων ἔντοσθε within my bodily frame, A. R. 607d , cf. D.H. Comp. 11 ; Ἀδμήτου μ. Cratin. 236 ; μέλη, τά , lyric poetry, choral songs, opp. Epic or Dramatic verse, Pl. R. 379a , 607a , al.; [μ.] ἐκ τριῶν συγκείμενον, λόγου τε καὶ ἁρμονίας καὶ ῥυθμοῦ ib. 398d . lyric portion of the Comic παράβασις, Heph. Poëm. 8.2 . music to which a song is set, tune, Arist. english_sentence_A: Now that which dissolves them is the heat in the body of the animal, in whatever manner they happen to be applied on each occasion; but their being broken up into fine or coarse parts they have from their own nature, so that, among cooling drugs too, those which are coarse-particled cannot bite, since they do not get so far as to penetrate the outer surface of the skin.
english_sentence_B: Their being broken up into fine or coarse parts, however, they have from their own nature. So also among the cooling drugs, those that are coarse-particled cannot bite, since they do not succeed in getting through the outer surface of the skin.

greek_sentence: ὡς γὰρ ὁμοιομερῶν ἁπάντων ὄντων, οὕτω ποιοῦνται τὸν λόγον, οὐ συγχωροῦντες οὔτε τὸν οἶνον οὔτε τοὔλαιον οὔτε τῶν ἄλλων οὐδὲν ἐκ διαφερόντων ταῖς δυνάμεσι συγκεῖσθαι μορίων, ἔτι δὲ τούτων μᾶλλον ἐπὶ ὄξους θαυμάζουσιν εἰ τολμῶμεν αὐτὸ λέγειν, ἀπολωλεκέναι μὲν τὴν ἔμφυτον τοῦ οἴνου θερμότητα, τὴν δ’ ἐκ σήψεως ἔχειν, ὅπερ δὴ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλει καὶ Θεοφράστῳ δοκεῖ.
english_sentence_A: For they construct their argument as though all of them were homoeomerous, not conceding that either wine or oil or any of the others is composed of parts differing in their powers; and still more than in these cases, with regard to vinegar they are amazed if we dare to say that it has lost the innate heat of the wine but possesses the heat that comes from putrefaction—which is indeed also the view of Aristotle and Theophrastus.
english_sentence_B: For they frame their argument as though all things were homoeomerous, not granting that either wine or oil or any of the other things is composed of parts differing in their powers; and still more than at these, in the case of vinegar they are astonished if we dare to say of it that it has lost the innate heat of the wine and has instead heat from putrefaction, which is indeed the view of both Aristotle and Theophrastus.

Fr. 271 (anap.): spring-water, drinking-water, οἶνον ἔμισγον καὶ ὕ. Od. 1.110 ; ἀφυσσάμεθ' ὕδωρ 9.85 ; ὕδατα καὶ . . δῖτοι Pl. R. 404a ; πότιμον ὕ. X. HG 3.2.19 ; ὕ. πίνων a water-drinker, D. 6.30 , cf. 19.46 , Ar. Eq. 349 ; ὕ. δὲ πίνων οὐδὲν ἂν τέκοι σοφόν Cratin. 199 , cf. Aristopho 10.3 , Bato 2.9 , al.: ὕδωρ κατὰ χειρός water for washing the hands, v. χείρ; φέρτε χερσὶν ὕ. Il. 9.171 ; ὕ. ἐπὶ χεῖρας ἔχευαν 3.270 , Od. 1.146 , al.; λοέσσας ὕδατι λευκῷ Il. 23.282 :—on γῆν καὶ ὕδωρ αἰτεῖν and διδόναι, v. γῆ 1.2b :—a curse was invoked upon those who refused fire (i.e. the right to borrow burning embers) or water or to direct a traveller on his way, Diph. 62 , cf. X. Oec. 2.15 :—prov., ὅρκους ἐγὼ γυναικὸς εἰς ὕ. γράφω S. Fr. 811 , cf. Men. Mon. 25 ; ἐν ὕδατι γράφειν Pl. Phdr. 276c ; ὅταν τὸ ὕδωρ πνίγῃ, τί δεῖ ἐπιπίνειν; if water chokes, what more can be done ? of a desperate case, Arist. EN 1146a35 , cf. ἐπιρροφέω 1 . rain-water, rain, ὅτε λαβρότατον χέει ὕ. Ζεύς Il. 16.385 ; ὗσαι ὕδατι λαβροτάτῳ Hdt. 1.87 ; ἐγίνετο ὕ. ἄπλετον Id. 8.12 ; πολύ Th. 6.70 , D. 59.99 ; ὕ. ἐπιγενόμενον πολύ X. HG 1.6.28 ; τὸ ὕ. τὸ γενόμενον τῆς νυκτός Th. 2.5 , cf. Hdt. 8.13 : more definitely, ὕδωρ ἐζ οὐρανοῦ X. An. 4.2.2 , Aristid. Or. 50(26).35 (but ἐζ οὐρανοῦ is a gloss in Th. 2.77 ): pl., ὕ. ὄμβρια Pi. O. 11(10).2 ; τὰ Διὸς, or παρὰ τοῦ Δ., ὕ. Pl. Lg. 761a , 761b ; τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕ. Thphr. HP 2.6.5 ; καινὸν ἀεὶ τὸν Δία ὕειν ὕδωρ, ὕδωρ τὸν θεὸν ποιῆσαι, Ar. Nu. 1280 , V. 261 (lyr.), cf. Thphr. Char. 3.4 : abs., ἐὰν πλείω ποιῇ ὕ. Id. CP 1.19.3 : κεραύνια ὕ. thunder-showers, Plu. 2.664f ; ὕ. πολλά, συνεχέα μαλθακῶς Hp. greek_sentence: τοιοῦτον γάρ τι κᾀπὶ τοῦ ὄξους πεπόνθαμεν, οὐ δυνάμενοι δι’ αἰσθήσεως ἰδεῖν αὐτοῦ τὴν γένεσιν, ἀπιστοῦμεν τῷ λόγῳ· ἀλλ’ εἰ μηδὲν ἄλλο, τὴν γοῦν τῆς ὄμφακος διαφορὰν πρὸς αὐτὸ κατανοήσαντες δίκαιοι πιστεύειν ἐσόμεθα ὡς οὐκ ὀξὺς μόνον, ἀλλὰ δριμύς τις ἕτερος ἀναμέμικται χυμὸς αὐτῷ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο τελέως ὁ τῆς ὄμφακος ἐμψύχει χυλὸς, ὥστε καὶ πρὸς καῦσον ἄκρως ἁρμόττει, κατὰ τοῦ στόματος τῆς γαστρὸς ἢ τῶν ὑποχονδρίων ὅλων ἐπιτιθέμενος, καὶ πρὸς ἅπαν ὅ τι περ ἂν ἐμψύξαι βουληθῶμεν, [631] οὐχ ὁμοίως δ’ ὄξος.
english_sentence_A: For we have experienced something of this sort also in the case of vinegar: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. But, if nothing else, having at least observed the difference of the unripe grape from it, we shall be right to believe that not only a sour flavour but also some other, pungent flavour has been mixed into it; and for this reason the juice of the unripe grape cools completely, so that it is also supremely suited for causus, when applied over the mouth of the stomach or the whole of the hypochondria, and for everything whatsoever that we may wish to cool, [631] whereas vinegar is not so in like manner.
english_sentence_B: For we have experienced something of this sort in the case of vinegar too: being unable to see its generation through sense-perception, we disbelieve the argument. But, if nothing else, once we have considered at least its difference from the unripe grape, we shall be right to believe that not a sour flavour only, but also some other, pungent flavour is mixed into it.

greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν οὖν ὀξὺ μόνον ὅ τι περ ἂν ᾖ ψυχρὸν πάντως ἐστὶν εἴτ’ οὖν ἄπιος, εἴτε μῆλον, εἴτε ῥοῦς, εἴτε ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν βάτων καρπὸς, εἴτε ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς μορέας, εἴθ’ ὁ ἀπὸ τῆς ῥοιᾶς, εἴθ’ ὅστις οὖν ἄλλος ἢ καρπὸς, ἢ χυλὸς, ἢ φυτὸν, ὡς ὀξυλάπαθον καὶ ὀξαλὶς, ἣν δὴ καὶ ὀξύδα προσαγορεύουσιν.

english_sentence_B: For it is not strictly one thing, nor sour only, but also pungent. Now whatever is sour only is in every case cold, whether a pear, or an apple, or sumach, or the fruit from brambles, or that from the mulberry, or that from the pomegranate, or any other whatever, be it fruit, or juice, or plant, such as oxylapathon and oxalis, which they also call oxys.

lsj_entry_text: ἀλαζ-ονεία, ἡ, false pretension, imposture, Pl. Grg. 525a , D. 22.47 , etc., cf. Arist. EN 1127a13 , Thphr. Char. 23 ; ὑπ' ἀλαζονείας Ar. Ra. 919 : in pl., Id. [That penult. is long appears from Ar.ll. cc., Men. 737 .]
greek_sentence: ὅ δὲ χρὴ πρότερον συμβουλεῦσαι τοῖς τὰ τοιαῦτα χωρὶς ἀλαζονείας σοφιστικῆς αὐτῆς ἕνεκεν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπισκοπουμένοις, ἤδη μοι καιρὸς εἰπεῖν, ὡς οὐ χρὴ μόνῳ τῷ λόγῳ γεγυμνάσθαι δι’ ὧν ἀεὶ παρακελεύομαι μεθόδων λογικῶν, ἃς ἐν τοῖς περὶ τῶν ἀποδείξεων ὑπομνήμασιν εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν αἴσθησιν τὴν γευστικὴν ἐπὶ τῶν χυμῶν γυμνάζειν ἐπιμελῶς, ἀρχομένους ἀπὸ τῶν ἐναργεστάτην ἐχόντων ἡντιναοῦν ποιότητα μίαν.
english_sentence_A: What it is necessary first to advise those who investigate such things, without sophistical imposture, for the sake of truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not only be trained in reasoning, by means of the logical methods which I constantly recommend, and which I set out in my commentaries on demonstrations, but must also carefully exercise the sense of taste upon the humours (flavours), beginning from those that possess some single quality whatsoever in the most evident manner.
english_sentence_B: What must first be advised to those who examine such matters without sophistical imposture, for the sake of the truth itself, it is now time for me to say: that one must not be trained in reason alone, through the logical methods which I am always urging and which I set out in the commentaries On Demonstration, but must also diligently train the gustatory sense on flavours, beginning from those that possess one single quality, whichever it may be, in the most evident form.

greek_sentence: ἐντεῦθεν γὰρ ὁρμώμενος ἑτοιμότερον ἐπί τε τὴν τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ἀμυδρῶν χυμῶν ἀφίξῃ διάγνωσιν ἐπί τε τὴν τῶν ὡς ἐγὼ μέν φημι γλυκέων, ὡς δ’ ἄλλοι τινὲς, ὑδατωδῶν, οἷος ὅ τε τῶν καλάμων ἐστὶ τῶν χλωρῶν καὶ ἀγρώστεως καὶ προσέτι πυρῶν καὶ κριθῶν καὶ ζειῶν καὶ ἄλλων πολλῶν, ὧν καὶ Θεόφραστος μέμνηται, ζητῶν εἴτ’ εἴδη πλείονα θετέον ἐστὶν τῶν γλυκέων χυμῶν, εἴτε τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον αὐτοὺς ὑποληπτέον διαφέρειν ἀλλήλων.
english_sentence_A: For setting out from here you will arrive more readily both at the discrimination of all the other faint flavours and at that of those which, as I for my part say, are sweet, but as certain others say, watery, such as is the flavour of green reeds and of dog's-tooth grass and, in addition, of wheat and barley and emmer and many others, which Theophrastus too mentions, inquiring whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.
english_sentence_B: For setting out from this you will arrive more readily at the discernment of all the other faint flavours, and at that of those which I call sweet but certain others call watery, such as the flavour of green reeds and of agrostis-grass, and moreover of wheat and barley and zeia and many others, which Theophrastus also mentions when he inquires whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.

english_sentence_A: For setting out from here you will arrive more readily both at the discrimination of all the other faint flavours and at that of those which, as I for my part say, are sweet, but as certain others say, watery, such as is the flavour of green reeds and of dog's-tooth grass and, in addition, of wheat and barley and emmer and many others, which Theophrastus too mentions, inquiring whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.
english_sentence_B: For setting out from this you will arrive more readily at the discernment of all the other faint flavours, and at that of those which I call sweet but certain others call watery, such as the flavour of green reeds and of agrostis-grass, and moreover of wheat and barley and zeia and many others, which Theophrastus also mentions when he inquires whether several species of sweet flavours are to be posited, or whether they are to be supposed to differ from one another by the more and the less.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξύς, εῖα, ύ, Ion. fem. ὀξέα Hdt. 9.23 , al., v.l. in Hp. Mul. 1.64 , al. (in codd. freq. ὀξέη, and so Babr. 73.1 metri gr.) : ὀξεῖα, poet. for neut. pl. ὀξέα, Hes. O. 7.70 ; Σείριος ὀξὺς ἐλλάμπων Archil. 61 ; πῦρ ὀ. Anaxipp. 1.12 ; so χιὼν ὀξεῖα Pi. english_sentence_A: But as they advance in time they become moister, and they take on sourness in addition to the acerbity, and, laying this aside little by little, they become sweet in turn as they are brought to completion.

english_sentence_A: And indeed, that all are concocted by the hot is clear, and that this is of two kinds—the one the proper innate heat of each, the other from without, from the sun, yet connate and proper to them—we surely know plainly, if we remember the elements that always underlie our account.

greek_sentence: ἐπεὶ δὲ καὶ [638] κατ’ ἀρχὰς μὲν ἔτι ξυλώδεις, ὥς καὶ Θεόφραστος ἔλεγε, ξηροί τέ εἰσιν ἅμα καὶ στρυφνοὶ, τὸ πλῆθος δ’ αὐτοὺς τῆς ἐπιῤῥεούσης ὑγρότητος ὀξεῖς ἐργάζεται, πρόδηλον ὡς γεωδέστερος μέν ἐστιν ὁ στρυφνὸς χυμὸς, ὑγρότερος δ’ ὁ ὀξὺς, ὥστε καὶ Πλάτων ὁρίζων ὀρθῶς ἔλεγεν· ὅσα τοιαῦτα τοῖς χυλοῖς ἐμφέρεται γεώδη μόρια, κατατηκόμενα ταῦτα καὶ συνάγοντα καὶ ἀποξηραίνοντα τὰ νοτερὰ τῶν τῆς γλώττης αἰσθητικῶν μορίων, τραχύτερα μὲν ὄντα στρυφνὰ, ἧττον δὲ τραχύνοντα αὐστηρὰ φαίνεται.
english_sentence_A: And since, at [638] the beginning, while they are still woody, as Theophrastus too said, they are at once dry and acerbic, whereas the abundance of the moisture flowing into them renders them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is earthier, the sour one moister; so that Plato too spoke correctly when he defined them: 'all such earthy particles as are carried in the juices, which, being dissolved (κατατηκόμενα) and contracting and drying up the moist portions of the sensitive parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less.' And we, in addition to this, shall correctly say that such a flavour is also cold in its mixture.
english_sentence_B: Since, moreover, [638] at the beginning, while still woody, as Theophrastus also said, they are at once dry and acerbic, and it is the quantity of the moisture flowing in upon them that makes them sour, it is evident that the acerbic flavour is more earthy and the sour one moister. Hence Plato too, in defining them, rightly said: all such earthy particles as are carried along in the juices, melting down and contracting and drying out the moist parts of the sensory parts of the tongue, appear acerbic when they are rougher, and harsh when they roughen less.

greek_sentence: ταυτὶ μὲν οὖν ἱκανῶς ἀλλήλοις ὡμολόγηται, τά τ’ ἀπὸ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῆς τῶν πραγμάτων εἰρημένα καὶ τὰ διὰ τῆς τῶν εὑρημένων κατὰ τὴν αἴσθησιν ἐπαγωγῆς· οὐδὲν δ’ ἂν εἴη χεῖρον ἔτι καὶ ταῦτα προσθεῖναι, μεμνημένους πάλιν κᾀνταῦθα τῆς τῶν ὀνομάτων χρήσεως, ὡς στύφειν μὲν ἄμφω λέγεται, τό τ’ αὐστηρὸν καὶ τὸ στρυφνὸν, ἐν δὲ τῷ μᾶλλον [640] καὶ ἧττον διαφέρει.

greek_sentence: καὶ μὴν καὶ ὅτι πολλαὶ τοῖς φαρμάκοις ὑπάρχουσι ποιότητες οὐ διάφοροι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ μαχόμεναι πρὸς ἀλλήλας, ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ παντάπασιν ὑπεναντίαι, δέδεικται μὲν ἔμπροσθεν αὐτάρκως, ἄρξασθαι δ’ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ καὶ νῦν ἀναγκαῖον.
english_sentence_A: And indeed, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also in conflict with one another, and sometimes even wholly opposed, has been sufficiently shown before; but it is necessary now too to begin from this point.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, that drugs possess many qualities, not only different but also conflicting with one another, and sometimes even wholly contrary, has been shown sufficiently earlier; but it is necessary to begin from this point now as well.

english_sentence_A: And if it appears neither sour nor sweet nor bitter, but, as far as is at all possible, having a single unmixed quality, that of astringency, then at that point to test it by experience in the manner I have often laid down for you before.
english_sentence_B: And if it should appear neither sour, nor sweet, nor bitter, but, as far as is possible, to have one unmixed quality, that of astringency, then you should at once test it by trial in the manner I have often proposed to you before.

greek_sentence: ἐὰν γὰρ ἅμα τό τε στύφειν ἔχῃ καὶ τὸ δάκνειν ἤ τινα ἄλλην ἐναργῆ ποιότητα καὶ δύναμιν ἐπιμεμιγμένην τῇ στύψει, περιττὸν καὶ μάταιον εἰς πεῖραν ἄγειν τὸ τοιοῦτον φάρμακον, ἐπειδὰν δοκιμάζῃς ἐνέργειαν στύψεως.
english_sentence_A: For if it has at once both the astringent and the biting, or some other evident quality and power mingled with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to the test when you are examining the activity of astringency.
english_sentence_B: For if it has at the same time both being astringent and biting, or some other evident quality and power mixed in with the astringency, it is superfluous and vain to bring such a drug to trial when you are assessing the action of astringency.

greek_sentence: χαλκῖτις οὖν καὶ μίσυ [641] καὶ χάλκανθος καὶ λεπὶς χαλκοῦ καὶ σῶρυ, στύφοντά τε ἅμα καὶ δάκνοντα, δρᾷ μὲν κατ’ ἀμφοτέρας τὰς ποιότητας εἰς ἕκαστον τῶν ὁμιλούντων σωμάτων, οὐ μὴν διδάξαι γε ἡμᾶς δύναται σαφῶς εἴτε διὰ τὴν στύψιν ἔχει τὸ καίειν, εἴτε διὰ τὴν δριμύτητα.

greek_sentence: καταλιπεῖν οὖν ἄμεινον αὐτὰ καὶ γεύεσθαι πολλῶν ἐφεξῆς ἄλλων ἐπισκοπούμενον εἰλικρινῆ στύψιν ἰδίᾳ καὶ καθ’ ἑαυτὴν ὡς οἷόν τ’ ἐστὶ μάλιστα, κᾀπειδὰν τοιαύτην εὕρῃς, οὕτως ἤδη κρίνειν τὸ φάρμακον αἷς πολλάκις ἔμπροσθεν ἤκουσας μεθόδοις, οἷον εἴ σοι γευομένῳ φαίνοιτο βαλαύστιον, ἢ κικὶς, ἢ κύτινος, ἢ ὑποκυστὶς, ἢ στρύχνος, ἢ γλαύκιον, ἢ ἀκακία, ἢ ῥοῦ χυλὸς, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἕτερον ἀκριβῶς μὲν εἶναι στρυφνὸν, ἔκδηλον δ’ ἑτέραν ποιότητα μηδεμίαν ἔχον, ἐξετάζειν ἐπὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἤδη καὶ βασανίζειν ἀκριβῶς ἐνέργειαν στύψεως.
english_sentence_A: It is better, therefore, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for a pure astringency, separately and by itself as far as is at all possible, and when you have found such a one, then at that point to judge the drug by the methods you have often heard before: for instance, if on tasting balaustion, or oak-gall, or kytinos, or hypokistis, or strychnos, or glaukion, or acacia, or juice of sumach, or some other such thing, it should appear to you to be precisely acerbic, while having no other manifest quality, then on such things to examine and test precisely the activity of astringency.
english_sentence_B: It is better, then, to leave these aside and to taste many others in succession, looking for an astringency that is pure, by itself and on its own as far as possible; and when you find such, then at last judge the drug by the methods you have often heard of before. greek_sentence: ἐπεὶ δ’ ὡς ὑπὲρ ἀναγκαίου μὲν, ἀγνώστου δὲ διέρχονται, διχῇ μέμψασθαι τοὺς ἄνδρας δίκαιον, ὅτι τε τὸ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον ὑπέλαβον ὡς ἀναγκαῖον, ὅτι τε προαπέγνωσαν αὐτοῦ τῆς εὑρέσεως.
english_sentence_A: But since they treat of it as something necessary, yet unknowable, it is just to blame these men on two counts: both because they took what is not necessary to be necessary, and because they despaired in advance of its discovery.

english_sentence_A: Indeed, even some of those that are mixed in their qualities, namely those that are moderately sweet and bitter and pungent, were clearly found to be cooling, since evidently the power of being astringent and of cooling prevails in them, so that the other powers are obscured.
english_sentence_B: And some even of those mixed with other qualities, namely the moderately sweet, bitter and pungent, were clearly found to cool, evidently because in them the power of astringing and cooling prevails, so that the others are obscured.

greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι καὶ [646] ὅσα στύφει τε ἅμα καὶ ὀξέα ταῖς ποιότησίν ἐστιν, ἅπαντα καὶ ταῦτά μοι εὑρέθη πειρωμένῳ σαφῶς ψύχοντα· τὰ δὲ γλυκέα μόνον ἅπαντα κατὰ τὸ ποσὸν τῆς γλυκύτητος εὐθὺς καὶ τῆς θερμότητος μετέχειν, ὥστ’ οὐδὲν μὲν τῶν λίαν γλυκέων ψυχρόν· εἴη δ’ ἄν τι καὶ μετρίως γλυκὺ ψυχρὸν, ἐπειδὰν τὸ πλεῖστον αὐτοῦ τῆς τοῦ σώματος οὐσίας ὑδατῶδες ᾖ, οὐ μὴν οὕτω γε ψυχρὸν, ὡς τὸ στρυφνὸν ἱκανῶς ἢ τὸ ὀξὺ, ἀλλ’ ὡς καὶ πρόσθεν που λέλεκται περὶ τῶν χλιαρᾶς θερμασίας μετεχόντων.
english_sentence_A: And indeed, [646] all those things too that are astringent and at the same time sour in their qualities were, as I found on trial, all of them clearly cooling; whereas all those that are merely sweet [I found] to partake straightaway of heat too, in proportion to the amount of their sweetness, so that none of the very sweet things is cold; yet something moderately sweet might also be cold, whenever the greater part of the substance of its body is watery—not, however, cold to such a degree as that which is strongly acerbic or sour, but in the way that has been stated somewhere earlier concerning the things that partake of a lukewarm warmth.
english_sentence_B: And indeed [646] all things that are at once astringent and sour in their qualities, these too I found on testing to be clearly cooling; whereas all things that are sweet only I found to partake of heat directly in proportion to the quantity of their sweetness, so that none of the very sweet things is cold.

english_sentence_A: But everything sweet is hot, and yet does not immoderately exceed the heat that is in us; rather, just as hot water, which we take pleasure in touching, and especially when we have been chilled, is most pleasant and most beneficial so long as it warms us [650] to the point of diffusing the parts of the body that have been congealed by the cold, yet without dissolving or cutting and separating their continuity, so too every sweet food is in every case hot, yet does not reach so great a degree of heat as to cause distress, but remains within the limits of what diffuses, smooths and softens.
english_sentence_B: But everything sweet is hot, and does not immoderately exceed the heat in us. Rather, it is like hot water, which we take pleasure in touching, especially when we have been chilled: so long as it warms us only to the point of diffusing the parts of the body congealed by the cold [650], and does not dissolve them or cut and separate their continuity, it is most pleasant and most beneficial.

greek_sentence: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τῶν σιτίων ἄλλοτε ἄλλο τοῖς τοιούτοις ἥδιον φαίνεται.
english_sentence_A: And for this reason, among foods too, now one, now another appears more pleasant to such people.
english_sentence_B: For the pleasant is twofold in kind. One kind refills what has been emptied, and this was nourishment.

lsj_entry_text: δι-θάλασσος, Att. δί-ττος [θα], ον, divided into two seas, of the Euxine, Str. 2.5.22 , cf. D.P. 156 ; of the Atlantic, Str. 1.1.8 . between two seas, where two seas meet, as is often the case off a headland, Act.Ap. 27.41 ; βραχέα καὶ διθάλαττα shallows and meetings of currents, in the Syrtes, D.Chr. 5.9 .
greek_sentence: διττοῦ γὰρ ὄντος τῷ γένει τοῦ ἡδέος, ἑτέρου μὲν τοῦ τὸ κεκενωμένον ἀναπληροῦντος, ὅπερ ἦν ἡ τροφὴ, ἑτέρου δὲ τοῦ τὸ ἠλλοιωμένον ἐξιωμένου, φάρμακον δ’ ἤδη τοῦτο συμβαίνει τοῖς ἐδέσμασιν, ὅταν μὴ μόνον τοῖς σώμασι κεκενωμένοις, ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ ποιότητα μεταβεβλημένοις προσφέρηται, κατὰ διττὸν ἡδύνεσθαι ἤδη τρόπον, ὡς τροφαῖς τε ἅμα καὶ φαρμάκοις.
english_sentence_A: For since what is pleasant is of two kinds in genus, one being that which fills up what has been emptied, which was nourishment, the other that which heals what has been altered, and this is now a drug, it comes about for foods, when they are administered to bodies that are not only emptied but also changed in quality, that they are now found pleasant in a twofold manner, as nourishments and drugs at the same time.
english_sentence_B: The other kind heals what has been altered, and this is already a drug. So it happens to foods, when they are given not only to bodies that have been emptied but also to bodies that have been changed in quality, that they now give pleasure in a twofold way, as nourishment and drugs at once.

lsj_entry_text: φάρμακον [v. sub fin.], τό, drug, whether healing or noxious: in Hom. the sense is freq. determined by an epith., φάρμακα, πολλὰ μὲν ἐσθλὰ . . , πολλὰ δὲ λυγρά Od. 4.230 ; τόδε φ. ἐσθλόν 10.287 , cf. 292 ; φ. ἤπια, ὀδυνήφατα (v. infr. 2 ); κακὰ φ. ib. 213 ; φ. λυγρά ib. 236 ; φ. οὐλόμενον ib. 394 ; ἀνδροφόνον 1.261 ; θυμοφθόρα φ. 2.329 ; so, after Hom. , προσανέα φ. Pi. P. 3.52 ; παιώνια A. Ag. 848 ; χρήσιμον Pl. R. 382c ; θανάσιμα Ph. Bel. 103.31 ; ὀλέθριον Luc. Herm. 62 . healing remedy, medicine, in Hom. mostly of those applied outwardly, ἐπιθήσει φάρμαχ' ἅ κεν παύσῃσι μελαινάων ὀδυνάων Il. 4.191 ; ἐπ' ἄρ' ἤπια φάρμακα πάσσε ib. 218 ; ὀδυνήφατα φ. πάσσων 5.401 , 900 , cf. 11.515 , 830 , 15.394 ; προσάλειφεν ἑκάστῳ φ. Od. 10.392 ; φ. περιαλείφειν Ar. Eq. 906 ; also of potions, πιὼν φάρμακ' Od. 10.326 ; φ. πεπωκώς Hdt. 4.160 , cf. Pi. l. c.; παρὰ τοῦ ἰατροῦ Pl. R. 406d , cf. Grg. 467c ; φ. χριστόν E. Hipp. 516 ; ἔγχριστον Theoc. 11.1 ; ἐπίχριστον Str. 17.1.10 ; ἐπίπαστον Theoc. l. c.; καταπλαστόν Ar. Pl. 716 ; ποτόν E. Hipp. l.c.; freq. in Medic. writers, Sor. 1.4 , Gal. 6.265 , etc.; of medicines for cattle, PFlor. 222.11 (iii A. D.). c. gen. (v. infr. 11 ), φ. νόσου a medicine for it, remedy against it, A. Pr. 251 , 606 (lyr.); βηχός Phryn.Com. 60 : κεφαλῆς for a head-ache, Pl. Chrm. 155b ; στραγγουρίας Arist. HA 612b16 , cf. 624a16 ; μέθης Amphis 37 ; δίψης AP 6.170 ( Thyill. ); but ὑγιείας φ. a medicine to restore or maintain health, Aristid. Or. 37(2).11 . enchanted potion, philtre: hence, charm, spell, Od. 4.220 sq., Ar. Pl. 302 , Theoc. 2.15 , PSI 1.64.20 (i B. C.); φαρμάκοις τὸν ἄνδρ' ἔμηνεν Ar. Th. 561 ; τοιαῦτα ἔχω φ. such charms have I, Hdt. 3.85 , cf. Apoc. 9.21 . poison, S. Tr. 685 , E. Med. 385 ; πιεῖν τὸ φ. Antipho 6.15 , Pl. Phd. 57a , 115a ; φάρμακα ἐσβεβληκέναι ἐς τὰ φρέατα Th. 2.48 ; φ. δηλητήρια SIG 37 A 1 (Teos, v B. C.); τοξικὸν φ. BGU 21 ii 14 (iv A. D.). lye for laundering, Stud.Pal. 22.56.12 (iii A. D.). generally, remedy, cure, Hes. Op. 485 , Alc. 35 , etc.; μεῖζον . . τῆς νόσου τὸ φ. the cure too strong for, i. e. worse than, the disease, S. Fr. 589.4 , cf. Com.Adesp. 455 ; φ. πραΰ, of a bridle, Pi. O. 13.85 ; φ. τινι for a thing, Thgn. 1134 (pl.), Archil. 9 ; πρός τι Arist. Pol. 1321a16 ; ποττὸν ἔρωτα Theoc. 11.1 ; but most freq. φ. τινός remedy against . . χλαῖνα . . φ. ῥίγευς Hippon. 19 ; Ζεὺς πάντων φ. μοῦνος ἔχει Simon. 87 ; τὸ σιγᾶν φ. βλάβης ἔχω A. Ag. 548 ; φ. πόνων, λύπης, E. Ba. 283 , Fr. 1079 ; δόλοι . . χρείας ἀνάνδρου φ. ib. 288 ; φόβου Pl. Lg. 647e ; λήθης φάρμακα (of γράμματα) E. Fr. 578.1 ; v. εὐδιανός. c. gen. also, a means of producing something, φ. σωτηρίας Id. Ph. 893 ; μνήμης καὶ σοφίας φ. Pl. Phdr. 274e ; ὑπομνήσεως ib. 275a , cf. 230d ; ἀθανασίας Antiph. 86.6 ; ἡσυχίας Arist. Pol. 1273b23 ; φ. μανίας, of the oil applied to wrestlers, D.L. 1.104 . ἐπὶ θανάτῳ φ. ἑᾶς ἀρετᾶς εὑρέσθαι a remedy or consolation in his own virtue, Pi. english_sentence_A: But if these things are so, the less sweet among foods will also be less hot, while the more sweet will be hotter by just as much as it is sweeter.

greek_sentence: πολὺ γὰρ, ὡς καὶ Θεόφραστος καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ἔλεγε, τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἡλιακῆς θερμασίας οἷον ἐμπύρευμά τι ταῖς τε ῥαξὶ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑπάρχει καρποῖς, ὑφ’ οὗ τὸ ὑδατῶδες ἐν αὐτοῖς ἔτι καὶ οἷον ἡμίπεπτον, εἰς πέψιν ἄγεται καὶ κατεργάζεται τῷ μεταβάλλοντι συνεξομοιούμενον, ὥστε κᾂν ἀποθλίψῃς τὸν χυλὸν ὀπώρας ἡστινοσοῦν, εὑρήσεις μὲν εὐθέως ζέοντα καθάπερ τὸ γλεῦκος, ἐν δὲ τῷ μᾶλλόν τε καὶ ἧττον διαφέρουσαν τὴν ζέσιν εἰς ὅσον ἂν καὶ ὁ καρπὸς τοῦ καρποῦ διαφέρει θερμότητος.
english_sentence_A: For, as both Theophrastus and Aristotle said, there is present in grapes and in the other fruits a great deal of what is, as it were, a kind of ember-like residue (empyreuma) from the sun's warmth, by which that which is still watery in them and, as it were, half-concocted is brought to concoction and worked up, being assimilated to that which changes it; so that if you press out the juice of whatever fruit you please, you will find it at once fermenting (ζέοντα) just like must, though the fermentation (ζέσις) differs in degree of more and less to the extent that one fruit differs from another in heat.
english_sentence_B: For, as both Theophrastus and Aristotle said, there is present in grapes and in the other fruits much of what comes from the sun's warmth, as it were a sort of ember, by which the watery element in them, still as it were half-concocted, is brought to concoction and worked up, being assimilated to what changes it; so that, if you press out the juice of any fruit whatsoever, you will find it at once seething just like must, but its seething differing by more and less to the extent that one fruit differs from another in heat.

VC 14 ; Ep. ὅτεῳ Od. 2.114 , and as disyll., Il. 12.428 , 15.664 ; so Hdt. 1.86 , al., Democr. 100 , Heraclit. 15 , SIG 194.21 (Amphipolis, iv B. C.); Arc. ὀσ<*>έοι IG 5(2).262.14 (Mantinea, v B. Aër. 21 ); dat. ὁτέοισι(ν) Il. 15.491 , Hdt. 2.82 , Att. ὅτοισι S. Ant. 1335 , Ar. Eq. 758 , ὅτοις S. Tr. 1119 ; acc. ὅτινας Il. 15.492 , Aeol. ὄττινας Sapph. 12 : in a few forms only the first part is inflected, Cret. gen. sg. ὦτι prob. in Leg.Gort. 1.5 , 2.50 , 11.50 , al., GDI 4993 ii 10 : neut. pl. ἄτι Leg.Gort. 2.47 , al.: of the forms with double inflexion Hom. has only ὅν τινα Il. 2.188 , al., ἥν τινα 3.286 , al., οἵ τινες Od. 4.94 , al., οὕς τινας Il. 4.240 , al., ἅς τινας Od. 8.573 ; ᾧτινι first in Hes. Op. 31 , ἧστινος A. Ag. 1358 , ᾗ τινι δή Th. 8.87 , οἷστισι Ar. Pax 1279 : Att. Inscrr. have ἧστινος ᾗτινι along with masc. and neut. ὅτου ὅτῳ, and this rule holds with few exceptions in Trag. and Att. Prose before iv B. C.; ᾡτινιοῦν occurs in Lys. 1.37 , etc.: ὅτῳ rarely as fem., E. IT 1071 .—For the Ion. and Ep. form ἅσσα, Att. ἅττα, v. ἅσσα .—On the concord and construction cf. ὅς B. 1.1 , 3 , 11.3 , 111.2a ,b:—Radic. sense, any one who, anything which, whosoever, whichsoever; ὣς ἀπόλοιτο καὶ ἄλλος, ὅτις τοιαῦτά γε ῥέζοι Od. 1.47 ; ἀθανάτων ὅς τίς σε φυλάσσει 15.35 , etc.: freq. without express antec., χαίρει δέ μιν ὅς τις ἐθείρῃ Il. 21.347 ; ἆσσον ἴτω ὅς τις δέπας οἴσεται 23.667 : hence freq. in maxims or sentiments, οὐκ ἔστιν ὅ. πάντ' ἀνὴρ εὐδαιμονεῖ Ar. Ra. 1217 ; μακάριος ὅ. οὐσίαν καὶ νοῦν ἔχει Men. 114 ; οὗτος βέλτιστος ἂν εἴη, ὅ. . . Fr. 354.5 ; οὐδὲν ὅ τι οὐ . . everything, Hdt. 5.97 , Th. 7.87 :—in these phrases the case of ὅστις commonly depends on that of οὐδείς; but sts. the reverse, v. οὐδείς 1.2 : also joined with Sup. , τρόπῳ ὅτῳ ἂν δύνωνται ἰσχυροτάτῳ Foed. ap. Th. 8.90 (πάντες ὅσοι being commonly used in pl., not πάντες οἵτινες; but πᾶσιν . . ὅστις ἐρωτᾷ IG 12.410 ). referring to a definite object, prop. only when a general notion is implied, Πολυκράτεα . . , δι' ὅντινα κακῶς ἤκουσε, not the man through whom, but one through whom . . , Hdt. 3.120 ; τελευταῖόν σε προσβλέψαιμι νῦν, ὅστις πέφασμαι φύς τ' ἀφ' ὧν οὐ χρῆν may I see thee now for the last time, I who am one born from sinful parentage, S. OT 1184 , cf. A. Pr. 38 , Ag. 1065 ; but in quite definite sense, βωμόν, ὅστις νῦν ἔξω τῆς πόλεώς ἐστι Th. 6.3 : sts. even with οὗτος or ὅδε as antec., Hdt. 1.167 , 2.99 , 6.47 , E. Hipp. 943 , Theoc. 8.87 . ἐφ' ὅτῳ, = ἐφ' ᾧτε , D.S. 16.4 ; so ἐφ' ὅτῳ τε Delph. 3(2).236 (ii B. C.). in indirect questions, Hom. , etc., εἴπ' ἄγε μοι καὶ τόνδε . . , ὅς τις ὅδ' ἐστί Il. 3.192 , cf. 167 , etc.; ἔσπετε νῦν μοι, Μοῦσαι, ὅς τις δὴ κτλ. who it was that . . , 14.509 ; ξεῖνος ὅδ', οὐκ οἶδ' ὅς τις Od. 8.28 : in dialogue, when the person questioned repeats the question asked by τίς, as οὗτος τί ποιεῖς;—ὅ τι ποιῶ ; Ar. Ra. 198 ; ἀλλὰ τίς γὰρ εἶ;—ὅστις ; πολίτης χρηστός Id. Ach. 595 , cf. Pl. 462 , Pl. Euthphr. 2c , etc. rare and late in direct questions, ὅ τι ἐστὶ τὸ ἐμποδίζον ; A.D. Adv. 140.12 ; ἀνθ' ὅτου . . ; = why? Jul. Ep. 82p.109B. -C.; cf. ὅπως. limited or made more indefinite by the addition of Particles: ὅστις γε being one who (cf. ὅσγε), S. OT 1335 , OC 810 , Ar. english_sentence_A: But when the watery and half-concocted part has been changed and worked up, and the warmth that produces the fermentation has been dissipated by transpiration, the proper qualities of the juices appear unmixed, so that it is then also that we discern what sort the wines are according to their own proper nature.
english_sentence_B: And once the watery and half-concocted element has been changed and worked up, and the warmth that produces the seething has been breathed out, the proper qualities of the juices appear unmixed, so that it is then that we also discern what sort the wines are according to their own nature.

greek_sentence: καὶ πρόδηλον, ὡς τὸ μὲν γλυκὺ θερμότερόν ἐστι τοῦ στρυφνοῦ, τὸ δὲ πικρὸν τοῦ γλυκέος.
english_sentence_A: There is indeed, after the boiling, in some of the wines a pure sweetness, at once pleasant and proper to the nature of the juice itself, not like the earlier one, which was a kind of mixture of the proper sweetness and of that arising from the boiling of the half-concocted and watery residue; so that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they grow old, and it happens to the harsh ones among them, in aging, first to take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next to increase in pungency while gradually ceasing from sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, to become quite pungent and to take on bitterness continually, and finally, when they thicken, to turn entirely bitter—then it is evident that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.
english_sentence_B: So that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they age, and it happens that the harsh among them, in growing old, first take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next increase in pungency and gradually lose their sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, become quite pungent and take on ever more bitterness, and finally, when they thicken, become completely bitter, it is also plain that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.

english_sentence_A: There is indeed, after the boiling, in some of the wines a pure sweetness, at once pleasant and proper to the nature of the juice itself, not like the earlier one, which was a kind of mixture of the proper sweetness and of that arising from the boiling of the half-concocted and watery residue; so that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they grow old, and it happens to the harsh ones among them, in aging, first to take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next to increase in pungency while gradually ceasing from sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, to become quite pungent and to take on bitterness continually, and finally, when they thicken, to turn entirely bitter—then it is evident that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.
english_sentence_B: So that, if it is agreed that all wines become hotter as they age, and it happens that the harsh among them, in growing old, first take on a certain sweetness and pungency as they lay aside their astringency, next increase in pungency and gradually lose their sweetness, and then again, over a longer time, become quite pungent and take on ever more bitterness, and finally, when they thicken, become completely bitter, it is also plain that the sweet is hotter than the acerbic, and the bitter hotter than the sweet.
