greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ εἴπερ ἡ γλυκύτης ὑπὸ [656] συμμετρίας θερμοῦ γίγνεται, δῆλον ὡς ἡ στρυφνότης ὑπὸ τοῦ ψυχροῦ κρατοῦντος ἀποτελεσθήσεται.
english_sentence_A: But if sweetness arises from [656] a due proportion of heat, it is clear that acerbity will be produced by the cold prevailing.
english_sentence_B: But if sweetness is produced by [656] a due proportion of heat, it is clear that acerbity will be brought about by the cold when it prevails.

greek_sentence: ὡς οὖν ὁ στρυφνὸς οἶνος ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ γλυκύτερος μὲν πρῶτον, ἐφεξῆς δὲ δριμύτερός τε καὶ πικρότερος ἀποτελεῖται καὶ τελευτῶν ἐκπικροῦται, κατὰ δὲ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ὅ τε ῥιγώσας ὀξύτερος εὐθὺς γίγνεται καὶ εἰ τελέως ἀποψυγείη τελέως ὀξύνεται, ὅ τ’ εὐθέως ἐν τῆ συγκομιδῇ τῶν καρπῶν ὑετοῦ κατασχόντος ὀθνείας ὑγρότητος ἀναπλησθεὶς, ὅ τ’ ἄλλως ὕδατος προσλαβὼν, ὀξεῖς ἑτοίμως οἱ τοιοῦτοι πάντες ἐπὶ μικραῖς προφάσεσιν ἀποτελοῦνται.
english_sentence_A: Just as, then, acerbic wine over time becomes first sweeter, then more pungent and more bitter, and finally turns wholly bitter, so in the same way the wine that has been chilled at once becomes sourer, and if it is completely cooled off it turns completely sour; and the wine that straightaway at the gathering of the fruits, when rain has set in, has been filled with foreign moisture, and the one that has otherwise taken on water—all such wines readily become sour on slight occasions.
english_sentence_B: Just as, then, the acerbic wine over time is rendered first sweeter, and next more pungent and more bitter, and in the end becomes thoroughly bitter, so in the same manner the wine that has been chilled becomes sourer at once, and if it should be completely chilled it becomes completely sour; and the wine that, rain having set in right at the gathering of the fruit, has been filled with extraneous moisture, and the wine that has otherwise taken on water: all such wines readily turn out sour upon slight occasions.

english_sentence_A: For to the extent that the hot is more capable of finding a way through than the cold, to that extent also the pungent juice passes more readily than the sour through the pores of the sentient bodies, so that the one, arriving first, as it were makes a road, and the other follows not long after; and in this the mixed and hard-to-interpret character of the sensation is brought about, since sensation can neither declare vinegar simply cold—for it perceives in it a certain fiery pungency—nor simply hot.
english_sentence_B: For to the degree that the hot is more penetrating than the cold, to that degree the pungent flavour also passes through the pores of the sentient bodies more readily than the sour one, so that the one, arriving first, as it were opens the way, and the other follows not far behind. In this way the mixed and hard-to-express character of the sensation is produced: the sensation can declare vinegar neither simply cold, for it perceives in it a certain fiery pungency, nor simply hot.

P. 3.71 , cf. 2.96 , 4.285 ; τίς ἂν εὔπατρις ὧδε βλάστοι; οὐδεὶς τῶν ἀ. κτλ. S. El. 1082 ; οἵ τ' ἀ. πρὸς τῶν ἀγενῶν κατανικῶνται Id. Phdr. 274a :—in political sense, aristocrats, esp. in the phrase καλοὶ κἀγαθοί (v. sub καλοκἀγαθός). brave, valiant, since courage was attributed to Chiefs and Nobles, Il. 1.131 , al.; τῷ κ' ἀγαθὸς μὲν ἔπεφν', ἀγαθὸν δέ κεν ἐξενάριξεν 21.280 ; cf. Hdt. 5.109 , etc. good, capable, in reference to ability, ἀ. βασιλεύς Il. 3.179 ; ἰητήρ 2.732 ; θεράπων 16.165 , 17.388 ; πύκτης Xenoph. 2.15 ; ἰητρός Hp. Prog. 1 ; προβατογνώμων A. Ag. 795 ; ἄρχοντες Democr. 266 : freq. with qualifying words, ἀ. ἐν ὑσμίνῃ Il. 13.314 ; βοὴν ἀ. 2.408 , 563 , al.; πύξ Od. 11.300 ; βίην Il. 6.478 ; γνώμην S. OT 687 ; πᾶσαν ἀρετήν Pl. Lg. 899b , cf. Prt. 356b . good, in moral sense, first in Thgn. 438 , cf. Heraclit. 104 , S. El. 1082 , X. Mem. 1.7.1 , Pl. Ap. 41d , etc.; ψυχῆς ἀγαθῆς πατρὶς ὁ ξύμπας κόσμος Democr. 247 : freq. with other Adjs., ὁ πιστὸς κἀ. S. Tr. 541 ; δικαίων κἀ. ib. 1050 :—ironical, τὸν ἀ. Κρέοντα Id. Ant. 31 . ὦ ἀγαθέ, my good friend, as a term of gentle remonstrance, Pl. Prt. 311a , etc. ἀ. δαίμων, v. sub δαίμων; ἀ. τύχη, v. sub τύχη; ἀ. θεός = Lat. bona dea, Plu. Caes. 9 , Cic. 19 . of things, good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη . . ἀ. κουροτρόφος Od. 9.27 , etc.; ἀ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει X. Cyn. 13.17 : c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀ. good for it, Id. Mem. 3.8.3 ; ἑλκῶν Thphr. HP 9.11.1 . of outward circumstances, αἰδὼς οὐκ ἀ. κεχρημένῳ ἀνδρὶ παρεῖναι Od. 17.347 ; εἰπεῖν εἰς ἀγαθόν to good purpose, Il. 9.102 ; ὁ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀ. περ for his own good end, 11.789 ; οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη 2.204 :—ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf., it is good to do so and so<*> Il. 7.282 , 24.130 , Od. 3.196 , etc. morally good, πρῆξις Democr. 177 ; ἔργα Emp. 112.2 , cf. Ep.Rom. 2.7 , etc. ἀγαθόν, τό, good, blessing, benefit, of persons or things, ὦ μέγα ἀ. σὺ τοῖς φίλοις X. Cyr. 5.3.20 ; φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀ. εἶναί φασι Id. Mem. 2.4.2 , cf. Ar. Ra. 74 , etc; as term of endearment for a baby, blessing!, treasure!, Men. Sam. 28 :— ἀγαθόν τινα δεδρακέναι, πεποιηκέναι confer a benefit on . . , Th. 3.68 , Lys. 13.92 ; ἐπ' ἀγαθῷ τινος for one's good, Th. 5.27 , X. Cyr. 7.4.3 ; ἐπ' ἀ. τοῖς πολίταις Ar. Ra. 1487 ; οὐκ ἐπ' ἀ. for no good end, Th. 1.131 ; ἐπ' οὐδενὶ ἀ. τῆς Ἑλλάδος X. HG 5.2.35 :—in pl., ἡ ἐπ' ἀγαθοῖς γεναμένη (sic) κατασπορά PFlor. 21.10 (iii A.D.):—τὸ ἀ. or τἀ., the good, Epich. 171.5 , cf. Pl. R. 506b , 508e , Arist. Metaph. 1091a31 , etc.:—in pl., ἀγαθά, τά, goods of fortune, treasures, wealth, Hdt. 2.172 , Lys. 13.91 , X. Mem. 1.2.63 , etc.; ἀγαθὰ πράττειν fare well, Ar. Av. 1706 ; also, good things, dainties, Thgn. 1000 , Ar. Ach. 873 , etc.: good qualities, τοῖς ἀ., οἷς ἔχομεν ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ Isoc. 8.32 , cf. Democr. 37 ; good points, of a horse, εἰ τἄλλα πάντα ἀ. ἔχοι, κακόπους δ' εἴη X. Eq. 1.2 . Comp. and Sup. are usu. supplied from other stems, viz. Comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων<*> βελτίων, κρείσσων ʽκάρρωνʼ, λωΐων (λώʽωνʼ), Ep. βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος:— Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος (λῷστος), Ep. βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος:— later, reg. Comp. ἀγαθώτερος LXX Jd. 11.25 , 15.2 , D.S. 8 Fr. 12 , Plot. 5.5.9 , Diod.Rh. p.53.9H. : Sup. ἀγαθώτατος D.S. 16.85 , Hld. 5.15 , etc. ( -ότατος POxy. 1757.26 (ii A.D.)). Adv. usually εὖ, q.v.: ἀγαθῶς Hp. Off. 9 , Arist. Rh. 1388b6 , LXX 1 Ki. 20.7 . (Etym. dub. ( ὅτι ἄγει ἡμᾶς ἐπὶ τὸν ὀρθὸν βίον Stoic. 3.49 ); perh. cognate with ἄγαμαι, hence admirable.)

greek_sentence: ὡς γὰρ καὶ πρόσθεν εἴρηται, σχεδὸν ἅπαντες οἱ τῶν δένδρων καρποὶ κατὰ τὴν πρώτην γένεσιν, ὡς καὶ Θεόφραστος ἔλεγε, στρυφνοὶ γευομένοις εἰσὶν, εἶτ’ ἐπειδὰν ὑγρότητος πληρῶνται, προσλαμβάνουσι μὲν ὀξύτητος, ἀφαιροῦσι δὲ τῆς στρυφνότητος.
english_sentence_A: For, as was said earlier too, nearly all the fruits of trees, at their first generation, as Theophrastus also said, are acerbic to those who taste them; then, when they become filled with moisture, they take on sourness and lose some of their acerbity.
english_sentence_B: For, as was also said before, nearly all the fruits of trees in their first growth, as Theophrastus too used to say, are acerbic to those who taste them; then, when they are filled with moisture, they take on sourness and lose some of their acerbity.

english_sentence_A: To take an immediate example, among unripe grapes some partake more of acerbity, some more of sourness, and some of both in equal measure.

english_sentence_B: But for cooling burning fevers (kausoi) they are all reasonably suitable.

Sc. 457 ; βέλος Il. 4.185 , etc.; also of non-metallic substances, λᾶας 16.739 ; μοχλός Od. 9.382 ; σκόλοπες Il. 12.56 , 64 ; ὀξεῖα κορυφή, of a mountain-peak, Od. 12.74 ; so πάγοι ὀξέες 5.411 ; λίθος ὀξὺς πεποιημένος sharpened so as to serve as a knife, Hdt. 7.69 , cf. 3.8 ; κυρβασίας ἐς ὀξὺ ἀπηγμένας brought to a point, Id. 7.64 ; ὄρεα ἐς ὀ. τὰς κορυφὰς ἀ. Id. 2.28 ; τὸ ὀ. the apex of a triangle, ib. 16 ; of the heart, Arist. Resp. 478b5 ; τὸ ὀ. τοῦ ᾠοῦ Id. GA 752b8 ; ὀ. γωνία an acute angle, Id. Top. 107a16 , al., Euc. 1 Def. 12 , Archim. Spir. 16 ; Χρόνος ὀξὺς ὀδόντας Simon. 176 ; ἡ ὀξεῖα, name of a surgical instrument, Hermes 38.282 , Heliod. ap. Orib. 44.23.59 ; but also, a pointed splinter of bone, ib. 46.20.5 . in reference to the senses, of feeling, sharp, keen, ὀδύναι Il. 11.268 ; ὀ. ἠέλιος the piercing sun, h.Ap. 374 ; ὀξειᾶν ἀκτίνων πατήρ, i.e. the Sun, Pi. O. 7.70 ; Σείριος ὀξὺς ἐλλάμπων Archil. 61 ; πῦρ ὀ. Anaxipp. 1.12 ; so χιὼν ὀξεῖα Pi. P. 1.20 ; so also of grief and the like , ἄχος Il. 19.125 ; μελεδῶναι Od. 19.517 : and generally, sharp, severe, μάχη ὀξέα . . γίνεται keenly contested, Hdt. 9.23 ; ὀ. πυρετός Hp. VM 16 ( Sup. ); [ἡ νόσοσ] ὀξεῖα φοιτᾷ καὶ ταχεῖ' ἀπέρχεται S. Ph. 808 ; νόσοι, μανίαι, Pi. O. 8.85 , N. 11.48 ( Comp. ), cf. Hp. Acut. tit., Archig. ap. Gal. 9.887 ; πάθαι Pi. P. 3.97 ; ἐπιμομφά Id. O. 10(11).9 , etc. of the sight, ὀξύτατον ὄμμα Id. N. 10.62 ; ὄψις . . ὀξυτάτη τῶν διὰ τοῦ σώματος . . αἰσθήσεων Pl. Phdr. 250d : freq. in neut. as Adv., ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι to be keenest of sight, Il. 17.675 ; ὀξύτατα καθορᾶν Pl. R. 516c ; so ὀξὺ νοεῖν notice a thing sharply, Il. 3.374 ; ὀξὺ προϊδεῖν Od. 5.393 ; ὀξύτερον βλέπει Ar. Pl. 1048 , Lys. 1202 (lyr.) : prov., ὀξύτερον τοῦ Λυγκέως βλέπειν Id. Pl. 210 , cf. Macar. Prov. 6.41 ; also ὀξὺ ἄκουσεν heard with sharp ear, Il. 17.256 , cf. Pl. Lg. 927b ; ὀξεῖαν ἀκοὴν . . λόγοις διδούς keen attention, S. El. 30 . of things that affect the sight, dazzling, bright, αὐγὴ Ἠελίου Il. 17.372 ; [Ἠελίου] ὀξύτατον πέλεται φάος εἰσοράασθαι 14.345 : hence of colours, Ar. Pax 1173 (v. φοινικίς 2 ) ; αἱ ὀξεῖαι χροιαί Arist. Phgn. 806b4 ; πορφύρα Plu. Cat.Mi. 6 , PHolm. 20.36 ; [ἐσθὴσ] ὀξυτέρα καὶ τηλαυγεστέρα Ael. NA 4.46 . of sound, shrill, piercing, ἀϋτή Il. 15.313 ; ὀξὺ βοήσας 17.89 ; ὀξὺ δὲ κωκύσασα 18.71 ; ὀξὺ λεληκώς 22.141 ; ὀξέα κεκληγώς 17.88 , etc.; of whinnying horses, ὀξεῖα χρέμισαν Hes. Sc. 348 ; of young pigs, ὀξὺ κεκράγατε Ar. Ach. 804 ; of the scream of birds of prey, ὀξέα κλάζων S. Ant. 112 (anap.) ; of metals, ἰάχεσκε σάκος ὀξέα καὶ λιγέως Hes. Sc. 233 ; also of the wail of the nightingale (cf. ὀξύφωνος), ὄρνιθος ὀ. φθόγγον S. Ant. 424 ; so ἐπηλάλαξαν τὸν ὀ. νόμον shrieked their shrill song, A. Th. 952 (lyr.) ; ὀξὺ μέλος, of the grasshopper, Ar. Av. 1095 (lyr.). of musical tones, in a technical sense, high-pitched, opp. βαρύς, φθόγγοι Pl. Ti. 80a , X. Cyn. 6.20 ; ὀξυτάτη χορδή Pl. Phdr. 268d ; φωνὴ ὀξεῖα, βαρεῖα, μέση Arist. Rh. 1403b29 ; τῷ ὀξεῖ ἐν φωνῇ μὲν ἐναντίον τὸ βαρύ, ἐν ὄγκῳ δὲ τὸ ἀμβλύ Id. Top. 106a13 . in Music, δι' ὀξειῶν ( Dor. -ᾶν) interval of a fifth, Philol. 6 , Arist. Pr. 920a24 . ἡ ὀξεῖα (sc. προσῳδία) the acute accent, D.T. 630.1 , A.D. Pron. 35.10 , al.; τὸν τόνον φυλάσσειν ὀ. ib. 60.1 ; ὀ. συλλαβή Pl. Cra. 399b ; ὀ. στοιχεῖον S.E. M. 1.113 . of taste, sharp, pungent, acid, φακῆ X. Cyr. 6.2.31 ; ὄξος Diph. 18.1 ; οἶνος Alex. 141.12 ; ἐξ ὀξέος καὶ ἁλμυροῦ ξυνθεὶς ζύμωμα Pl. Ti. 74c . of smell, Arist. de An. 421a30 ; ὀξύτατον ὄζειν τινός Ar. Ach. 193 . metaph., of the inner sense, sharp, keen, hasty, esp. quick to anger, passionate, epith. of Ares, Il. 2.440 ,al. ; μένος ὀξύ h.Hom. 8.14 ; καρδίη ὀξυτέρη Thgn. 366 ; θυμὸς ὀ. S. OC 1193 ; νέος καὶ ὀ. Pl. Grg. 463e ; οἱ ἀκρόχολοι ὀξεῖς Arist. EN 1126a18 : so in ὀξύ-θυμος, -κάρδιος, -χολος. sharp, quick, δεινοὶ καὶ ὀξεῖς Pl. Ap. 39b : c. inf., ἐπινοῆσαι ὀ. Th. 1.70 ; γνῶναι . . ὀξύτατοι τὰ ῥηθέντα D. 3.15 ; also εἰς πάντα τὰ μαθήματα ὀξεῖς Pl. R. 526b ; τὰς ἐνθυμήσεις ὀξύς Luc. Salt. 81 . of motion, quick, swift, post- Hom. , ὀξυτάτους ἵππους Hdt. 5.9 ( v.l. ὠκυτάτους ) ; ἱερακίσκος Ar. Av. 1112 ; ὀξυτέρῳ χαλινῷ S. Ant. 108 (lyr.) ; of a report, ὀξεῖα βάξις διῆλθ' Ἀχαιούς Id. Aj. 998 ; ὀξεῖαν ἐκβάλλει ῥοήν, of a dying man, Id. Ant. 1238 , cf. A. Ag. 1389 ; of a flame, fierce, Thphr. HP 5.9.3 ; ᾄξας ὀξὺς νότος ὥς S. Aj. 258 (anap.) ; τὸ εὔψυχον . . ὀξεῖς ἐνδείκνυνται are quick in displaying, Th. 4.126 ; opp. βραδύς, Id. 8.96 ; opp. ῥάθυμος, Arist. EE 1240a2 ; opp. ἡσύχιος, Id. EN 1116a9 ; ὀ. παράγγελμα Onos. 10.2 ; ὀ. καιρός an urgent crisis, Id. 6.1 , al.; ὁ ὀ. δρόμος the express post, POxy. 900.7 (iv A. D.), 2115.6 (iv A. D.) ; ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν ἐκχέαι αἷμα Ep.Rom. 3.15 : esp. in Adv. (v. infr.). regul. Adv. ὀξέως quickly, soon, βοηθεῖν, μεταχειρίσαι, Th. 6.10 , 12 , etc.; sharply, ὁρᾶν, αἰσθάνεσθαι, Pl. R. 567b , Phdr. 263c ; poet. ὀξείως Epigr.Gr. 986.3 (Philae) : Comp. ὀξυτέρως Hp. Epid. 3.17 .β' ; ὀξυτέρως ἀποθῄνσκειν ib. 1.2 ; but, neut. ὀξύ and pl. ὀξέα as Adv., v. supr. 11.2 , 3 : Comp. ὀξύτερον Th. 2.8 , Pl. Tht. 190a : Sup. ὀξύτατον Il. 17.675 , Pl. Lg. 741d ; or ὀξύτατα Id. R. 401e , al. (Cf. ὀξίνα, ὄκρις.)

lsj_entry_text: γλυκύς, εῖα ( -ῆα Herod. 4.2 ), ύ ( -ύν IG 14.1890 ), sweet to the taste or smell, νέκταρ Il. 1.598 ; οἶνος Epich. 124 , etc.; γλυκὺ ὄζειν Cratin.Jun. 1 , prob. in Crates Com. 2 ; opp. ὀξύς, Hp. Vict. 2.55 ; opp. δριμύς, Plu. 2.708e : mostly metaph., even in Hom. , pleasant, delightful, ἵμερος, ὕπνος, Il. 3.139 , Od. 2.395 ; γ. αἰών 5.152 , Hdt. 7.46 ; πόλεμος γλυκίων γένετ' ἠὲ νέεσθαι Il. 2.453 ; οὐδὲν γλύκιον ἧς πατρίδος οὐδὲ τοκήων Od. 9.34 , cf. Pi. N. 5.2 , E. Med. 1036 , etc.; γλυκύ [ἐστι], c. inf., A. Pr. 698 , Alex. 210 ; θανεῖν γλύκιστον B. 3.47 ; ὅτῳ . . μηδὲν ἦν ἰδεῖν γλυκύ S. OT 1335 (lyr.), cf. 1390 . of water, sweet, fresh, Xenoph. 1.8 , etc.; opp. πικρός, Hdt. 4.52 ; opp. ἁλμυρός, Arist. Mete. 355a33 , etc. after Hom. (but v. supr.), of persons, sweet, dear, γλυκεῖα ( v.l. -ῆα ) μᾶτερ Sapph. 90 ; γλυκεῖαι παῖδες ἀρχαίου Σκότου S. OC 106 : c. inf., γ. φρὴν συμπόταισιν ὁμιλεῖν Pi. P. 6.52 ; freq. in epitaphs, IG 14.1472 ( Sup. ), etc.; also ὑπὲρ τῆς γλυκυτάτης πατρίδος τελευτῆσαι POxy. 33i13 (ii A. D.); ὦ γλυκύτατε my dear fellow, Ar. Ach. 462 , cf. Ec. 124 ; sts. in bad sense, simple, silly, ὡς γ. εἶ! Pl. Hp.Ma. 288b ; also applied κατ' ἀντίφρασιν to a swine, Gal. 18(2).611 ; γλυκὺ πνεῖον, of mustard, Matro Conv. 90 . as Subst., ὁ γ. (sc. οἶνος) grape-syrup, Alex. 59 , 172.14 , Arist. Pr. 875b2 , Herod. 6.77 , POxy. 1088.51 ; also τὸ γ. Nic. Al. 386 , POxy. 234ii6 (ii/iii A. D.). of the eye of Polyphemus, Theoc. 6.22 . ἡ γ., = γλυκύρριζα , Thphr. HP 9.13.2 . ἡ γ., = χολή , Sch. Nic. Th. 594 . Comp. and Sup. γλυκίων Od. 9.34 ; γλύκιστος B. 3.47 , Ael. NA 12.46 , etc.; also γλυκύτερος, -τατος Pi. O. 1.109 , 19 , etc.; γλύσσων Xenoph. 38.2 . Adv. -κέως Poll. 4.24 . (Perh. fr. Δλυκύς, cf. Lat. dulcis.)

lsj_entry_text: δριμύς, εῖα, ύ, piercing, sharp, keen, βέλος Il. 11.270 : metaph., δριμεῖα μάχη 15.696 , Hes. Sc. 261 ; δ. χόλος Il. 18.322 ; μένος Od. 24.319 ; ἄχος Hes. Sc. 457 ; θυμός A. Ch. 391 (lyr.). of things which affect the eyes or taste, keen, pungent, acrid, of smoke, δριμύτατος καπνῶν Ar. V. 146 ; of radish, etc., opp. γλυκύς, X. Mem. 1.4.5 , cf. Pl.Com. 154 ( Sup. ); χυμός Arist. de An. 422b13 ; ὀσμαί ib. 421a30 ; δριμέσιν ἰητρεύειν with pungent drugs, Hp. Fract. 27 ; δ. οἶνος Luc. Merc.Cond. 18 . Adv. -έως: Comp. δριμύτερον, ὄζειν Arist. Pr. 907a13 ; ῥεύματος δριμύτερον γενομένου Hp. VM 18 . metaph., of persons, bitter, fierce, ἀλάστωρ A. Ag. 1501 (lyr.); ἄγροικος Ar. Eq. 808 , etc.; also, keen, shrewd, κρόταλον E. Cyc. 104 ; ἔντονοι καὶ δ. Pl. Tht. 173a ; δ. καὶ δικανικός ib. 175d ; δ. ἐν τῷ ἀποκρίνεσθαι Arist. Top. 156b37 ; λόγος δριμύτατος Id. SE 182b37 (but λέξις and λόγος δ. of striking turns of phrase, Hermog. Id. 1.2 , 2.5 ): neut. as Adv., δριμὺ βλέπειν look bitter, Ar. Ra. 562 ; but also to look sharply, keenly, Pl. R. 519a , Luc. Symp. 16 ; ἐνορᾶν Id. Cat. 3 , Ael. VH 14.22 , D.C. 59.26 :—regul. Adv. δριμέως, Anaxandr. 15.3 ; ἐρασθῆναι Ael. NA 7.15 ; δριμύτατα ἀλγεῖν Id. VH 12.1 .

greek_sentence: Ἐπεὶ δὲ τῶν ὀξέων ἴσως ἄν τῳ δόξειε λείπειν, ὅ τινας καὶ τῶν ἐλλογίμων ἰατρῶν ἐξηπάτησεν· τῷ γὰρ τοὺς οἴνους τοὺς ἀσθενεῖς ἔν τε τῷ ἦρι καὶ τῷ θέρει μεταβάλλειν τε καὶ ὀξύνεσθαι, χειμῶνος δ’ ἐν ταῖς οἰκείαις φυλάττεσθαι ποιότησιν, ὑπὸ θερμοῦ τισιν ἔδοξεν ἡ ὀξύτης γεννᾶσθαι.
english_sentence_A: But in the case of sour things something might perhaps seem to someone to be lacking, a point which has deceived even some of the reputable physicians: for because weak wines change and turn sour in spring and in summer, but in winter are preserved in their proper qualities, it seemed to some that sourness is generated by heat.

greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι τοὺς πίθους ἔνιοι τῶν τὰ γεωργικὰ γραψάντων ἀξιοῦσιν ἐν οἴκοις κατορύττεσθαι πρὸς ἄρκτον ἐστραμμένοις, ὡς τῆς μὲν ψύξεως φυλαττούσης αὐτῶν τὴν ποιότητα, τῆς δὲ θερμότητος μεταβαλλούσης.
english_sentence_A: And moreover some of those who have written on agricultural matters recommend that the storage jars be buried in rooms turned toward the north, on the grounds that cooling preserves their quality, whereas heat alters it.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, some of those who have written on agriculture recommend that the storage jars be buried in houses facing north, on the grounds that cold preserves their quality whereas heat changes it.

english_sentence_A: For some wines readily turn sour when they are stored away in southern and sun-exposed places; and it seems to me that one should make the beginning of the solution of the points stated from here.

greek_sentence: οὔτε γὰρ κίνησιν οὔτε θερμασίαν ἰσχυρὰν ἀσθενὴς ὑπομένει φύσις, ἀλλὰ διαφορεῖται πρὸς αὐτῆς μᾶλλον ἢ αὐξάνεται, ἐπεί τοι κᾀξεπίτηδες ἐν πολλοῖς χωρίοις κινοῦσί τε καὶ μεταφέρουσι τοὺς οἴνους, ὥσπερ οὖν καὶ ἡλιοῦσί γε καὶ θερμαίνουσιν, ὡς ἐνίους αὐτῶν ἀηδεῖς γίγνεσθαι τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καπνοῦ δεχομένους ποιότητα.
english_sentence_A: For a weak nature withstands neither strong motion nor strong warmth, but is dispersed by it rather than increased; since in fact in many regions they deliberately move and transport the wines, just as they also expose them to the sun and heat them, so that some of them become unpleasant, taking on the quality from the smoke.

greek_sentence: τῶν δὲ τὰ γεωργικὰ συγγραψάντων οὐδὲν θαυμαστὸν ἐνίους ὑπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὰ σφέτερα χωρία πείρας ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων οἴνων ἀποφήνασθαι προπετέστερον.
english_sentence_A: And it is no wonder that some of those who have written on agricultural matters, on the basis of the experience gained in their own regions, have pronounced rather rashly about all wines.

greek_sentence: ὑπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ὀνινάμενα καὶ βλαπτόμενα· καὶ γὰρ καὶ γυμνάσια σφοδρὰ καὶ ἥλιος ἰσχυρότερα μὲν ἐργάζεται τὰ θερμὰ καὶ ῥωμαλέα σώματα, καταβάλλει δὲ καὶ διαφορεῖ καὶ καταψύχει τὰ μὴ τοιαῦτα, καὶ τῶν οἴνων τοὺς μὲν θερμοὺς φύσει καὶ κίνησις ῥιπίζουσα καὶ ἥλιος ἐκθερμαίνων καὶ φλόγες πλησίον καιόμεναι πεπαίνουσι θᾶττον.
english_sentence_A: For indeed vigorous exercises and the sun make hot and robust bodies stronger, but cast down, disperse and chill those that are not of this kind; and of wines, those that are hot by nature are ripened more quickly both by motion that fans them and by the sun that heats them through and by flames burning nearby.
english_sentence_B: For vigorous exercises and the sun make hot and robust bodies stronger, but they lay low, disperse and chill those that are not such. And of wines, those that are hot by nature are ripened more quickly by motion that fans them, by sun that heats them thoroughly, and by flames burning nearby.

english_sentence_A: And this too seems somehow to agree with what was said at the beginning about the sour flavours.
english_sentence_B: And in a way this too seems to agree with what was said at the beginning about sour flavours.

Fr. 556 , And. 3.5 , Pl. R. 439e ; τῆς Πλειάδος βορείου γενομένης having appeared in the north, Arist. H A 542b11 . of the north wind, β. χειμών a winter during which northerly winds prevail, Hp. Cyn. 8.1 ); βορείοις in the time of northerly winds, Arist. H A 574a1 , al.; βορείων ὄντων ib. 592a14 : Comp. -ότερος Arat. 247 , Alex.Aphr. in Metaph. 446.34 : Sup. -ότατος Man. 4.241 . βόρειον, = ἐλλεβορίνη , Ps.- Dsc. 4.108 ; βόρειος, = ἀείζωον τὸ μέγα , ib. 88 .
lsj_first_sense_gloss: from the quarter of the north wind
greek_sentence: εἴπερ γὰρ ὅμοιόν τι πεπόνθασι ταῖς βορείαις καταστάσεσιν, ὡς λεπτομερεῖς ὑπάρχειν ἅμα καὶ ψυχροὺς, πρόδηλον ὡς ἡ γένεσις αὐτῶν οὐκ ἄνευ θερμότητος, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ τῷ ἀέρι.
english_sentence_A: For if indeed they have undergone something similar to the northerly conditions of the weather, so as to be fine-particled and at the same time cold, it is evident that their generation does not occur without heat, just as it does not for the air either.
english_sentence_B: For if they have been affected in a way similar to northerly conditions of the weather, so as to be at once fine-particled and cold, it is evident that their coming-into-being is not without heat, just as it is not for the air either.

english_sentence_A: All the sour flavours are indeed cold, yet they do not cool to such a degree as to kill.
english_sentence_B: All sour flavours are indeed cold, yet they do not chill to such a degree as to kill.

english_sentence_A: For these manifestly have their sourness mixed with some acerbity, just as vinegar has it mixed with pungency.
english_sentence_B: For in these it has appeared to me most nearly unmixed and alone, partaking of no acerbity, as the fruits of trees do.

english_sentence_A: Now what is properly named sour among the flavours is perceptible to the tongue alone, as is also the pungent.
english_sentence_B: These fruits plainly have their sourness admixed with a certain acerbity, just as vinegar has its sourness admixed with pungency.

GA 728b35 , cf. Plu. in Hes. 84 . π. ἄγριος,= χελιδόνιον τὸ μικρόν, Dsc. 2.181 . (Cf. Lith. pūraĩ (pl.) 'wheat', and perh. πυρήν.)
greek_sentence: μεταβάλλει δὲ τὰ μὲν εὐθὺς εἰς ἄλληλα, τὰ δὲ διὰ μέσων ἑτέρων, οἷον αὐτίκα ἡ γῆ μὲν εἰς πυροὺς καὶ κριθὰς καὶ τἄλλα τὰ τοιαῦτα.
english_sentence_A: And some things change directly into one another, others through other things as intermediates; as, for instance, earth changes into wheat and barley and the other such things, and each of these in turn into the flesh of a human being, yet it is not possible for earth itself to become flesh, passing over the change that lies in between.
english_sentence_B: Some things change into one another directly, others through other intermediate things.

lsj_entry_text: ἔνιοι, αι, α, some; never in Ep. , Lyr., or Att. Poets before Men. , exc. Ar. Pl. 867 (cf. however ἐνίοτε); first used in Ion. Prose, as Hdt. 1.120 , 8.56 , Hp. Praec. 6 ; πολλοὶ μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Lys. 25.19 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . ἔνιοι δὲ . . Pl. Tht. 151a , X. Mem. 4.2.38 ; ἔνιοι μὲν . . οἱ δὲ . . Pl. Mx. 238e ; ἔνιοί τινες Isoc. 15.258 : later in sg., οὐ πᾶσα κίνησις θερμαίνει, ἀλλ' ἐνία ψύχει Arist. Pr. 884b13 , cf. Thphr. Vert. 1 ; περὶ ψυχῆς ἐνίας θεωρῆσαι Arist. greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι καὶ τῶν εἰς ἄλληλα μεταβαλλόντων ἔνια μὲν ἑτοίμην τε καὶ διὰ ταχέων, ἔνια δὲ καὶ χαλεπὴν καὶ χρόνιον ﻿ [669] ἔχει τὴν ἀλλοίωσιν.
english_sentence_A: And indeed, among the things that change into one another, some have a ready and swift alteration, others a difficult and protracted [669] one.
english_sentence_B: And indeed, of the things that change into one another, some have a ready and quick alteration, others a difficult and protracted [669] one.

lsj_entry_text: ταχύς [υ], εῖα, ύ : of motion, swift, fleet, opp. βραδύς, of persons and animals, either abs., Il. 18.69 , etc.; or more fully, πόδας ταχύς 13.249 , 482 , 17.709 , etc.; ταχὺς ἔσκε θέειν Od. 17.308 ; θείειν τ. Il. 16.186 , Od. 3.112 ; κύνες, ἔλαφος, πτώξ, ἵππος, Il. 3.26 , 8.248 , 17.676 , 23.347 , etc.; οἰωνόν, ταχὺν ἄγγελον 24.292 , cf. Od. 15.526 ; τ. βαδιστής a quick walker, E. Med. 1182 ; σφοδροὶ καὶ τ. X. Cyr. 2.1.31 . of things, τ. πόδες Il. 6.514 , cf. Od. 13.261 , etc.; τ. ἰός, ὀϊστοί, Il. 4.94 , Od. 22.3 , etc.; πτερά Ar. Av. 1453 ; -ύτατα ἅρματα Pi. O. 1.77 ; νῆες, τριήρεις, Hdt. 8.23 , Th. 6.43 , etc.; [ ἴχνοσ] τὸ τοῦ ποδὸς μὲν βραδύ, τὸ τοῦ δὲ νοῦ ταχύ E. Ion 742 . of thought and purpose, quick, hasty, φρονεῖν γὰρ οἱ ταχεῖς οὐκ ἀσφαλεῖς S. OT 617 : c. inf., βλάπτειν τ. Ar. Ra. 1428 ; τ. βουλεῦσαί τι ἀνήκεστον Th. 1.132 , cf. 118 , Luc. Dem.Enc. 12 ; also τ. πρὸς ὀργήν Plu. Cat.Mi. 1 ; τὸ ταχύ speed, haste, E. Ph. 452 , X. Eq. 7.18 , etc. of actions, events, etc., rapid, sudden, πήδημα S. Aj. 833 ; ᾅδης, μόρος, E. Hipp. 1047 , Mosch. 3.26 ; πόλεμος Th. 4.55 , 6.45 ; φυγή Id. 4.44 ; μεταβολή Pl. R. 553d ; short, τ. ἐλπίδες fleeting hopes, Pi. P. 1.83 ; ἐπαυρέσεις Th. 2.53 ; ἀτραπός Ar. Ra. 127 ; ταχεῖ σὺν χρόνῳ S. OC 1602 ; τ. διήγησις short, rapid, Arist. Rh. 1416b30 . Adv., regul. ταχέως, quickly, opp. βραδέως, Il. 23.365 , Hes. Th. 103 , etc.:—rarely in sense perhaps (cf. τάχα 11 ), Plb. 16.25.8 . the Adv. is also expressed by periphr., διὰ ταχέων in haste, Th. 1.80 , 3.13 , Pl. Ap. 32d , X. An. 1.5.9 ; ἐκ ταχείας S. Tr. 395 ; cf. τάχος 11 . neut. ταχύ as Adv., Pi. P. 10.51 , N. 1.51 , S. Ph. 349 , E. HF 885 (lyr.), Ar. Eq. 109 , Gal. 16.665 , etc.; ἤδη ἤδη τ. τ. Sammelb. 4321.21 , BGU 956.3 (both iii A.D.); ἄρτι ἄρτι τ. τ. Arch.Pap. 5.393 (ii A.D.); also τάχα (q.v.). the Adj. ταχύς is freq. construed with Verbs, where we should use the Adv., ταχέες δ' ἱππῆες ἄγερθεν Il. 23.287 ; ταχεῖά γ' ἦλθε χρησμῶν πρᾶξις A. Pers. 739 ; ὁρμάσθω ταχύς S. Ph. 526 ; δεῦρ' ἀφίξεται τ. Id. OC 307 ; τ. χάρις διαρρεῖ Id. Aj. 1266 , cf. Th. 2.75 , 5.66 . Degrees of Comparison: Comp. : the form ταχύτερος, α, ον, is used by Hdt. , ἐποίησα ταχύτερα ἢ σοφώτερα 3.65 , cf. 7.194 ; also in Arist. Mu. 394b3 , Arr. Ind. 9.6 , Aret. SD 1.16 , but not in good Att. ; ταχύτερον as Adv., Hdt. 4.127 , 9.101 , Hp. Prog. 17 . the more usual form is θάσσων, neut. θᾶσσον, gen. ονος, Att. θάττων, neut. θᾶττον, Il. 15.570 , 13.819 (elsewh. only neut. in Hom. ), etc.:—neut. as Adv., freq. in Hom. , Od. 2.307 , al.; θᾶσσον ἂν . . κλύοιμι sooner, i.e. rather, would I hear, S. Ph. 631 ; θᾶσσον also often stands for the Positive, Il. 2.440 , Od. 15.201 , 16.130 , Pi. P. 4.181 , Ar. Nu. 506 , V. 187 , Ra. 94 ; οὐ θᾶσσον οἴσεις; i.e. make haste and bring, S. Tr. 1183 , cf. OT 430 ; θᾶττον νοήματος quicker than thought, X. Mem. 4.3.13 , cf. Ar. V. 824 , etc.; with a Conj., ὅτι θᾶσσον, like ὅτι τάχιστα , Theoc. 24.48 ; ἐπειδὴ θᾶττον συνεσκότασεν as soon as . . , D. 54.5 ; ἐπειδὰν θ. συνιῇ τις Pl. Prt. 325c ; ὅταν θ. φθέγγηται ὁ κόκκυξ Arist. HA 563b17 , cf. 611a5 ; ἐὰν or ἢν θ. as soon as . . , X. Cyr. 3.3.20 , An. 6.5.20 , Pl. Alc. 1.105a ; ἂν θ. Men. Pk. 174 ; εἰ θ. Pl. Ep. 324b ; ὡς θ. Plb. 1.66.1 , 3.82.1 ; θ. rarely = sooner than, before, ἐξήλαυνον μεσημβρίας οὐ πολλῷ τινι θ. Aristid. Or. 51 ( 27 ). 13 (cf. τάχιον infr. 3 ). the form ταχίων [ι], neut. ιον, is freq. in late Prose, as LXX Wi. 13.9 , 1 Ma. 2.40 , Ph. Bel. 69.14 , 17 , 73.23 , Gem. 1.20 , D.H. 6.42 , D.S. 20.6 , J. (v. infr.), Plu. 2.240d , Ev.Jo. 20.4 , Alciphr. 3.4 ; also in Hp. Mul. 1.1 , Men. 402.16 ; but condemned by Phryn. 58 , Hdn. Philet. p.436 P.; τὴν ταχίονα τῆς τροφῆς παράθεσιν earlier, sooner, Gal. 19.206 :—Adv. τάχιον earlier, πλέεται . . περὶ τὸν Σεπτέμβριον μῆνα . . , οὐδὲν δὲ κωλύει κἂν τ. Peripl.M.Rubr. 24 ; τ. τῆς ὑποσχέσεως sooner than they had promised, Rev.Ét.Gr. 6.159 (Iasus); τ. τοῦ παραγγέλματος J. BJ 4.4.2 ; εἰς μακρὸν αὐτῶν γῆρας καὶ βίου μῆκος ὅμοιον τοῖς τ. ἐπερχομένων Id. AJ 1.3.7 ; ἀποπαύεται οὔτε τ. ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα οὔτε βράδιον ἐτῶν πεντήκοντα Sor. 1.20 , cf. 48 , al.; formerly, ἐπεσκεύασαν τὸ παρόχιον, . . τ. γενόμενον γυμνάσιον IGRom. 3.639 (Lycia, ii A.D.), cf. 4.1517 (Sardis), 1632.14 (Philadelphia), 1665.5 (Tira), Keil-Premerstein Dritter Bericht p.79 (iii A.D.), Hermes 63.229 (Callatis); cf. supr. 2 fin. Sup. : the form ταχύτατος is rare, ταχύτατα ἅρματα Pi. O. 1.77 ; ταχύτατα as Adv., X. HG 5.1.27 codd., Antiph. 87 codd.; but both passages have been corrected. the usual form is τάχιστος, η, ον, used by Hom. only in neut. pl. τάχιστα as Adv., most quickly, most speedily, ὅττι τάχιστα as soon as may be, as soon as possible, Il. 4.193 , 9.659 , al.; ὅτι τάχιστα S. OT 1341 (lyr.), Th. 3.31 , etc.; so ὅσον τ. A. Ch. 772 , S. OT 1436 , etc.; ᾳ (prob.) τ. Pi. O. 13.79 ; ὅπως τ. A. Ag. 605 , S. OT 1410 , Ar. V. 167 ; ὡς τ. IG 12.76.23 , Hdt. 1.210 , Th. 4.15 , E. Rh. 147 , X. An. 1.3.14 : these are ellipt. phrases, as may be seen from the foll. examples, ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι τάχιστα Pl. Lg. 710b , X. Cyr. 5.4.3 ; ᾗ δυνατὸν τ. Id. HG 6.3.6 ; ὡς or ᾗ ἠδύνατο τ. Id. Cyr. 3.2.14 , An. 1.2.4 ; ὡς δύναιτο τ. Hdt. 1.79 ; ὡς or ᾗ ἂν δύνωμαι τ. X. HG 4.1.38 , Cyr. 7.1.9 , cf. IG 12.106.18 . τάχιστα after Particles of Time, as soon as, ἐπεὶ ( Ion. ἐπεί τε) τάχιστα A. Pr. 201 , Hdt. 1.27 , 75 , 7.163 , X. An. 7.2.6 , PCair.Zen. 34.12 (iii B.C.); ἐπειδὴ τ. Pl. Prt. 310d , Is. 9.3 , D. 27.16 , etc.; ἐπεὰν τ. Hdt. 4.134 , 7.129 , 8.144 ; ἐπὰν τ. X. An. 4.6.9 ; ἐπειδὰν τ. Id. Cyr. 1.3.14 , An. 3.1.9 ; ὅταν τ. Id. Cyr. 4.5.33 : also ὡς τ. separated by one or more words, ὡς ἡμέρη τ. ἐγεγόνεε Hdt. 1.11 , cf. 19 , 47 , 65 , al., X. Cyr. 1.3.2 , Mem. 1.2.16 , al.; ὡς δὲ τ. ἐξῆλθε . . κόρον ἔτεκε IG 42(1).121.4 (Epid., iv B.C.); ὡς γὰρ τ. εἰσῆλθον Men. Pk. 287 ; ὡς ἂν τ. λάβῃς τὴν ἐπιστολήν PCair.Zen. 241.1 (iii B.C.); but ὡς τ. γὰρ ἀπεδήμησας ib. 472.7 (iii B.C.); ὅπως τ. A. Pr. 230 :—the same notion is sometimes expressed by the part., ἀπαλλαγεὶς τάχιστα, = ὡς ἀπηλλάγη τ ., Plu. Dem. 8 , cf. 25 . freq. also in Prose, τὴν ταχίστην (in full, τὴν τ. ὁδόν X. An. 1.2.20 , Luc. Rh.Pr. 4 ) as Adv., by the quickest way, i.e. most quickly, Hdt. 1.24 , 73 , 81 , 86 , Hyp. Eux. 7 , Men. Pk. 75 , Plb. 1.33.4 , etc. (Cf. Lith. (dial.) deñgti, Lett. diêgt, both = 'run quickly', Polish dążyć 'hurry'.)

lsj_entry_text: βραδύς, εῖα, ύ: Comp. βραδύτερος Th. 4.8 ; metath. βαρδύτερος Theoc. 29.30 ; βραδίων Artem. 1.70 : Sup. βραδύτατος Ar. Fr. 357 , also βράδιστος (metath. βάρδιστος Il. 23.310 , 530 , Doroth(?).ap. Heph. Astr. 3.30 ) Aret. SD 1.6 , βραδίστατος Ael. Fr. 325 :—slow, κιχάνει τοι β. ὠκύν Od. 8.329 , etc.: c. inf., ἀλλά τοι ἵπποι βάρδιστοι θείειν slowest at running, Il. 23.310 ; β. λέγειν E. HF 237 , etc.; τὸ β. delay, Pl. Lg. 766e . Adv. βραδέως, χωρεῖν Th. 5.70 ; θεῖν Pl. Prt. 336a , etc.: Comp. -ύτερον Hp. Prog. 22 , Pl. Tht. 190a ; βραδυτέρως Aen.Tact. 16.12 ; βράδιον Hes. Op. 528 , Sor. 1.117 (condemned by Luc. Sol. 7 ): Sup. -ύτατα Pl. Ti. 39b . of the mind, dull, sluggish, ἐπιλήσμων καί β. Ar. Nu. 129 ; opp. ἀγχίνους, Pl. Phdr. 239a ; βράδιστοι τὴν γνώμην Aret.l.c.: c. inf., προνοῆσαι βραδεῖς Th. 3.38 ; τὸ β. καὶ μέλλον slowness and deliberation, Th. 1.84 . Adv. βραδέως, βουλεύεσθαι ib. 78 ; β. ὀλίγην ὀργὴν ποιεῖσθαι Pl. Phdr. 233c . in Egypt, of illiterates, βραδέως, βραδύτερον γράφειν, PTeb. 316.101 (i A. D.), PRyl. 173.13 (i A. D.); also βραδέα γράφουσα BGU 446.19 (ii A. D.). of Time, tardy, late, σὺν χρόνῳ β. μολών S. Tr. 395 , cf. Th. 7.43 ; βραδεῖαν . . ὁδὸν πέμπων S. Aj. 738 . Adv., ἕως βραδέως ἦν τῆς ἡμέρας D.L. 2.139 : neut. as Adv., ὀψὲ καὶ βραδὺ τῆς ἡλικίας Hld. 2.29 ; βράδιον ἀπογαλακτίζειν Sor. l.c.
greek_sentence: ὅσα μέν ἐστιν ἐγγὺς ταῖς ὁμοιότησι, ταχεῖαν ἔχει, ὅσα δὲ ποῤῥωτέρω, βραδυτέραν.
english_sentence_A: Those that are close in their similarities have a swift one, those that are further removed, a slower one.
english_sentence_B: Those that are near in their similarities have a quick alteration, those that are further off a slower one.

lsj_entry_text: ἀνομοιότης, ητος, ἡ, unlikeness, dissimilarity, Pl. Prm. 159e , Plt. 273d , Thphr. CP 1.2.2 , Hierocl. in CA 26p.481M. : in pl., Pl. Plt. 294 , Arist. Po. 1448a10 .
greek_sentence: ἐχρῆν οὖν, οἶμαι, γενέσθαι τι τοῖς ζώοις ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως ὄργανον ὁμοιότητος καὶ ἀνομοιότητος τῶν οὐσιῶν διακριτικὸν, ὃ διαγιγνῶσκον τὰς φύσεις τὸ μὲν οἰκεῖον αἱρήσεται, τὸ δ’ ἀλλότριον φεύξεται.
english_sentence_A: It was necessary, therefore, I think, that there come to be in animals, by the agency of nature, some organ capable of discriminating the similarity and dissimilarity of substances, which, by diagnosing their natures, will choose what is akin and shun what is alien.
english_sentence_B: It was necessary, therefore, I think, that some organ should be produced by nature for animals that discriminates the similarity and dissimilarity of substances, so that, recognising their natures, it would choose what is proper and flee what is alien.

lsj_entry_text: γλῶσσα, Ion. γλάσσα, Herod. 3.84 , al., SIG 1002.7 (Milet.), Schwyzer 692 (Chios), Att. γλῶττα, ης, ἡ, tongue, Od. 3.332 , etc. γ. λάρυγγος, = γλωττίς , larynx, Gal. UP 7.13 . tongue, as the organ of speech, γλώσσης χάριν through love of talking, Hes. Op. 709 , A. Ch. 266 ; γλώσσῃ ματαίᾳ Id. Pr. 331 , cf. Eu. 830 ; γλώσσης ἀκρατής Id. Pr. 884 (lyr.); μεγάλης γ. κόμποι S. Ant. 128 ; γλώσσῃ δεινός, θρασύς, Id. OC 806 , Aj. 1142 ; ἡ γ. ὀμώμοχ' ἡ δὲ φρὴν ἀνώμοτος E. Hipp. 612 : with Preps., ἀπὸ γλώσσης by frankness of speech, Thgn. 63 ; φθέγγεσθαι Pi. O. 6.13 (but ἀπὸ γ. ληίσσεται, opp. χερσὶ βίῃ, of fraud opp. violence, Hes. Op. 322 ); also, by word of mouth, Hdt. 1.123 , Th. 7.10 , Arr. An. 2.14.1 ; τῷ νῷ θ' ὁμοίως κἀπὸ τῆς γ. λέγω S. OC 936 ; τὰ γλώσσης ἄπο, i.e. our words, E. Ba. 1049 ; ἀπὸ γ. φράσω by heart, opp. γράμμασιν, Cratin. 122 ; οὐκ ἀπὸ γλώσσης not from mere word of mouth, but after full argument, A. Ag. 813 ; μὴ διὰ γλώσσης without using the tongue, E. Supp. 112 ; ἐν ὄμμασιν . . δεδορκὼς κοὐ κατὰ γλῶσσαν κλύων S. Tr. 747 :—phrases: πᾶσαν γλῶτταν βασάνιζε try every art of tongue, Ar. V. 547 ; πᾶσαν ἱέναι γλῶσσαν let loose one's whole tongue, speak withoutrestraint, S. El. 596 ; πολλὴν γ. ἐγχέας μάτην Id. Fr. 929 ; κακὰ γ. slander, Pi. P. 4.283 : pl., ἐν κερτομίοις γλώσσαις, i.e. with blasphemies, S. Ant. 962 (lyr.), cf. Aj. 199 (lyr.): βοῦς, κ ῇς ἐπὶ γλώσσῃ, v. βοῦς, κλείς . of persons, one who is all tongue, speaker, of Pericles, μεγίστη γ. τῶν Ἑλληνίδων Cratin. 293 , cf. Ar. Fr. 629 (s. v. l.). ἡ γ. τοῦ ταμιείου the advocacy of the fiscus, Philostr. VS 2.29 . language, ἄλλη δ' ἄλλων γ. μεμιγμένη Od. 19.175 , cf. Il. 2.804 ; γλῶσσαν ἱέναι speak a language or dialect, Hdt. 1.57 ; γ. Ἑλληνίδα, Δωρίδα ἱέναι, Id. 9.16 , Th. 3.112 , cf. A. Pers. 406 , Ch. 564 ; γλῶσσαν νομίζειν Hdt. 1.142 , 4.183 ; γλώσσῃ χρῆσθαι Id. 4.109 ; κατὰ τὴν ἀρχαίαν γ. Arist. Rh. 1357b10 ; dialect, ἡ Ἀττικὴ γ. Demetr. Eloc. 177 ; but also Δωρὶς διάλεκτος μία ὑφ' ἥν εἰσι γ. πολλαί Tryph. ap. Sch.D.T. p.320 H. obsolete or foreign word, which needs explanation, Arist. Rh. 1410b12 , Po. 1457b4 , Plu. 2.406f : hence Γλῶσσαι, title of works by Philemon and others. people speaking a distinct language, LX X. Ju. 3.8 (pl.), interpol. in Scyl. 15 . anything shaped like the tongue (cf. γλῶσσαι ὡσεὶ πυρός Act.Ap. 2.3 ). in Music, rced or tongue of a pipe, Aeschin. 3.229 , Arist. HA 565a24 , Thphr. HP 4.11.4 , etc. tongue or thong of leather, shoe-latchet, Pl.Com. 51 , Aeschin.Socr. 57 . tongue of land, App. Pun. 121 , cf. 95 . ingot, γ. χρυσῆ LXX Jo. 7.21 . marking on the liver, in divination, Hsch. (γλῶσσα from γλωχ-y[acaron], cf. γλώξ, γλωχίς; γλάσσα from Γλαχ-y[acaron], weak grade of same root.)
greek_sentence: τοῦτ’ οὖν ἐστιν ἡ γλῶττα, τῷ περιττῷ τῆς αἰσθήσεως οὐ ψυχρῶν μόνον, ἢ θερμῶν, ἢ ξηρῶν, ἢ ὑγρῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν οἰκείων τε καὶ οὐκ οἰκείων ἔχον διάγνωσιν.
english_sentence_A: This, then, is the tongue, which, through the surplus of its sensation, possesses a diagnosis not only of things cold, or hot, or dry, or moist, but also of things akin and not akin.
english_sentence_B: This, then, is the tongue: by the exceptional degree of its sensation it has discernment not only of cold or hot or dry or moist things, but also of things proper and not proper.

greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ πυροὶ καὶ κριθαὶ καὶ κύαμοι καὶ ἐρέβινθοι καὶ τἄλλα ὅσα τοιαῦτα, διὰ ὑγρότητα κατ’ ἀρχὰς ἐγγὺς ἀποίων ὄντα τὴν γεῦσιν, ἐν τῷ χρόνῳ πεπαινόμενά τε καὶ ξηραινόμενα γίνεται γλυκύτερα, γεώδους δὲ καὶ ξηρᾶς ἐν ἀχύροις καὶ χόρτῳ καὶ ἀγρώστει καὶ καλάμοις ξηροῖς καὶ ξύλοις, ὧν ἔνια πρὶν ἀποξηρανθῆναι γλυκέα τε ἡμῖν ἐστι καὶ τροφὴν τῷ σώματι δίδωσιν ἐνίοτε, οἷον ὅ τε τοῦ φοίνικος ἐγκέφαλος, οὕτω γὰρ ὀνομάζουσι τὸ ἀνώτατον μόριον αὐτοῦ, καὶ τῆς ἀγρώστεώς τε καὶ τῶν καλάμων αἱ μαλακαὶ ῥίζαι, καὶ μάλιστα τῶν κατ’ Αἴγυπτον, ἤδη δὲ καὶ τῶν πλείστων δένδρων αἱ βλάσται.
english_sentence_A: For wheat, barley, beans, chickpeas and all the others of this kind, being at the beginning, because of their moisture, nearly without quality in taste, become sweeter in time as they ripen and dry out; while an earthy and dry substance predominates in chaff, hay, dog's-tooth grass, dry reeds and wood, some of which, before they have been dried out, are sweet to us and sometimes give nourishment to the body, such as the 'brain' of the date-palm — for so they name its uppermost part — and the soft roots of dog's-tooth grass and of reeds, and especially of those in Egypt, and indeed also the shoots of most trees.
english_sentence_B: Earthy and dry substance predominates in chaff, hay, couch-grass, dry reeds and wood. Some of these, before they have dried out, are sweet to us and sometimes give nourishment to the body: for instance the 'brain' of the date-palm (for so they name its topmost part), the soft roots of couch-grass and of reeds, especially those in Egypt, and also the shoots of most trees.

english_sentence_A: And since there are many dissimilarities, it is necessary that in this matter the non-sweet qualities too be many; these it is impossible to explain in words, but it is possible to recall them to mind, since all men know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic [673] things is one, that from sour things another, and that from salty things different, that from bitter things different again.
english_sentence_B: And since the dissimilarities are many, it is necessary that in this case the qualities that are not sweet also come to be many. These it is impossible to express in words, but it is possible to call them to mind, since all human beings know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic things [673] is one thing and that from sour things another, and that the one from salty things is different again, and the one from bitter things different again.

greek_sentence: πολλῶν δ’ οὐσῶν ἀνομοιοτήτων πολλὰς ἀναγκαῖον ἐν τῷδε καὶ τὰς μὴ γλυκείας γίγνεσθαι ποιότητας, ἃς ἑρμηνεῦσαι μὲν ἀμήχανον, ἀναμνῆσαι δ’ ἐγχωρεῖ, πάντων ἀνθρώπων ἀκριβῶς εἰδότων, ἑτέραν μὲν τὴν ἐκ τῶν στρυφνῶν [673] αἴσθησίν τε καὶ διάθεσιν ἐν τῇ γλώττῃ γιγνομένην, ἑτέραν δὲ τὴν ἐκ τῶν ὀξέων, καὶ ἄλλην μὲν τὴν ἐκ τῶν ἁλμυρῶν, ἄλλην δὲ τὴν ἐκ τῶν πικρῶν.
english_sentence_A: And since there are many dissimilarities, it is necessary that in this matter the non-sweet qualities too be many; these it is impossible to explain in words, but it is possible to recall them to mind, since all men know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic [673] things is one, that from sour things another, and that from salty things different, that from bitter things different again.
english_sentence_B: And since the dissimilarities are many, it is necessary that in this case the qualities that are not sweet also come to be many. These it is impossible to express in words, but it is possible to call them to mind, since all human beings know precisely that the sensation and condition arising in the tongue from acerbic things [673] is one thing and that from sour things another, and that the one from salty things is different again, and the one from bitter things different again.

greek_sentence: Ὥσπερ οὖν ὅσα τῶν ἐδεσμάτων ὁμοιότατα ταῖς τῶν τρεφομένων ὑπάρχει φύσεσιν, γλυκύτητά τ’ ἐμφαίνεται καὶ σκευασίας οὐδεμιᾶς προσδεῖται, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον ὅσα ποῤῥώτερα τὴν κρᾶσίν ἐστιν τὰ μὲν ἡδυσμάτων, τὰ δὲ καὶ συναμφοτέρων προσδεῖται, καὶ οὐδέν γε θαυμαστὸν αὐτῶν τῶν ἡδυσμάτων μηδὲν ἐδώδιμον ὑπάρχον εἰς ἡδονὴν συντελεῖν τῷ δι’ ἑαυτοῦ σκευασθέντι.
english_sentence_A: Just as, then, those foods which are most similar to the natures of the things being nourished display sweetness and require no preparation, in the same way those which are further removed in their mixture require, some of them, seasonings, and others both together; and it is indeed no wonder that, although none of the seasonings themselves is edible, it contributes to the pleasure of what has been prepared by means of it.
english_sentence_B: Just as, then, those foods that are most similar to the natures of the things being nourished both display sweetness and need no preparation besides, in the same way those that are further removed in their mixture need, some of them, seasonings, and others both together. And it is not at all surprising that the seasonings themselves, although none of them is edible, contribute to the pleasantness of what has been prepared by means of them.

greek_sentence: δυοῖν γὰρ ἀμέτροιν συνελθόντοιν ἐγχωρεῖ τὸ μικτὸν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν σύμμετρον ἀποτελεσθῆναι καὶ διὰ τοῦτο γλυκὺ φανῆναι, τῶν ἀμέτρων οὐκ ὄντων τοιούτων.
english_sentence_A: For when two immoderate things come together it is possible for the mixture from both to be rendered well-proportioned and for this reason to appear sweet, though the immoderate things are not themselves such.

greek_sentence: τὸ δ’ ὀῤῥῶδες περίττωμα ψυχρόν τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ὑγρὸν, ὥστε τὸ μὲν σύμπαν γάλα τοῦ συμμέτρου τῇ θερμότητι σώματος ἀπολείπεσθαι συχνῷ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο εἰς ὀξύτητα μεταβάλλει ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ μᾶλλον ἢ πικρότητα.
english_sentence_A: But of these the oily one is especially well-tempered, and the thick one falls a little short of it; whereas the whey-like residue is cold and moist, so that milk as a whole falls considerably short of the body that is moderate in heat, and for this reason it changes from itself into sourness rather than bitterness.
english_sentence_B: The whey-like residue is cold and moist, so that milk taken as a whole falls considerably short of a body moderate in heat, and for this reason it changes of itself into sourness rather than into bitterness.

english_sentence_B: For what is extremely sweet, and for this reason no longer admits any addition of sweetness, must change into the next quality in order; but to what is deficient, completion accrues from concoction.

lsj_entry_text: ὀξύς, εῖα, ύ, Ion. fem. ὀξέα Hdt. 9.23 , al., v.l. in Hp. Mul. 1.64 , al. (in codd. freq. ὀξέη, and so Babr. 73.1 metri gr.) : ὀξεῖα, poet. for neut. pl. ὀξέα, Hes. Sc. 348 :—sharp, keen, whether of a point or an edge, in Hom. and Hes. mostly of weapons or anything made of metal, ἄκων Il. 10.335 , al.; ἄορ 21.173 , Hes. Sc. 457 ; βέλος Il. 4.185 , etc.; also of non-metallic substances, λᾶας 16.739 ; μοχλός Od. 9.382 ; σκόλοπες Il. 12.56 , 64 ; ὀξεῖα κορυφή, of a mountain-peak, Od. 12.74 ; so πάγοι ὀξέες 5.411 ; λίθος ὀξὺς πεποιημένος sharpened so as to serve as a knife, Hdt. 7.69 , cf. 3.8 ; κυρβασίας ἐς ὀξὺ ἀπηγμένας brought to a point, Id. 7.64 ; ὄρεα ἐς ὀ. τὰς κορυφὰς ἀ. Id. 2.28 ; τὸ ὀ. the apex of a triangle, ib. 16 ; of the heart, Arist. Resp. 478b5 ; τὸ ὀ. τοῦ ᾠοῦ Id. GA 752b8 ; ὀ. γωνία an acute angle, Id. Top. 107a16 , al., Euc. 1 Def. 12 , Archim. Spir. 16 ; Χρόνος ὀξὺς ὀδόντας Simon. 176 ; ἡ ὀξεῖα, name of a surgical instrument, Hermes 38.282 , Heliod. ap. Orib. 44.23.59 ; but also, a pointed splinter of bone, ib. 46.20.5 . in reference to the senses, of feeling, sharp, keen, ὀδύναι Il. 11.268 ; ὀ. ἠέλιος the piercing sun, h.Ap. 374 ; ὀξειᾶν ἀκτίνων πατήρ, i.e. the Sun, Pi. O. 7.70 ; Σείριος ὀξὺς ἐλλάμπων Archil. 61 ; πῦρ ὀ. Anaxipp. 1.12 ; so χιὼν ὀξεῖα Pi. P. 1.20 ; so also of grief and the like , ἄχος Il. 19.125 ; μελεδῶναι Od. 19.517 : and generally, sharp, severe, μάχη ὀξέα . . γίνεται keenly contested, Hdt. 9.23 ; ὀ. πυρετός Hp. VM 16 ( Sup. ); [ἡ νόσοσ] ὀξεῖα φοιτᾷ καὶ ταχεῖ' ἀπέρχεται S. Ph. 808 ; νόσοι, μανίαι, Pi. O. 8.85 , N. 11.48 ( Comp. ), cf. Hp. Acut. tit., Archig. ap. Gal. 9.887 ; πάθαι Pi. P. 3.97 ; ἐπιμομφά Id. O. 10(11).9 , etc. of the sight, ὀξύτατον ὄμμα Id. N. 10.62 ; ὄψις . . ὀξυτάτη τῶν διὰ τοῦ σώματος . . αἰσθήσεων Pl. Phdr. 250d : freq. in neut. as Adv., ὀξύτατον δέρκεσθαι to be keenest of sight, Il. 17.675 ; ὀξύτατα καθορᾶν Pl. R. 516c ; so ὀξὺ νοεῖν notice a thing sharply, Il. 3.374 ; ὀξὺ προϊδεῖν Od. 5.393 ; ὀξύτερον βλέπει Ar. Pl. 1048 , Lys. 1202 (lyr.) : prov., ὀξύτερον τοῦ Λυγκέως βλέπειν Id. Pl. 210 , cf. Macar. Prov. 6.41 ; also ὀξὺ ἄκουσεν heard with sharp ear, Il. 17.256 , cf. Pl. Lg. 927b ; ὀξεῖαν ἀκοὴν . . λόγοις διδούς keen attention, S. El. 30 . of things that affect the sight, dazzling, bright, αὐγὴ Ἠελίου Il. 17.372 ; [Ἠελίου] ὀξύτατον πέλεται φάος εἰσοράασθαι 14.345 : hence of colours, Ar. Pax 1173 (v. φοινικίς 2 ) ; αἱ ὀξεῖαι χροιαί Arist. Phgn. 806b4 ; πορφύρα Plu. Cat.Mi. 6 , PHolm. 20.36 ; [ἐσθὴσ] ὀξυτέρα καὶ τηλαυγεστέρα Ael. NA 4.46 . of sound, shrill, piercing, ἀϋτή Il. 15.313 ; ὀξὺ βοήσας 17.89 ; ὀξὺ δὲ κωκύσασα 18.71 ; ὀξὺ λεληκώς 22.141 ; ὀξέα κεκληγώς 17.88 , etc.; of whinnying horses, ὀξεῖα χρέμισαν Hes. Sc. 348 ; of young pigs, ὀξὺ κεκράγατε Ar. Ach. 804 ; of the scream of birds of prey, ὀξέα κλάζων S. Ant. 112 (anap.) ; of metals, ἰάχεσκε σάκος ὀξέα καὶ λιγέως Hes. Sc. 233 ; also of the wail of the nightingale (cf. ὀξύφωνος), ὄρνιθος ὀ. φθόγγον S. Ant. 424 ; so ἐπηλάλαξαν τὸν ὀ. νόμον shrieked their shrill song, A. Th. 952 (lyr.) ; ὀξὺ μέλος, of the grasshopper, Ar. Av. 1095 (lyr.). of musical tones, in a technical sense, high-pitched, opp. βαρύς, φθόγγοι Pl. Ti. 80a , X. Cyn. 6.20 ; ὀξυτάτη χορδή Pl. Phdr. 268d ; φωνὴ ὀξεῖα, βαρεῖα, μέση Arist. Rh. 1403b29 ; τῷ ὀξεῖ ἐν φωνῇ μὲν ἐναντίον τὸ βαρύ, ἐν ὄγκῳ δὲ τὸ ἀμβλύ Id. Top. 106a13 . in Music, δι' ὀξειῶν ( Dor. -ᾶν) interval of a fifth, Philol. 6 , Arist. Pr. 920a24 . ἡ ὀξεῖα (sc. προσῳδία) the acute accent, D.T. 630.1 , A.D. Ach. 193 . metaph., of the inner sense, sharp, keen, hasty, esp. quick to anger, passionate, epith. of Ares, Il. 2.440 ,al. ; μένος ὀξύ h.Hom. 8.14 ; καρδίη ὀξυτέρη Thgn. 366 ; θυμὸς ὀ. S. OC 1193 ; νέος καὶ ὀ. Pl. Grg. 463e ; οἱ ἀκρόχολοι ὀξεῖς Arist. EN 1126a18 : so in ὀξύ-θυμος, -κάρδιος, -χολος. sharp, quick, δεινοὶ καὶ ὀξεῖς Pl. Ap. 39b : c. inf., ἐπινοῆσαι ὀ. Th. 1.70 ; γνῶναι . . ὀξύτατοι τὰ ῥηθέντα D. 3.15 ; also εἰς πάντα τὰ μαθήματα ὀξεῖς Pl. R. 526b ; τὰς ἐνθυμήσεις ὀξύς Luc. Salt. 81 . of motion, quick, swift, post- Hom. , ὀξυτάτους ἵππους Hdt. 5.9 ( v.l. ὠκυτάτους ) ; ἱερακίσκος Ar. Av. 1112 ; ὀξυτέρῳ χαλινῷ S. Ant. 108 (lyr.) ; of a report, ὀξεῖα βάξις διῆλθ' Ἀχαιούς Id. Aj. 998 ; ὀξεῖαν ἐκβάλλει ῥοήν, of a dying man, Id. Ant. 1238 , cf. A. Ag. 1389 ; of a flame, fierce, Thphr. HP 5.9.3 ; ᾄξας ὀξὺς νότος ὥς S. Aj. 258 (anap.) ; τὸ εὔψυχον . . ὀξεῖς ἐνδείκνυνται are quick in displaying, Th. 4.126 ; opp. βραδύς, Id. 8.96 ; opp. ῥάθυμος, Arist. EE 1240a2 ; opp. ἡσύχιος, Id. EN 1116a9 ; ὀ. παράγγελμα Onos. 10.2 ; ὀ. καιρός an urgent crisis, Id. 6.1 , al.; ὁ ὀ. δρόμος the express post, POxy. 900.7 (iv A. D.), 2115.6 (iv A. D.) ; ὀξεῖς οἱ πόδες αὐτῶν ἐκχέαι αἷμα Ep.Rom. 3.15 : esp. in Adv. (v. infr.). regul. Adv. ὀξέως quickly, soon, βοηθεῖν, μεταχειρίσαι, Th. 6.10 , 12 , etc.; sharply, ὁρᾶν, αἰσθάνεσθαι, Pl. R. 567b , Phdr. 263c ; poet. ὀξείως Epigr.Gr. 986.3 (Philae) : Comp. ὀξυτέρως Hp. Epid. 3.17 .β' ; ὀξυτέρως ἀποθῄνσκειν ib. 1.2 ; but, neut. ὀξύ and pl. ὀξέα as Adv., v. supr. 11.2 , 3 : Comp. ὀξύτερον Th. 2.8 , Pl. Tht. 190a : Sup. ὀξύτατον Il. 17.675 , Pl. Lg. 741d ; or ὀξύτατα Id. R. 401e , al. (Cf. ὀξίνα, ὄκρις.)

english_sentence_B: And so this biting is common to three flavours, the sour, the bitter and the pungent; but it belongs to the sour as being at once cold and fine-particled (for this was shown earlier), and to the bitter and the pungent as being hot.

english_sentence_A: But concerning the one properly called pungent there is, to begin with, no need even of demonstration.
english_sentence_B: But concerning what is properly called pungent there is no need of demonstration at all.

greek_sentence: φθάνει μὲν γὰρ ἡ ἐκ τῆς αἰσθήσεως ἐνέργεια τὴν ἐκ τοῦ λόγου πίστιν, ὥστ’ οὐδ’ ἠμφισβήτησεν οὐδεὶς ὑπὲρ αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ καὶ Πλάτων ὡς περὶ θερμοτάτου πάντων ἀποφαίνεται καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης καὶ Θεόφραστος καὶ τῶν ἰατρῶν οὐδείς ἐστιν οὔτε τῶν παλαιῶν οὔτε τῶν νεωτέρων, ὃς ἕτερόν τι γιγνώσκει.
english_sentence_A: For the activity that comes from sense-perception anticipates the conviction that comes from reasoning, so that no one has even disputed about it; rather Plato declares it to be the hottest of all, as do Aristotle and Theophrastus, and there is no physician, either among the ancients or among the more recent, who holds any other view.
english_sentence_B: For the evidence (ἐνέργεια, perhaps for ἐνάργεια) that comes from sense-perception anticipates the conviction that comes from reason, so that no one has ever disputed about it. Rather, Plato declares it to be the hottest of all, and so do Aristotle and Theophrastus, and there is no one among the physicians, either of the ancients or of the more recent, who holds any other view.

greek_sentence: κατὰ γὰρ τὸν τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ λόγον ἐστὶ τὸ θερμαί νειν, ὥστ’ εἰ καὶ τῶν ἰδιωτῶν ὁντιναοῦν ἔροιο, τί καλεῖ δριμὺ [680] βρῶμα, φαίη ἂν, οἶμαι, τὸ θερμαῖνον ἰσχυρῶς ἐν τῷ γεύεσθαι, καθάπερ τὸ πέπερι καὶ τὸ πύρεθρον καὶ τὸ κάρδαμον καὶ τὰ σκόροδα καὶ τὰ κρόμμυα καὶ πάνθ’ ὅσα τοιαῦτα.
english_sentence_A: For heating belongs to it according to the very account of its substance, so that even if you were to ask any layman whatsoever what he calls a pungent [680] food, he would say, I think, that which heats strongly in being tasted, such as pepper and pellitory and cress and garlic and onions and all things of this sort.
english_sentence_B: For heating belongs to it by the very account of its substance, so that if you were to ask any layman whatsoever what he calls a pungent [680] food, he would say, I think, that it is what heats strongly in the tasting, as pepper does, and pellitory, cress, garlic, onions and all things of this kind.

greek_sentence: ὄντος γὰρ καὶ τοῦ πικροῦ χυμοῦ καὶ τοῦ ὀξέος δριμέων ἀμφοῖν, ἐν ᾧπερ ἂν σώματι σφοδρὰν εὑρίσκομεν τὴν δριμύτητα, κᾂν μήτε πικρὸν ᾖ κᾂν μήτε ὀξὺ, δριμὺ προσαγορεύειν εἰθίσμεθα, καίτοι πολλῶν ὄντων κατ’ εἶδος τῶν τοιούτων σωμάτων.
english_sentence_A: For although both the bitter flavour and the sour are pungent, both of them, in whatever body we find the pungency to be vehement, even if it is neither bitter nor sour, we are accustomed to call it pungent, although such bodies are many in species.
english_sentence_B: For although the bitter flavour and the sour are both pungent, in whatever body we find the pungency to be intense, even if it is neither bitter nor sour, we are accustomed to call it pungent, and this although such bodies are many in species.

english_sentence_A: It is yellowish in colour, and as heavy in smell as [682] that of hemlock, except insofar as it also gives off a slight fragrance of a somewhat aromatic kind.
english_sentence_B: It is yellowish in colour, and as heavy in smell as [682] hemlock, except insofar as it gives off a slight, aromatic sort of fragrance.

english_sentence_A: All the pungent flavours, however—for it was about these that the discussion was—one must recognise as being hot in the highest degree; next after them the bitter ones, and then after these the sweet.
english_sentence_B: All pungent flavours, for it was about these that the discussion was, one must recognise as being extremely hot; next after them come the bitter, and then, next after these, the sweet.

greek_sentence: ἐν ἅπασι δ’ αὐτοῖς ἱκανοῦ τοῦ πλάτοις ὑπάρχοντος, ὁ μὲν μᾶλλον δριμὺς καὶ πικρὸς καὶ γλυκὺς μᾶλλον δηλονότι καὶ θερμός ἐστιν, ὁ δ’ ἧττον εἰς τοσοῦτον ἀπολείπεται θερμότητος, εἰς ὅσον καὶ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς κατὰ τὴν γεῦσιν ποιότητος.
english_sentence_A: And since in all of them there is a considerable latitude, the one that is more pungent and bitter and sweet is obviously also hotter, while the one that is less so falls short in heat by just as much as it also falls short of the exact quality in respect of taste.
english_sentence_B: And since in all of them there is a considerable range, the one that is more pungent, or bitter, or sweet is evidently also more hot, while the one that is less so falls short of heat to the same degree as it falls short of the exact quality in taste.

greek_sentence: ὅρος δὲ τοῦ μὲν πικροῦ χυμοῦ τὸ ῥύπτειν ἐστὶν, τοῦ δὲ δριμέος τὸ καίειν, τοῦ δὲ γλυκέος τὸ τρέφειν, ὅταν γε τελέως ἔχωσι κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστον φύσιν, τουτέστιν ὅταν ὡς οἶόν τε μάλιστα ὑπάρχωσιν ἑτέραις ποιότησιν ἄμικτοι, οἷον ὁ πικρὸς ἔστι μὲν πάντως θερμὸς, ἀλλ’ ὁ μὲν ἄρτι γενόμενος ἐκ τῆς τοῦ γλυκέος μεταβολῆς ἧττόν τε πικρός ἐστι καὶ ἧττον θερμὸς, ὁ δὲ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον ἐξηλλαγμένος ἐσχάτως τε πικρός [683] ἐστι καὶ ἤδη πλησίον ἥκει τοῦ δριμέος, ὡς μὴ ῥύπτειν ἔτι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ διαβιβρώσκειν καὶ δάκνειν, οἷον ἀριστολοχία μὲν καὶ ἴρις καὶ πάναξ αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον, ἀποῤῥύπτουσί τε καὶ καθαροποιοῦσι τὰ ἕλκη.
english_sentence_A: The defining mark of the bitter juice is cleansing, of the pungent burning, and of the sweet nourishing, at least when each of them is complete according to its own nature, that is, when they are, as far as is at all possible, unmixed with other qualities. For instance, the bitter is in every case hot; but the one that has just come into being from the transformation of the sweet is both less bitter and less hot, whereas the one that has been altered to the greatest extent is extremely bitter [683] and has already come close to the pungent, so that it no longer only cleanses but also erodes and bites.
english_sentence_B: The defining mark of the bitter flavour is to cleanse, of the pungent to burn, of the sweet to nourish, at least when each of them is in a perfect state according to its own nature, that is, when they are as far as possible unmixed with other qualities. lsj_entry_text: δια-βρωτικός, ή, όν, corrosive, Alex.Aphr. Pr. 1.99 , Gal. 1.280 ( Sup. ).
greek_sentence: καὶ πρῶτον μὲν θερμοὺς ἀκριβῶς αὐτοὺς εἴπωμεν, εἶτα διαβρωτικούς τε καὶ καυστικοὺς καὶ ἐσχαρωτικοὺς καὶ συντηκτικούς· ἐπὶ μὲν τοῦ δέρματος ἐπιτιθεμένους ἅπαντας τοὺς τοιούτους εἶναι, εἴσω δὲ τοῦ σώματος λαμβανομένους, ὅσοι μὲν ὅλαις ταῖς οὐσίαις ἐναντιώτατα διάκεινται πρός τινα ζῶα, σηπτικούς τε πάντας εἶναι καὶ δηλητηρίους ἐκείνων τῶν ζώων.
english_sentence_A: And first let us say that they are precisely hot, then corrosive and caustic and eschar-producing and colliquative; that all such are of this kind when applied to the skin, but when taken inside the body, all those which in their whole substances are disposed most opposite to certain animals are putrefying and deleterious to those animals; but those which are so only in respect of the excess of their heat, if they are coarse-particled and earthy, are ulcerating to the internal parts, but if fine-particled, diuretic and sudorific, and, simply put, cutting and dispersing.

english_sentence_A: For they are of a nature to differ from these not only by strong heat, but also in that the bitter ones are all not only hot but also dry in their power—as one might most clearly liken them, closely resembling ash—whereas in the pungent ones, those at least which are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and for this very reason we eat not a few of such bodies.
english_sentence_B: For not only are they by nature such as to differ from them in strong heat, but also in this: all the bitter are not only hot but also dry in power, as one might most clearly compare them, like ash; whereas in the pungent, at least those that are not bitter, much moisture is sometimes mixed in, and it is for this reason that we eat not a few bodies of this kind.

greek_sentence: εὐθὺς δὲ ταῦτα καὶ τῇ συστάσει μὲν ξηρότερα φαίνεται, καὶ τῷ δαπανᾶσθαι δ’ ἀεὶ καὶ ἀποῤῥεῖν αὐτῶν τὸ ὑγρὸν, ἐξατμιζόμενον ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τὸ καταλειπόμενον ἀποδείκνυσθαι γεωδέστερόν τε καὶ ξηρότερον.
english_sentence_A: And straightaway these appear drier in their consistency, and, because their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, vaporised by the heat, it is necessary that what is left behind be rendered more earthy and drier.
english_sentence_B: And these at once appear drier in their consistency as well; and since their moisture is continually being consumed and flowing away, evaporated by the heat, what is left must necessarily turn out more earthy and drier.

lsj_entry_text: ἥσσων, ἧσσον, gen. ονος; Att. ἥττων, Ion. ἥσσων (not ἕσσων) Hdt. (v. infr.), Democr. 50 , Hp. VC 2 : formed from ἦκα (prop. ἠσσ-, cf. ἤκιστος), but in sense Comp. of κακός, μικρός: c. gen. pers., inferior; esp. in force, weaker, αἴθ' ὅσον ἥ. εἰμὶ τόσον σέο φέρτερος εἴην Il. 16.722 ; of horses, 23.322 , al.; ῥώμῃ ἥσσονες τῶν Περσέων Hdt. 8 113 , cf. 9.62 ; γυναικῶν ἥσσονες S. Ant. 680 ; Κύπριδος E. Andr. 631 ; ἔς τι in a thing, Hdt. 3.102 : c. inf. modi, ἥσς. τινὸς θέειν not so good at running, ib. 105 ; οὐδενὸς ἥσς. γνῶναι second to none in judging, Th. 2.60 ; ἱππεύειν ἥττ. τῶν ἡλίκων inferior to them in riding, X. Cyr. 1.3.15 . abs., οἱ ἥσς. the weaker party, A. Supp. 203 , 489 ; οὐχ ἥσσους γενέσθαι to have the best of it, Th. 4.72 ; τὸ λαμβάνειν τὰ τῶν ἡττ. X. An. 5.6.32 : c. dat. modi, ἥσσονες ναυμαχίῃ Hdt. 5.86 : c. acc. modi, τὸν νοῦν ἥσς. S. El. 1023 , cf. X. Cyr. 1.4.4 ; of things, τὸν ἥττω λόγον κρείττω ποιεῖν 'to make the worse appear the better cause', Pl. Ap. 18b , cf. Ar. Supp. 379 (lyr.). less, fewer, ἵνα πλείω μὲν ἀκούωμεν, ἥττονα δὲ λέγωμεν Zeno Stoic. 1.68 . c. gen. rei, giving way or yielding to a thing, a slave to . . , τοῦ τῆσδ' ἔρωτος εἰς ἅπανθ' ἥσς. S. Tr. 489 ; τῶν αἰσχρῶν Id. Ant. 747 ; ὀργῆς Id. Fr. 929 ; γάμων E. IA 1354 ; κέρδους Ar. Pl. 363 ; ἡδονῶν Pl. Prt. 353c ; γαστρὸς ἢ οἴνου ἢ ἀφροδισίων ἢ πόνου ἢ ὕπνου X. Eq.Mag. 1.3 , 2.78 . neut. ἧσσον, ἧττον, as Adv., less, ὀλίγον δέ τί μ' ἧσς. ἐτίμα Od. 15.365 , cf. E. Hipp. 264 (anap.); ἧσσόν τι Th. 3.75 ; ἧσς. ἑτέρων Id. 1.84 ; ὁμοίως τε τρωθεὶς καὶ ἧσς. Hp.l.c.: mostly with Verbs, but also with Adjs., ἀριστοκρατίαι . . αἱ μὲν ἧττ., αἱ δὲ μᾶλλον μόνιμοι Arist. Pol. 1307a14 , cf. Mete. 340b8 : with a Comp. , ἧττ. ἀκριβέστερον Id. greek_sentence: αὐτὸ μὲν γὰρ τὸ γλυκὺ πρὸς τῷ θερμὸν ὑπάρχειν ἢ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττον, ἐξ ἀνάγκης δήπου καὶ ὑγρὸν ἢ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττόν ἐστιν.
english_sentence_A: For the sweet itself, in addition to being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is surely of necessity also moist to a greater or lesser degree.
english_sentence_B: For the sweet itself, besides being hot to a greater or lesser degree, is of necessity, surely, also moist to a greater or lesser degree.

greek_sentence: εἰ δέ γε τῇ τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν φύσει μάλιστα οἰκεῖον ὑπάρχει, αὕτη δ’ ἦν εὔκρατος, ὑγρὰ καὶ θερμὴ, τὸ δ’ οἷον ὑπεροπτηθέντος τούτου γιγνόμενον ὅμοιον τιτάνῳ καὶ τέφρᾳ, ξηρὸν καὶ θερμὸν ἐξ ἀνάγκης ἀποτελεῖται.
english_sentence_A: And if indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this was well-tempered, moist and hot, then that which comes to be, as it were, when this has been over-roasted, being like lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot.
english_sentence_B: If indeed it is most akin to the nature of our body, and this nature was well-tempered, moist and hot, then what comes into being when the sweet is, as it were, over-roasted, being similar to lime and ash, is of necessity rendered dry and hot.

greek_sentence: καὶ μέντοι καὶ δι’ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ῥύπτειν τε πέφυκε καὶ καταθραύειν καὶ τέμνειν τοὺς γλίσχρους καὶ παχεῖς χυμοὺς, ὥσπερ ἡ τέφρα καὶ τὸ νίτρον.
english_sentence_A: And indeed for this very reason it is of a nature to cleanse and to break up and to cut the viscous and thick humours, just like ash and nitre.
english_sentence_B: And indeed for this very reason it is by nature cleansing, and apt to break up and cut viscous and thick humours, as ash and nitre are.

lsj_entry_text: ἀερώδης, ες, like air, of the soul, Epicur. Fr. 314 ; Astrol., of signs, connected with the air, Vett.Val. 7.26 ; light of texture, Sch. E. Or. 1431 . = ἀέρινος 2 , τὴν χρόαν Dsc. 5.152 (dub.). τὸ ἀ. the airy nature, Placit. 2.11.2 , al., cf. Arist. Mu. 395a20 . full of air, Id. PA 669b2 .
greek_sentence: οὐδὲ γὰρ ἀερώδης αὐτῶν ἐστιν οὐδὲ λεπτομερὴς, ἀλλὰ οὐδὲ ὑδατώδης ἡ σύστασις, ἀλλ’ ὥσπερ καὶ μικρῷ πρόσθεν εἴρηται, γεωδεστέρα, κατειργασμένη ἀκριβῶς ὑπὸ τοῦ θερμοῦ καὶ οἷον ὑπερωπτημένης αὐτῶν τῆς οὐσίας.
english_sentence_A: For their consistency is neither airy nor fine-particled, nor indeed watery, but, as was also said a little earlier, more earthy, thoroughly worked over by the heat, their substance being, as it were, over-roasted.
english_sentence_B: For their consistency is neither airy nor fine-particled, nor yet watery, but, as was said a little before, more earthy, thoroughly worked up by the heat, their substance having been, as it were, over-roasted.

lsj_entry_text: δριμύς, εῖα, ύ, piercing, sharp, keen, βέλος Il. 11.270 : metaph., δριμεῖα μάχη 15.696 , Hes. Sc. 261 ; δ. χόλος Il. 18.322 ; μένος Od. 24.319 ; ἄχος Hes. Sc. 457 ; θυμός A. SE 182b37 (but λέξις and λόγος δ. of striking turns of phrase, Hermog. Id. 1.2 , 2.5 ): neut. as Adv., δριμὺ βλέπειν look bitter, Ar. Ra. 562 ; but also to look sharply, keenly, Pl. R. 519a , Luc. Symp. 16 ; ἐνορᾶν Id. Cat. 3 , Ael. VH 14.22 , D.C. 59.26 :—regul. Adv. δριμέως, Anaxandr. 15.3 ; ἐρασθῆναι Ael. NA 7.15 ; δριμύτατα ἀλγεῖν Id. VH 12.1 .
greek_sentence: ὡς μὲν οὖν τοῖς στύφουσι [687] παραβαλεῖν, εἴη ἂν οὐκ ὀλίγῳ τινὶ λεπτομερέστερα τὰ πικρὰ τῶν φαρμάκων, ὡς δὲ τοῖς δριμέσι, παχυμερέστερα καὶ διὰ τοῦτ’ οὔτε διεξέρχεται ῥᾳδίως τῶν γλίσχρων τε καὶ παχέων χυμῶν, ὥσπερ ὅσα λεπτομερέστερα ταῖς οὐσίαις ἐστὶν, οὔτ’ ἀδυνατεῖ τέμνειν ὁμοίως τοῖς παχυμερέσιν.
english_sentence_A: As compared, then, with the astringent things, [687] the bitter drugs would be not a little more fine-particled; but as compared with the pungent ones, more coarse-particled; and for this reason they neither pass easily through the viscous and thick humours, as do all those things that are more fine-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut, like the coarse-particled ones.
english_sentence_B: So, compared with astringent drugs, bitter drugs would be finer-particled by no small amount, but compared with pungent ones, [687] more coarse-particled. For this reason they neither pass easily through viscous and thick humours, as do the things that are finer-particled in their substances, nor are they unable to cut them, as the coarse-particled ones are.

english_sentence_A: For now it suffices to know at least this much, that the bitter quality as a whole belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and in addition to these, moreover, fine-particled and earthy.
english_sentence_B: For now it is enough to know this much at least: every bitter quality belongs to substances that are at once hot and dry, and, in addition to these, fine-particled and earthy.

greek_sentence: καὶ γὰρ ἂν μάχεσθαι δόξειεν οὕτω γε τῷ γεώδει τὸ λεπτομερὲς, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ἁπλῶς λεπτομερὲς, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἐν γεώδει συστάσει τοιοῦτο εἶναί φημι τὸ πικρὸν, οἷον τίτανος καὶ τέφρα καὶ πᾶν ὅ τι περ ἂν ἀκριβῶς κατοπτηθῇ, καὶ γένηται σποδιὰ, μᾶλλον δ’ ἂν ἴσως ἀληθέστερον εἰκάζοιτο λιγνύϊ τινὶ καὶ αἰθάλῃ [688] φλογὸς, ἣ καὶ γευομένοις πικρὰ φαίνεται.
english_sentence_A: For in that way the fine-particled would seem to be in conflict with the earthy; but I say that the bitter is not fine-particled simply, but is such as it is within an earthy constitution, like lime and ash and everything whatever that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinder-ash; or rather, perhaps, it might more truly be likened to a kind of smoky vapour and soot [688] of flame, which also appears bitter to those who taste it.
english_sentence_B: For taken in that way the fine-particled would seem to conflict with the earthy. But I say that the bitter is not simply fine-particled; rather, it is fine-particled as in an earthy consistency, such as lime and ash and everything that has been thoroughly roasted and has become cinders.

greek_sentence: τούτων δ’ ἔτι λεπτομερέστερα, καί τοι γεώδη ταῖς συστάσεσιν ὑπάρχοντα, τίτανός τε καὶ κανθαρὶς καὶ ὁ θαλάττιος λαγωός· ὧν τινὰ μὲν ἄχρι τῶν καθ’ ἧπαρ ἀνέρχεται χωρίων, ἔνια δὲ καὶ μέχρι κύστεως καὶ θώρακος, ἐν τῷ τοσούτῳ διαστήματι ﻿ [689] τῆς φορᾶς τὸ πυρῶδες προσκτώμενα, ἀριστολοχία δὲ καὶ ἴρις ἔτι καὶ τούτων αὐτῶν λεπτομερέστερά ἐστιν· καὶ γὰρ καὶ ὑγρᾶς οὐσίας μᾶλλον τούτων μετέχει καὶ ἀερώδους, δῆλον δ’ ἐκ τοῦ μήθ’ οὕτως εἶναι ξηρὰ καὶ κραῦρα μήθ’ οὕτως βαρέα καὶ διὰ τοῦτ’ ἐξέφυγε τὸ γένος τῶν δηλητηρίων.
english_sentence_A: Still more fine-particled than these, although earthy in their constitution, are lime, cantharis and the sea-hare; of these some ascend as far as the regions about the liver, and some even as far as the bladder and the thorax, acquiring the fiery quality in so great an interval [689] of their transport, while aristolochia and iris are more fine-particled even than these themselves; for they partake more than these of moist substance and of airy substance, and this is clear from their being neither so dry and brittle nor so heavy, and for this reason they have escaped the class of deleterious things.

greek_sentence: καὶ μὲν δὴ καὶ ἡ κανθαρὶς ὀλίγη ποτὲ ληφθεῖσα καὶ οἷς προσῆκε μιχθεῖσα πρὸς τῷ μηδὲν ἀδικεῖν τὴν κύστιν ἔτι καὶ διακαθαίρει νεφροὺς, καὶ τά γε δραστικώτερα τῶν οὐρητικῶν φαρμάκων ἔχει τι καὶ κανθαρίδος.
english_sentence_A: And indeed cantharis too, when taken on occasion in small quantity and mixed with the things with which it ought to be, besides doing no harm to the bladder, further also thoroughly cleanses the kidneys, and the more active of the diuretic drugs contain something of cantharis as well.
english_sentence_B: For they partake more than these do of moist and of airy substance. This is clear from their being neither so dry and brittle nor so heavy, and for this reason they have escaped the class of deleterious drugs.

greek_sentence: Ὁ δὲ πικρὸς χυμὸς ὅτι τοῖς ξηροῖς τῇ κράσει σώμασι συνυπάρχει κᾀκ τοῦ δυσσηπτότατα πάντων εἶναι τὰ πικρὰ καὶ ἥκιστα σκώληκάς τε καὶ ἄλλ’ ἄττα ζῶα γεννᾷν, οἷα δὴ πέφυκεν ἐν ῥίζαις καὶ βοτάναις καὶ καρποῖς σηπομένοις ἐγγίγνεσθαι πάρεστι συλλογίσασθαι.
english_sentence_A: That the bitter flavour coexists with bodies that are dry in mixture it is possible to infer also from the fact that bitter things are of all things the most difficult to putrefy and least of all generate worms and certain other animals, such as are naturally produced in roots and herbs and fruits as they putrefy.
english_sentence_B: But concerning such matters there is another discussion. That the bitter flavour coexists with bodies that are dry in their mixture one may infer also from this: bitter things are, of all things, the most resistant to putrefaction.

greek_sentence: τὰ δ’ ἀκριβῶς πικρὰ, καλῶ δ’ οὕτως ὅσα μηδεμιᾶς ἑτέρας ποιότητος αἰσθητῆς μετέσχηκεν, ἅπασι [690] σχεδὸν τοῖς ζώοις, οὐκ ἀνθρώποις μόνοις, ἐστὶν ἄβρωτα, τῷ πᾶν μὲν ζῶον ὑγρὸν ἢ μᾶλλον ἢ ἧττον ὑπάρχειν, ξηρὰ δ’ εἶναι τὰ πικρὰ, τέφρᾳ καὶ κονίᾳ παραπλήσια.
english_sentence_A: But the things that are exactly bitter—and I so call those which partake of no other perceptible quality—are inedible to almost [690] all animals, not to human beings alone, because every animal is moist, to a greater or lesser degree, whereas bitter things are dry, similar to ash and lye.
english_sentence_B: But things that are exactly bitter (and I call so whatever has no share in any other perceptible quality) are inedible to almost all [690] animals, not to humans alone, because every animal is moist, to a greater or lesser degree, while bitter things are dry, closely resembling ash and lye.

lsj_entry_text: ἀψίνθ-ιον, τό, wormwood, Artemisia Absinthium, Hp. Morb. 3.11 , Mul. 1.74 , X. An. 1.5.1 , Thphr. HP 1.12.1 , Dsc. 3.23 ; ἀψινθίῳ κατέπασας Ἀττικὸν μέλι Men. 708 :—also ἄψινθος, ἡ, Aret. CD 1.13 , but ὁ, Apoc. 8.11 ; and ἀψινθία, ἡ, Alex. Trall. 1.10 . ἀψίνθιον, = ἀβρότονον , Ps.- Dsc. 3.24 . = Artemisia monosperma, Aq. Pr. 5.4 . ἀ. θαλάσσιον, = σέριφον , Dsc. 3.23 .
greek_sentence: ἀψίνθιον μὲν γὰρ οὐ πικρὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ στρυφνόν ἐστιν, ἡ θάλαττα δ’ ἁλμυρὰ μᾶλλον ἢ πικρὰ καὶ πλείστου μετέχουσα τοῦ ποτίμου, καθάπερ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλει πάλαι τοῦθ’ ἱκανῶς ἐπιδέδεικται.
english_sentence_A: For wormwood is not only bitter but also acerbic, and the sea is salty rather than bitter, and partakes of a very great deal of the potable, just as this was long ago sufficiently demonstrated by Aristotle.
english_sentence_B: For wormwood is not only bitter but also acerbic, and the sea is briny rather than bitter, and has a very large share of drinkable water, as Aristotle long ago adequately demonstrated.

lsj_entry_text: ἁλυκ-ός, ή, όν, salt, Hp. Acut. 42 , Aër. 1 , Ar. Lys. 403 , LXX Ge. 14.3 ; brackish, Thphr. HP 4.3.5 .
greek_sentence: τὸ δὲ τῆς ἐν Παλαιστίνῃ Συρίᾳ λίμνης ὕδωρ, ἣν ὀνομάζουσιν οἱ μὲν θάλασσαν νεκρὰν, οἱ δὲ λίμνην ἀσφαλτῖτιν, ἔστι μὲν καὶ γευομένοις οὐχ ἁλυκὸν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πικρόν.
english_sentence_A: But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea, others the Asphaltite Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter.
english_sentence_B: But the water of the lake in Palestinian Syria, which some name the Dead Sea and others the Asphalt Lake, is, to those who taste it, not only salty but also bitter.

lsj_entry_text: λευκός, ή, όν, light, bright, clear (opp. μέλας in all senses), αἴγλη Od. 6.45 ; λευκὸν ( v.l. λαμπρόν ) . . ἠέλιος ὥς Il. 14.185 ; λ. φάος S. Aj. 708 (lyr.), cf. infr. 11.3 ; αἰθήρ E. Andr. 1228 (anap.); of metallic surfaces, λέβης Il. 23.268 ; λ. γαλήνη a glassy calm, Od. 10.94 ; of water, clear, limpid, Il. 23.282 , Od. 5.70 , A. Supp. 23 (anap.); λ. νᾶμα E. HF 573 ; - ότατος ποταμῶν Call. Jov. 19 . metaph., clear, distinct, of the voice, Arist. Top. 106a25 , S.E. M. 6.41 : in literary sense, clear, λ. στίχος AP 11.347 ( Phil. ): prov., λευκὸς Ἑρμῆς, when a rogue was detected, Macar. 5.53 . Adv. -κῶς, πάντα φαίνειν, of Hermes, Corn. ND 16 : Comp. -ότερον , διαλεχθῆναι Hld. 7.20 . of colour, white, freq. in Hom. , varying from the pure white of snow ([ ἵπποι] -ότεροι χιόνος Il. 10.437 ) to the grey of dust ( λευκοὶ ἐγένοντο κονισάλῳ 5.503 ); γάλα λ. 4.434 ; κρῖ 5.196 ; ἄλφιτα 18.560 ; ἡνία λεύκ' ἐλέφαντι 5.583 ; ὀδόντες 10.263 ; ὀστέα 16.347 ; ἱστία 1.480 ; φᾶρος 18.353 , etc.; λ. ἅρμα, = λεύκιππον , E. Ph. 172 ; of the white horses used by tyrants, λ. ζεῦγος D. 21.158 , cf. λεύκιππος; λ. λίθος marble, OGI 219.36 (Sigeum, iii B.C.), etc., cf. λευκόλιθος; λευκῷ<ʼν>λίθῳ λ. στάθμη a white line on a white stone, prov. of explanations which do not explain, S. Fr. 330 ; ἡ λ. ῥίζα white root (= ἡ τοῦ δρακοντίου, acc. to Gal. 19.118 ), Hp. Morb. 2.48 , Nat.Mul. 32 ; freq. of white or grey hair, λ. κάρη Tyrt. 10.23 ; θρίξ S. Ant. 1092 ; λ. γῆρας Id. Aj. 625 (lyr.); λευκὰ γήρᾳ σώματα E. HF 909 , etc. of the human skin, white, fair, sts. as a sign of youth and beauty, χρώς, πήχεε, Il. 11.573 , Od. 23.240 ; λ. παρειά, παρηΐς, S. Ant. 1239 , E. Med. 923 ; σάρξ, δέρη, ib. 1189 (v.l.), IA 875 (troch.); freq. with the notion of bare, κῶλον, πούς, Id. Ba. 665 , 863 (lyr.), Ion 221 (lyr.); cf. λευκόπους. of persons, white-skinned, Pl. R. 474e : hence, weakly, womanish, Ar. Th. 191 , Ec. 428 , X. HG 3.4.19 ; λευκῶν ἀνδρῶν οὐδὲν ὄφελος Macar. 5.55 ; cf. λευκόπρωκτος, λευκόχρως. λευκαὶ φρένες in Pi. P. 4.109 is expld. by Hsch. μαινόμεναι, frantic, passionate (cf. λευκῶν πραπίδων· κακῶν φρενῶν, Id.). λ. χρυσός, pale gold, i.e. gold alloyed with silver (prob. the same as ἤλεκτρον), opp. ἄπεφθος χρυσός, Hdt. 1.50 . metaph., bright, fortunate, happy, λευκὸν ἦμαρ νυκτὸς ἐκ μελαγχίμου A. Pers. 301 , cf. Ag. 668 ; a joyful day or holiday, Call. Aet. 1.1.2 ; λ. ἡμέρα a happy day, S. Fr. 6 , cf. Sch. Call. Iamb. in PSI 9.1094.39 ; variously expld. in Phylarch. 83 J. , Plu. Per. 27 ; ἡ λ. ψῆφος the vote of acquittal, Luc. Harm. 3 , cf. Hsch. λεύκη, ἡ, λευκόν, τό , as Subst., v. sub vocc. (Cogn. with Lat. lux, etc.)
greek_sentence: ἔχει δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐξ ἑαυτοῦ γεννωμένους ἅλας ὑποπίκρους ὁμοίως καὶ κατὰ τὴν ὄψιν εὐθὺς ἅμα πάσης θαλάσσης λευκότερόν τε καὶ παχύτερον φαίνεται, ἅλμῃ κατακορεῖ προσεοικὸς, εἰς ἣν οὐδ’ ἂν ἐμβάλῃς ἅλας, ἔτι τακήσονται, πλεῖστον γὰρ τούτων μετέχει.
english_sentence_A: And it has, likewise, the salts generated from it somewhat bitter; and to the sight it straightway appears at the same time both whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling a saturated brine, into which, not even if you throw in salts, will they still dissolve, for it partakes of a very great deal of them.
english_sentence_B: The salts generated from it are likewise somewhat bitter. To the sight too it appears at once whiter and thicker than any sea, resembling saturated brine, in which salts will no longer dissolve even if you throw them in, for it already contains a very great quantity of them.

lsj_first_sense_gloss: anything that comes off the surface
greek_sentence: καὶ εἴ τις εἰς αὐτὴν καταδὺς ἀνακύψειεν, ἄχνην ἁλῶν ἂν εὐθέως κύκλῳ περὶ πᾶν ἴσχει τὸ σῶμα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτό τε βαρύτερόν ἐστι τῆς ἄλλης θαλάττης [691] τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκεῖνο τοσοῦτον ὅσον ἡ θάλαττα τῶν ποταμῶν.
english_sentence_A: And if someone, having plunged into it, should come up again, he at once has a film of salt all round his whole body; and for this reason too that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as the sea is heavier than rivers.
english_sentence_B: And if someone dives down into it and then comes up again, he would at once have a crust of salt (ἄχνην ἁλῶν) all round his whole body. For this reason that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as sea-water is heavier than rivers.

greek_sentence: καὶ εἴ τις εἰς αὐτὴν καταδὺς ἀνακύψειεν, ἄχνην ἁλῶν ἂν εὐθέως κύκλῳ περὶ πᾶν ἴσχει τὸ σῶμα, καὶ διὰ τοῦτό τε βαρύτερόν ἐστι τῆς ἄλλης θαλάττης [691] τὸ ὕδωρ ἐκεῖνο τοσοῦτον ὅσον ἡ θάλαττα τῶν ποταμῶν.
english_sentence_A: And if someone, having plunged into it, should come up again, he at once has a film of salt all round his whole body; and for this reason too that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as the sea is heavier than rivers.
english_sentence_B: And if someone dives down into it and then comes up again, he would at once have a crust of salt (ἄχνην ἁλῶν) all round his whole body. For this reason that water is heavier than the rest of the sea [691] by as much as sea-water is heavier than rivers.

greek_sentence: ὥστ’ οὐδ’ εἰ βούλοιο κατὰ τοῦ βάθους καθεὶς ἑαυτὸν φέρεσθαι κάτω, δυνηθείης ἄν· οὕτως ἐξαίρει τε καὶ κουφίζει τὸ ὕδωρ, οὐχ ὡς φύσει κοῦφον ὑπάρχον, ὅπερ ἤδη τις εἷπε τῶν παλαιῶν σοφιστῶν, ἀλλ’ ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης ἔλεγε, διὰ βαρύτητα δίκην πηλοῦ βαστάζον τὰ κουφότερα.
english_sentence_A: So that not even if you wished, letting yourself down toward the depth, to be carried downwards, would you be able to: so much does the water raise and buoy one up, not because it is light by nature, which one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it supports the lighter things, like mud.
english_sentence_B: So even if you wanted to let yourself down into the depth and be carried downwards, you would not be able to; so strongly does the water lift and buoy one up. This is not because it is light by nature, as one of the ancient sophists once said, but, as Aristotle said, because through its heaviness it carries lighter things, as mud does.

english_sentence_A: And moreover, just as in the sea boats carry greater cargoes without being sunk than those in lakes and rivers, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times more than those in the sea.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, just as in the sea ships carry greater loads than in lakes and rivers without being sunk, in the same way in the Dead Lake they carry many times the loads they carry in the sea.

english_sentence_A: For the water in it is heavier than sea-water by as much as sea-water is heavier than lake-water and river-water.

english_sentence_A: And it is possible for you yourself to generate sea-water, by dissolving salt in drinkable water, and to learn by how much heavier such water turns out to be than sweet water.
english_sentence_B: You yourself can also produce sea-water by dissolving salt in potable water, and so learn how much heavier such water turns out than sweet water.

lsj_entry_text: φιλοτιμ-ία, Ion. -ιη, ἡ, love of honour or distinction, ambition, freq. in bad sense in early writers, Pi. Fr. 210 , E. IA 527 , Ar. Th. 383 , Arist. EN 1125b22 ; κακίστη δαιμόνων Φ. E. Ph. 532 ; ἄκαιρος Isoc. Ep. 2.9 ; πλεονεξία καὶ φ. Th. 3.82 ; with φιλονικία, Pl. Lg. 860e ; also in good sense, Isoc. 5.110 , X. Mem. 3.3.13 , Hier. 7.3 , Pl. R. 553c : the object is added in gen., φ. τῶν καλῶν ib. 555a , cf. X. Cyr. 8.1.35 ; also φ. ἐπὶ τοῖς καλοῖς Pl. Smp. 178d ; ὑπὲρ τῶν ὅλων, περί τι, Plb. 1.52.4 , 5.71.6 ; πρὸς τὰ καλά Id. 6.55.4 , cf. Pl. lsj_entry_text: ἅλς (A), ἁλός [α], ὁ: dat. pl. ἅλασιν (v. infr.):— salt, πάσσε δ' ἁλὸς θείοιο Il. 9.214 , cf. Od. 17.455 ; ἁλὸς μέταλλον a salt-mine, Hdt. 4.185 ; ἁλὸς χόνδροι lumps of rock-salt, ib. 181 : sg. also Ar. Ach. 835 , Philyll. 28 , Axionic. 8 : more freq. in pl., Od. 11.123 , Hdt. 4.53 , al., etc.:—prov. phrases: οὐ σύ γ' ἂν . . σῷ ἐπιστάτη οὐδ' ἅλα δοίης Od. 17.455 ; φῄς μοι πάντα δόμεν· τάχα δ' . . οὐδ' ἅλα δοίης Theoc. 27.61 ; ἅλας συναναλῶσαι, i.e. to be bound by ties of hospitality, Arist. EN 1156b27 ; τῶν ἁλῶν συγκατεδηδοκέναι μέδιμνον to have eaten a bushel of salt together, i.e. to be old friends, Com.Adesp. 176 ; οἱ περὶ ἅλα καὶ κύαμον, of friends, Plu. 2.684e , cf. Arist. EE 1238a3 ; ὅρκον μέγαν, ἅλας τε καὶ τράπεζαν Archil. 96 ; ποῦ ἅλες; ποῦ τράπεζαι; D. 19.189 ; τοὺς ἅλας παραβαίνειν ib. 191 ; τοὺς τῆς πόλεως ἅλας περὶ πλείονος ποιήσασθαι τῆς ξενικῆς τραπέζης Aeschin. 3.224 ; ἁλῶν δὲ φόρτος ἔνθεν ἦλθεν, ἔνθ' ἔβη 'light come, light go', Zen. 2.20 ; ἅλασιν ὕει, of great abundance, Suid. in pl. of medical preparations, Dsc. 5.109 . brine, Call. Fr. 50 . ἃ. ἀμμωνιακός rock-salt, PLond. 1.78.90 . ἃ. Ἰνδικός sugar, Archig. ap. Paul.Aeg. 2.53 . ἅλες, οἱ, metaph., like Lat. sales, wit, possible but unlikely in Pl. Smp. 177b , Ep.Col. 4.6 ; certain in Plu. 2.854c ; ἅλες called "χάριτες" ib. 685a . (Cf.sq.)
greek_sentence: μᾶλλον δ’ ἂν ἔτι βαρύτερον ἐργάσαιο τὸ τοιοῦτο ὕδωρ, εἰ τήξας τοὺς ἅλας ὡς πλείστους ὑπὸ κυνὸς ἐπιτολὴν, ἡνίκα μάλιστα θάλπος ἐστὶ σφοδρότατον, ἐάσαις ἐξοπτηθῆναι, παραπλησίως τῷ κατὰ τὴν ἀσφαλτῖτιν λίμνην.
english_sentence_A: And you would make such water heavier still if, having dissolved as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog-star, when the heat is most intense, you should allow it to be baked out, in a manner similar to the water in the Asphalt Lake.
english_sentence_B: You could make such water heavier still if, after dissolving as much salt as possible at the rising of the Dog Star, when the heat is at its most intense, you let it be thoroughly baked, just like the water of the Asphalt Lake.

greek_sentence: φαίνεται γὰρ ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ ὕδατι μήτε ζῶον ἐγγιγνόμενόν τι μήτε φυτὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν εἰς αὐτὴν ἐμβαλόντων ποταμῶν ἀμφοτέρων, μεγίστους καὶ πλείστους ἐχόντων ἰχθύας, καὶ μάλιστα τοῦ πλησίον Ἰεριχοῦντος, ὃν Ἰορδάνην ὀνομάζουσιν, οὐδ’ εἷς τῶν ἰχθύων ὑπερβαίνει τὰ στόματα τῶν ποταμῶν.
english_sentence_A: For it appears that in that water neither any animal nor any plant comes into being; but even of the two rivers that empty into it, which contain very large and very numerous fish, and especially of the one near Jericho, which they call the Jordan, not a single one of the fish passes beyond the mouths of the rivers.
english_sentence_B: For it is evident that in that water neither any animal nor any plant comes into being; moreover, although both the rivers that empty into it contain very large and very numerous fish, and especially the one near Jericho, which they call the Jordan, not a single one of the fish passes beyond the mouths of the rivers.
