lsj_first_sense_gloss: pool of standing water left by the sea or a river
greek_sentence: κἂν εἰ συλλαβὼν δέ τις αὐτοὺς ἐμβάλοι τῇ λίμνῃ, διαφθειρομένους ὄψεται ταχέως· οὕτως τ’ ﻿ [694] ἀκριβῶς πικρὸν ἅπασίν ἐστι καὶ ζώοις καὶ φυτοῖς πολέμιον, αὐχμῶδές τε καὶ ξηρὸν καὶ τὴν φύσιν οἷόν περ αἴθαλος ὑπὸ τῆς κατοπτήσεως γεγενημένον.
english_sentence_A: And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing; so [694] precisely bitter is it, and hostile to all things, both animals and plants, parched and dry and in its nature having become, as it were, soot through the roasting.
english_sentence_B: And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing. So hostile to all things, both animals and plants, is what is exactly bitter, being parched and dry and in its nature like soot produced by roasting.

Mithrid., i B.C.).—πολέμιος is older than πολεμικός, being always used by Pi. and Trag., and mostly by Hdt. and Th. ; in X. and later writers, πολέμιος is mostly used in the sense of hostile, πολεμικός in that of warlike, skilled in war.
greek_sentence: κἂν εἰ συλλαβὼν δέ τις αὐτοὺς ἐμβάλοι τῇ λίμνῃ, διαφθειρομένους ὄψεται ταχέως· οὕτως τ’ ﻿ [694] ἀκριβῶς πικρὸν ἅπασίν ἐστι καὶ ζώοις καὶ φυτοῖς πολέμιον, αὐχμῶδές τε καὶ ξηρὸν καὶ τὴν φύσιν οἷόν περ αἴθαλος ὑπὸ τῆς κατοπτήσεως γεγενημένον.
english_sentence_A: And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing; so [694] precisely bitter is it, and hostile to all things, both animals and plants, parched and dry and in its nature having become, as it were, soot through the roasting.
english_sentence_B: And if someone were to catch them and throw them into the lake, he will see them quickly perishing. So hostile to all things, both animals and plants, is what is exactly bitter, being parched and dry and in its nature like soot produced by roasting.

greek_sentence: δύναμις δ’ αὐτῶν οὐ ξηραντικὴ μόνον ἐπὶ μᾶλλόν ἐστι τῶν ἄλλων ἁλῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ λεπτυντικὴ, διότι μᾶλλον τῶν ἄλλων ἐξώπτηνται.
english_sentence_A: Their power is not only drying to a greater degree than that of the other salts, but also thinning, because they have been roasted more than the others.
english_sentence_B: Their power is not only drying to a greater degree than that of the other salts, but also thinning, because they have been roasted more thoroughly than the others.

lsj_entry_text: στυπτικός, ή, όν, (στύφω) astringent, Diocl.Fr. 130 , Thphr. Od. 21 , Dsc. 1.30.3 ( Comp. ), Ath.Med. ap. Orib. inc. 23.27 , Plu. 2.624e , Sor. 1.61 , Gal. 6.426 , Antyll. ap. Orib. 10.24.6 ; τὰ ς. astringents, Hp. Aph. 7.37 , Theo Sm. p.14H. Adv. -κῶς Paul.Aeg. 3.18 .
greek_sentence: πᾶσι μὲν γὰρ τοῖς ἁλσὶν ὑπάρχει τι καὶ στυπτικὸν ἀμυδρὸν, ᾧ δὴ καὶ σφίγγουσι καὶ πιλοῦσι τὰ ταριχευόμενα τῶν κρεῶν καὶ μάλισθ’ ὅταν ὦσι χόνδροι τε καὶ δύσθραυστοι.
english_sentence_A: For in all salts there is also something faintly astringent, by which indeed they bind and compact the meats that are being salted, and especially when they are in coarse lumps and hard to break.
english_sentence_B: For all salts possess something faintly astringent as well, by which they bind and compact meats that are being pickled, and especially when they are coarse-grained and hard to break.

greek_sentence: οὕτω δὲ δὴ καὶ τὸ νίτρον αὐτὸ καὶ ἀφρὸς αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ συνθέτῳ προσηγορίᾳ καλούμενον ἀφρόνιτρον ἔτι μᾶλλον τῶν ἄλλων πέφυκε ῥύπτειν, ὡς ἂν ἥκιστα μὲν στύφοντα, πικρὰ δ’ ἀκριβῶς ὑπάρχοντα.
english_sentence_A: So too nitre itself and its foam, and what is called by the composite name aphronitron, are by nature even more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent while being precisely bitter.
english_sentence_B: In the same way nitre itself, its foam, and what is called by a compound name aphronitre are by nature still more cleansing than the others, inasmuch as they are least astringent and thoroughly bitter.

english_sentence_A: For the salty flavour is near to the bitter, since both are earthy and hot; yet they differ by no obscure difference, in that the bitter has been thinned and worked up more by dry heat.

english_sentence_A: So too, of the salts themselves, those that are harder and denser and more earthy—and such are almost all the mined salts—are less hot and fine-particled, whereas those that are friable and loose-textured are at once both more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are somewhat bitter, being in a way intermediate between the hard salts and aphronitron.
english_sentence_B: In the same way, among the salts themselves, those that are harder, denser and more earthy (and almost all the mined salts are of this kind) are less hot and less fine-particled, whereas those that are easily crumbled and porous are at once more fine-particled and hotter in power, and some of them are slightly bitter, standing in a way between the hard salts and aphronitre.

english_sentence_B: For this too is sufficiently fine-particled, but less hot than aphronitre.

greek_sentence: διὸ καὶ τὰς ὑπεραυξανομένας σάρκας ἀλυπότερον ἀποτήκει, δάκνει δ’ αὐτὰς ἤδη τὸ ἄνθος τοῦ νίτρου, δάκνει δὲ καὶ τὸ ἀφρόνιτρον, οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ τὸ νίτρον αὐτὸ, καίτοι γε ἧττον ἐκείνων ὑπάρχον θερμόν.

english_sentence_A: For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as that of the fine-particled does, but being held back and always remaining and lingering, and sitting for a longer time upon one place of our body, it naturally becomes painful, like a thorn fixed in the flesh.
english_sentence_B: For no part of it passes through painlessly and quickly, as happens with fine-particled substance; instead, being held back, always remaining and lingering, and staying for a longer time at one place in our body, it reasonably becomes distressing, like a stake fixed in the flesh.

greek_sentence: ὥσπερ γὰρ τῶν προσπιπτόντων τῇ ﻿ [699] γλώττῃ χυμῶν οἱ μὲν οἰκειότατοι γλυκεῖς ἦσαν, οἱ δ’ οὐκ οἰκεῖοι πολλὰς ἐκέκτηντο διαφορὰς, οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀτμῶν οἱ μὲν οἰκεῖοι τῷ κατὰ τὸν ἐγκέφαλον πνεύματι φίλιοί τ’ εἰσὶ καὶ ἡδεῖς, οἱ δ’ οὐκ οἰκεῖοι διαφέρουσι μὲν ἀλλήλων οὐκ ὀλίγαις διαφοραῖς, ὀνόματα δ’ αὐταῖς ἁπάσαις οὐ κεῖται καθάπερ ἐπὶ τῶν χυμῶν.

english_sentence_B: This watery component itself, then, seems somehow to have already been worked up, thinned and heated, and for this reason to be readily brought into vapours; and it is in this way that the rose is both odorous and dries out very quickly.

english_sentence_A: The bodies named after them are both the elements common to all things and those which are called wet and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these, and those which are compared with the well-proportioned member of the same genus or of the same species, and those compared with anything whatever that happens to be at hand.
english_sentence_B: The bodies named after them are, first, the elements common to all things; second, those called moist and dry and cold and hot according to the predominance of one of these qualities; third, those so called when compared with the well-balanced body of the same genus or of the same species; and fourth, those so called in comparison with anything whatever that happens to come along. Now the difference among these has been discussed many times.

english_sentence_A: Now concerning the difference among these it has been said many times, and no less has it also been said in what way nutriment differs from a drug, and that nutriment is mastered and overcome by the thing being nourished, whereas the drug, conversely, itself overcomes and masters the body of which it is a drug; for the conception of each of the two lies in the relative.
english_sentence_B: It was also shown that a drug naturally alters either according to some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or according to some pairing of those mentioned, or according to its whole substance.

english_sentence_A: It was shown also that a drug is naturally such as to alter either in respect of some one quality, whichever it may be, heating or cooling or drying or moistening, or in respect of some conjugation of those mentioned, or in respect of its whole substance, as do some of the deleterious drugs and not a few of the alexipharmic ones and all the purgatives and many of those called epispastic.
english_sentence_B: Some of the deleterious drugs act in this last way, as do not a few of the protective remedies, all the purgatives, and many of those called attractive.

english_sentence_A: And indeed also that some are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances, others fine-particled and airy, and others as it were watery and intermediate between those mentioned—these points too, having been demonstrated in the preceding discourses, let them stand for me as assumptions with a view to what is going to be said.
english_sentence_B: Moreover, some are coarse-particled and earthy in their substances, others fine-particled and airy, and others as it were watery and intermediate between those mentioned; since these things too were shown in the preceding discussions, let them stand as hypotheses for me with respect to what is going to be said.

greek_sentence: Ἡ χρεία τῶν φαρμάκων τοῖς ἀνθρώποις γίγνεται πολλάκις μὲν ὡς αὐτὸ τοῦτο μόνον, ἤτοι θερμαινόντων ἢ ψυχόντων ἢ ὑγραινόντων ἢ ξηραινόντων, ἢ κατὰ συζυγίαν τινὰ τούτων ἐνεργούντων, ἐνίοτε δὲ ὡς ἤδη τὸ πέρας τοῦ μετρίου κεχαλασμένον, ἐπιτεινόντων τε καὶ συναγόντων, [707] ἢ τὸ συντεταμένον χαλώντων, ἢ ἀραιούντων τὸ πεπυκνωμένον ἢ πυκνούντων τὸ μανὸν, ἢ μαλαττόντων τὸ σκληρὸν ἢ σκληρυνόντων ἀμέτρους μαλακότητας, ἢ κενούντων τὸ πλῆρες ἢ πληρούντων τὸ κενὸν, ἤ τι τοιοῦτον ἕτερον ἐργαζομένων.
english_sentence_A: The need for drugs arises for human beings often simply as this alone, namely of drugs that either heat or cool or moisten or dry, or that act according to some conjunction of these; but sometimes as of drugs that tighten and draw together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relax what is tensed, or rarefy what has been condensed or condense what is loose, or soften what is hard or harden immoderate softnesses, or empty what is full or fill what is empty, or that accomplish some other such thing.
english_sentence_B: The use of drugs for human beings often arises simply for this alone, namely their heating or cooling or moistening or drying, or their acting according to some combination of these; but sometimes it arises for their tightening and drawing together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relaxing what has been tensed, or rarefying what has been condensed, or condensing what is porous, or softening what is hard, or hardening immoderate softnesses, or emptying what is full, or filling what is empty, or effecting some other such thing.

english_sentence_A: The need for drugs arises for human beings often simply as this alone, namely of drugs that either heat or cool or moisten or dry, or that act according to some conjunction of these; but sometimes as of drugs that tighten and draw together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relax what is tensed, or rarefy what has been condensed or condense what is loose, or soften what is hard or harden immoderate softnesses, or empty what is full or fill what is empty, or that accomplish some other such thing.
english_sentence_B: The use of drugs for human beings often arises simply for this alone, namely their heating or cooling or moistening or drying, or their acting according to some combination of these; but sometimes it arises for their tightening and drawing together what has already been relaxed beyond the limit of the moderate, [707] or relaxing what has been tensed, or rarefying what has been condensed, or condensing what is porous, or softening what is hard, or hardening immoderate softnesses, or emptying what is full, or filling what is empty, or effecting some other such thing.

english_sentence_A: And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as do both those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been worn out by fatigue, they long to bathe and they drink cold water, and whatever may be capable of moistening and cooling at once, this they contrive to find out; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, often procure for themselves the remedies for these conditions.
english_sentence_B: And indeed, when they perceive dryness together with heat throughout the whole body, as those who have been scorched by the sun and those who have been fatigued long to bathe and drink cold water, they contrive to find whatever is capable of moistening and cooling at once; and many of the laymen, led by nature itself, do often provide themselves with the remedies for these conditions.

greek_sentence: ὑπὲρ μὲν δὴ τῶν τοιούτων τῆς δυνάμεως ἐν τοῖς πρὸ τούτου τέσσαρσιν ὑπομνήμασι διῆλθον· ἐν μὲν τῷ πρώτῳ καὶ δευτέρῳ τὰ τῶν σοφιστῶν ἐξελέγχων ἐπιχειρήματα καὶ δεικνὺς τὴν ἀληθῆ μέθοδον, ᾗ χρώμενος ἄν τις εὑρίσκοι τὰς τῶν φαρμάκων δυνάμεις, ἐν δὲ τῷ τρίτῳ τῶν σοφιστῶν ἀποχωρήσας, ἅπαντα διῆλθον ἐξ ἀρχῆς τὰ λογικὰ ζητήματα, δι’ ὧν ἄν τις μάλιστα διελθὼν καὶ ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι τεχνωθεὶς ἱκανὸς ἔσται πάντων τῶν φαρμάκων εὑρίσκειν τὰς δυνάμεις· ἐν δὲ τῷ δ΄ περὶ τῶν τῆς [710] γλώττης ἰδίων αἰσθητῶν ἐποιησάμην τὸν λόγον, ἃ δὴ χυμοὺς ὀνομάζουσιν, ἐπιδεικνύων ὡς ἄν τις ἐντεῦθεν ὁρμώμενος εὑρίσκοι τὰς πρώτας ποιότητάς τε καὶ δυνάμεις.
english_sentence_A: Concerning such matters of power, then, I have gone through in the four treatises before this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method by using which one might find the powers of drugs; in the third, having taken leave of the sophists, I went through from the beginning all the logical inquiries, by going through which especially, and being, as one might say, trained by them, one will be capable of finding the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse about the objects of sense proper to the [710] tongue, which indeed they name flavours (χυμοί), demonstrating how one, setting out from there, might find the primary qualities and powers.
english_sentence_B: Concerning the power of such things I have treated in the four commentaries preceding this one: in the first and second, refuting the arguments of the sophists and showing the true method, by using which one might discover the powers of drugs; in the third, having left the sophists aside, I went through from the beginning all the logical questions, by going through which most thoroughly and, as one might say, by being made skilled in the art (technōtheis), one will be competent to discover the powers of all drugs; and in the fourth I made my discourse concerning the sensibles proper to the [710] tongue, which they call flavours (chymoi), showing how someone setting out from there might discover the primary qualities and powers.

greek_sentence: Ἔστι δὲ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα σύμπαντα τὰ πρόσθεν εἰρημένα διὰ τῶν δ΄ ὑπομνημάτων αὐτῆς τῆς περὶ τῶν φαρμάκων θεωρίας ἴδια, πλὴν εἴ που κατὰ κοινωνίαν ὁ λόγος ἥψατο μεθόδου θεραπευτικῆς.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ ὅτι τε προγυμνάζειν ἔδοξέ μοι τοὺς μέλλοντας ἀκολουθήσειν τοῖς τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου λογισμοῖς, οἵ τε πλεῖστοι τῶν ἑταίρων καὶ μάλιστα ﻿ [714] οἷς χαριζόμενος ἐπὶ τήνδε τὴν πραγματείαν ἧκον, οὕτως ἠξίωσάν με διαπρᾶξαι, διὰ τοῦτο μεταχειριοῦμαι τὸν λόγον ἐν τῷδε τῷ γράμματι, τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀπὸ τῶν διαπυϊσκόντων τε καὶ μαλαττόντων ποιησάμενος.
english_sentence_A: But because it seemed good to me to train in advance those who are going to follow the reasonings of the therapeutic method, and because most of my companions, and especially [714] those to gratify whom I came to this treatise, asked me to carry it through in this way, for this reason I shall take up the discussion in this book, making my beginning from the suppurating and the softening drugs; since both are hot and moist, yet each in a different manner.
english_sentence_B: But since it seemed good to me to give a preliminary training to those who are going to follow the reasonings of the therapeutic method, and since most of my companions, and especially [714] those as a favour to whom I came to this treatise, asked me to do so, for this reason I shall take up the account in this book, making the beginning from the drugs that bring to suppuration and those that soften.

lsj_entry_text: ἑταῖρ-ος, Ep. and Dor. also ἕγαρος, Cleobul. ap. D.L. 1.93 , A. Pers. 988 (lyr.), ὁ:— comrade, companion, in Hom. esp. of the followers of a chief, comrades-in-arms, Il. 1.179 , al.; messmate, 17.577 ; fellowslave, Od. 14.407 , al.: joined with ἀνήρ, 8.584 , Hdt. 5.95 , Antipho 1.18 ; later, as a term of address, φίλ' ἑταῖρε Thgn. 753 , cf. Pl. Grg. 482a ; ὦταῖρε Scol. ap. Ar. V. 1238 , cf. Ev.Matt. 20.13 , al.: c. gen., δᾳιτὸς ἑταῖρε partner of my feast, h.Merc. 436 ; νυκτὸς ἑ. ib. 290 ; πόσιος καὶ βρώσιος ἑταῖροι messmates, Thgn. 115 ; ἑ. ἐν πρήγματι Id. 116 . metaph., of things, ἐσθλὸς ἑταῖρος, of a fair wind, Od. 11.7 , 12.149 ; φθόνος κενεοφρόνων ἑ. Pi. Fr. 212 ; γέλως ἑ. ὕβρεων Plu. 2.622b : c. dat., βίον..τὸν σοφοῖς ἕταρον AP 7.470 ( Mel. ). pupil, disciple, e.g. of Socrates, X. Mem. 2.8.1 , al., cf. Arist. Pol. 1274a28 ; Λεύκιππος καὶ ὁ ἑ. αὐτοῦ Δημόκριτος Id. Metaph. 985b4 : pl., fellow-pupils, Poll. 4.45 . of political partisans (cf. ἑταιρεία 1.2 ), Lys. 12.43 , Th. 8.48 ; οἱ περὶ αὐτὸν ἑ. his club-mates, D. 21.20 . members of a religious guild, OGI 573.1 (Cilicia, Jewish). rarely of lovers, Semon. 7.49 , Ar. Ec. 912 (lyr.). ἑταῖροι, οἱ, the guards, i.e. the cavalry of the Macedonian kings, Theopomp.Hist. 217 , Anaximen.Lamps. ap. Harp. s.v. πεζέταιρος , Arr. An. 3.16.11 , etc.; to be distinguished from the king's immediate retinue (cf. supr. 1 ), Theopomp. l.c., Arr. An. 2.12.6 , al.; of the Comites of the Roman Emperor, Βαρβίλλῳ τῷ ἐμῷ ἑτέρῳ (sic) PLond. 1912.105 (Epist. Claudii), cf. SIG 798.6 (Cyzicus, i A. D., pl.). as Adj., associate of, τὸ ἐπιθυμητικὸν ἡδονῶν ἑ. Pl. R. 439d : Sup. , τοῖς σεαυτοῦ ἑταιροτάτοις your closest companions, Id. Grg. 487d , cf. Phd. 89e , D.Chr. 1.44 ; σαργῶν γένος πέτρῃσιν ἑ. constant to the rocks, Opp. H. 4.267 : abs., of animals, gregarious, Id. C. 2.325 . ἑταίρα, Ion. ἑταίρη, Ep. ἑτάρη [α], ἡ, companion, Ἔρις..Ἄρεος..κασιγνήτη ἑτάρη τε Il. 4.441 ; Λάτω καὶ Νιόβα μάλα μὲν φίλαι ἦσαν ἔ. Sapph. 31 , cf. 11 ; φύζα, φόβου κρυόεντος ἑ. R. 603b ; Ποσειδάωνος ἑ., of a submerged city, Call. Del. 101 . courtesan, Hdt. 2.134 , Ar. Pl. 149 , Ath. 13.567a , 571d , etc.; opp. πόρνη (a common prostitute), Anaxil. 22.1 ; opp. γαμετή, Philetaer. 5 ; Ἀφροδίτη ἑ. Apollod.Hist. 17 .

lsj_entry_text: ὅμοιος or (as in Hom. , Ion. , and old Att. ) ὁμοῖος, α, ον (cf. ἐρῆμος, ἑτοῖμος) : later Ep. also ὁμοίιος (B, q.v.) ; Aeol. ὔμοιος Theoc. 29.20 (Adv. -ως IG 12(2).69a6 ) ; Arc. ὑμοῖος Schwyzer 665 A 15 (Orchom., iv B.C.) : (ὁμός) :—like, resembling, ὡς αἰεὶ τὸν ὁ. ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὁ. 'birds of a feather flock together', Od. 17.218 ; ὁ ὅ. τῷ ὁ. Pl. Grg. 510b ; ὁ ὅ. ὡς τὸν ὅ. Arist. EN 1155a34 ; τὸ ὅ. τῷ ὁ. φίλον ib. 1165b17 , v. infr. 6 ; ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν ὁ. as in similar cases (of persons), BGU 79.18 (ii A.D.), etc. : Comp. -ότερος more like, Pl. Phd. 79b : Sup. -ότατος most like, Hdt. 2.92 , S. Ant. 833 (lyr.), etc. the same, ἄμφω γὰρ πέπρωται ὁμοίην γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι Il. 18.329 ; χρὼς οὐκέθ' ὁ. Od. 16.182 ; hence (sc. ἑαυτῷ), always the same, unchanging, αἰεὶ πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὁμοῖοι Hes. Op. 114 ; ὅ. τὴν γνώμην the same as ever, Antipho 5.76 ; γνῶμαι πρὸς τοὺς αὐτοὺς κινδύνους ὁμοῖαι Th. 2.89 ; ἀεὶ ὅ. εἶ, ὦ Ἀπολλόδωρε Pl. Smp. 173d ; ἓν καὶ ὅ. one and the same, Id. Phdr. 271a . equal in force, a match for one, Il. 23.632 , Hdt. 9.96 . of things, suiting, according with, πολλά τε καὶ ὅ. ἑαυταῖς Id. R. 549e ; ὅ. τῇ φύσει Ar. Th. 167 . ὁμοῖον ἡμῖν ἔσται it will be all the same, all one to us, Hdt. 8.80 ; σὺ δ' αἰνεῖν εἴτε με ψέγειν θέλεις, ὁμοῖον A. Ag. 1404 , cf. 1239 , E. Supp. 1069 ; ἐν τῷ ὁ. καθειστήκει Th. 2.49 . τὸ ὅ. ἀνταποδιδόναι give 'tit for tat', Hdt. 1.18 ; so τὴν ὁμοίην (sc. δίκην, χάριν) ἀποδιδόναι τινί Id. 4.119 , 6.21 , 62 ; τὴν ὁ. φέρεσθαι παρά τινος to have a like return made one, ibid. ; ἐπ' ἴσῃ καὶ ὁμοίᾳ, v. ἴσος 11.2 . ἐν ὁμοίῳ ποιεῖσθαί τι hold a thing in like esteem, Id. 7.138 , 8.109 . ἐκ τοῦ ὁ. in like fashion, likewise, Th. 6.78 , 87 ; ἐκ τῶν ὁ. ceteris paribus, Pl. Phdr. 243d ; on equal terms, in fair fight, A. Ag. 1423 ; so ἐν τῷ ὁ. στρατεύεσθαι καὶ ὅτε . . as when . . , Th. 6.21 , etc. of the same rank or station, Hdt. 1.134 ; γαμεῖν ἐκ τῶν ὁ. Cleobul. ap. Stob. 3.1.172 , POxy. 124.2 (iii A.D.), PSI 2.120.33 (iv A.D.?) : hence οἱ ὅμοιοι, in aristocratic states, peers, all citizens who had equal right to hold state-offices, esp. at Sparta, X. HG 3.3.5 , Lac. 13.1 , 7 , Arist. Pol. 1306b30 ; Περσέων ὁμοίους τοῖσι πρώτοισι δυώδεκα Hdt. 3.35 . Geom., of figures, similar, Euc. 6 Def. 1 , 3 Def. 11 , al. ; of angles, similar, i.e. equal, Arist. Cael. 296b20 , 297b19 , 311b34 , cf. Thalesap. Procl. in Euc. 1p.251F. of Numbers, square, the product of two equal factors, Plot. 6.2.21 ; cf. ἀνόμοιος 2 . Construction : abs., freq. in Hom. , etc. (v. supr.). c. dat. of the person or thing which another resembles : so always in Hom. , Hes. , and usu. in Hdt. and Att. (v. supr.) : but sts. c. gen., τοῖσι τούτων ὁμοίοις χύμασι v.l. in Hp. Art. 12 (DielsZtschr.f.vergl. Sprachf. 47.200 ), v. l. in Hdt. 3.37 and Pl. R. 472d ; τουτέων οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλο ἔθνος ὁμοίας τὰς κεφαλὰς ἔχον οὐδέν (ellipt. as in b. infr.) Hp. Aër. 14 ; ὁ λεκτικὸς πῇ μὲν ὅμοιος Ἡροδότου, πῇ δὲ ἐνδεέστερος D.H. Pomp. 4 ; ὁμοία ἀνδριάντος Dion.Byz. 53 ; ὅμοιον ἱέρακος Cyran. 22 , cf. 12 . ellipt. phrases, κόμαι Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι, for κόμαι ταῖς τῶν Χαρίτων ὁμοῖαι, Il. 17.51 ; οὔ τις ὁμοῖα νοήματα Πηνελοπείῃ ᾔδη, for τοῖς τῆς Πηνελοπείης, Od. 2.121 : also in Prose, ἅρματα ὅ. ἐκείνῳ, for τοῖς ἐκείνου, X. Cyr. 6.1.50 ; ὁμοίαν ταῖς δούλαις ἐσθῆτα, for τῇ τῶν δουλῶν, ib. 5.1.4 ; cf. ἴσος 1.1 , συγγενής 111.2 . c. acc. of that in which a person or thing resembles another, ἀθανάτῃσι φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ὁμοίη Od. 6.16 , cf. 3.468 , Il. 5.778 ; ὀργὴν ὁ. τῷ κάκιστ' αὐδωμένῳ A. Th. 678 , cf. S. Aj. 1153 , etc. : also with Preps., ὁμοῖοι ἐν πολέμῳ Il. 12.270 ; ἐς φύσιν οὐδὲν ὁ. Batr. 32 ; ὅ. τινὶ πρός τι X. Cyn. 5.29 ; but οὐδὲν ὁμοῖον ἦν μοι πρὸς τοῦτον I had nothing in common with him, Is. 8.26 . c. inf., θείειν ἀνέμοισιν ὁμοῖοι like the winds in running, Il. 10.437 ; τῷ οὔ πώ τις ὁμοῖος κοσμῆσαι ἵππους like him to marshal or in marshalling horses, 2.553 , cf. 14.521 ; ὅμοιοι ἦσαν θαυμάζειν (s. v.l., θαυμάζοντες codd. dett.) X. An. 3.5.13 . ὅμοιον εἰπεῖν approximately, Men. Epit. 548 . folld. by a Relat., ὁμοίη, οἵην με τὸ πρῶτον ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσι νόησας like as when thou saw'st me first, h.Ven. 178 ; ὅμοιον . . , οἷόνπερ τὸ τῶν ποταμῶν X. HG 4.2.11 , cf. Hier. 7.5 , Cyr. 6.1.37 : folld. by ὅσπερ, Id. An. 5.4.34 ; by ὥσπερ, ὁ. ἀτμὸς ὥσπερ ἐκ τάφου πρέπει A. Ag. 1311 , cf. X. Smp. 4.37 ; by ὥστε, E. Or. 697 ; v. infr. c. folld. by καί (='as'), γνώμῃσι ἐχρέωντο ὁμοίῃσι καὶ σύ Hdt. 7.50 , cf. Th. 1.120 , Pl. Cri. 48b , Tht. 154a ; οὐδέν τι γενόμενος ἐς Ἀχαιοὺς ὅμοιος [ἢ] καὶ Καλλίστρατος . . Paus. 7.16.4 ; v. καί A. 111 . Adv., freq. in the neut. sg. and pl. ὅμοιον, ὅμοια (older ὁμοῖον, ὁμοῖα) in like manner with, c. dat., ὁμοῖα τοῖσι μάλιστα 'second to none', Hdt. 3.8 , cf. Th. 7.29 ; ὁμοῖα τοῖσι πλουσιωτάτοισι Hdt. 3.57 ; ὅμοιον μουσίσδει . . ταῖσιν ἀηδονίσι Theoc. 8.37 : folld. by a relat. Partic., ὁμοῖον ὥστε . . even as, S. Ant. 587 (lyr.) ; ὁ. ὡς εἰ . . Pl. Lg. 628d ; ὁμοῖα καὶ βοῦς ἐργάτης S. Fr. 563 . alike, ὅμοια χέρσον καὶ θάλασσαν ἐκπερῶν A. Eu. 240 . regul. Adv. ὁμοίως in like manner with, c. dat., Hdt. 1.32 , al. ; τοῖς μάλισθ' ὁ. D. Ep. 2.24 : folld. by a relat. Partic., ὁ. ὡς εἰ . . Hdt. 1.155 ; ὁ. ὥσπερ . . X. Cyr. 1.4.6 ; ὁ. καὶ . . Hdt. 7.86 , 8.60 .β' : abs., ὁ. δέ and in like manner, PEleph. 15.1 (iii B. C.), etc. alike, equally, Pi. P. 9.78 , Hdt. 7.100 ; Δαναοῖσι Τρωσί θ' ὁ. A. Ag. 67 (anap.) ; λέγειν . . σιγᾶν θ' ὁ. Id. Eu. 278 , etc. ; τῷ νῷ θ' ὁ. κἀπὸ τῆς γλώσσης S. OC 936 ; ὁ. μὲν . . , ὁ. δὲ . . Pl. Prt. 319d ; ὁ. ἀμφοῖν ἀκροάσασθαι D. 18.2 ; ὁ. ἔχειν to be uniform, Arist. Ph. 261b25 : prov., οὐδ' ὅκου χώρης οἱ μῦς ὁ. τὸν σίδηρον τρώγουσιν like any other food, Herod. 3.76 (but perh. all alike, cf. Ar. Eq. 1296 cod. R, Th. 5.15 (s. v.l.), Plu. 2.763c ) : Comp. -ότερον AP 11.233 ( Lucill. ) : Sup. -ότατα Ar. Fr. 281 .
greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ὁμοιοτάτην τῷ διαπυϊσκομένῳ σώματι θερμότητα γεννῶντα πρὸς τῷ μήτ’ ἀφαιρεῖν τι τῆς οὔσης ἐν αὐτῷ ὑγρότητος μήτε προστιθέναι, τὰ δ’ ὡς καὶ πλέονα τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἀνάπτοντα καὶ συνάγοντά τι τῆς ὑγρότητος.
english_sentence_A: For the former are so inasmuch as they generate a heat most similar to the body that is being brought to suppuration, in addition to neither removing anything of the moisture that is present in it nor adding to it; the latter inasmuch as they kindle a heat even greater than the natural one and draw together some of the moisture.
english_sentence_B: The former generate a heat most similar to that of the body being brought to suppuration, and besides neither take away any of the moisture present in it nor add any.

lsj_entry_text: πλέω, Ep. πλείω Od. 15.34 , 16.368 : Ep. impf. ἀπ-έπλειον 8.501 : also Ep. and Ion. πλώω (v. infr.): Att. contr. imper. πλεῖ E. Tr. 102 (anap.): fut. πλεύσομαι Od. 12.25 , Il. 11.22 (ἀνα-), Hdt. 2.29 , Th. 6.104 , etc.; later πλευσοῦμαι SIG 402.27 (Chios, iii B. C.), found in codd. of Th. 1.143 , 8.1 , (ἐπεσ-) Id. 4.13 , (συνεκ-) Lys. 13.25 , (ἀπο-) Pl. Hp.Ma. 370d , 371b , (συμ-) Isoc. 17.19 , etc.; Dor. πλευσοῦμαι Theoc. 14.55 ; but 3 pl. πλεύσονται GDI 5120 B 11 , 13 (Crete, iii B. C.); πλεύσω Philem. 116 (S.V.l.), Plb. 2.12.3 , AP 11.162 ( Nicarch. ), 245 ( Lucill. ), OGI 572.30 (Lycia, ii/iii A.D.), etc.: aor. 1 ἔπλευσα A. Ag. 691 (lyr.), etc.: pf. πέπλευκα S. Ph. 404 , etc.:— Pass. , fut. πλευσθήσομαι (περι-) Arr. An. 5.26.2 : aor. ἐπλεύσθην ib. 6.28.6 , Babr. 71.3 : pf. πέπλευσμαι X. Cyr. 6.1.16 , D. 56.12 : Hom. uses only pres., impf., and fut. πλεύσομαι (v. supr.).—Of the Ion. πλώω, Hom. uses opt. πλώοιεν Od. 5.240 , part. ἐπι-πλώων ib. 284 , πλώων h.Hom. 22.7 : impf. πλῶον Il. 21.302 ; also shortd. aor. ἔπλων, ως, ω, part. πλώς, in the compds. ἀπ-έπλω, ἐπ-έπλως, part. ἐπιπλώς, παρέπλω; and Hes. has ἐπ-έπλων; the pres., impf., and fut. forms occur as vv.ll. in Hdt. , inf. πλώειν 4.156 , part. πλωούσας 8.10 , 22 , 42 : impf. ἔπλωον ib. 41 ; Iterat. πλώεσκον Q.S. 14.656 : fut. πλώσομαι (ἀπο-) Hdt. 8.5 ( πλώσω Lyc. 1044 ); but the aor. 1 forms are read in Hdt. , ἔπλωσα 4.148 ; inf. πλῶσαι 1.24 ; part. πλώσας 4.156 , 8.49 (also once in Hom. in compd. ἐπι-πλώσας Il. 3.47 ): pf. παρα-πέπλωκα Hdt. 4.99 ; πέπλωκα occurs E. Hel. 532 , Ar. Th. 878 (paratrag.).—Only εε and εει are contracted in Att. (πλέει is f.l. in Th. 4.28 , and πλέετε v.l. in X. An. 7.6.37 ). [ Hom. uses πλέων as monosyll., πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον Od. 1.183 ]:—sail, go by sea, Λακεδαίμονος ἐξ ἐρατεινῆς Il. 3.444 ; Ἰλιόθεν 14.251 ; ἐπὶ Κέρκυραν Th. 1.53 ; εὐθὺ Λέσβου X. HG 1.2.11 ; π. ἐπὶ [σῖτον] to fetch it, Id. Oec. 20.27 ; ἐπί τι IG 12.105.9 ; μετὰ [νάκος] Pi. P. 4.69 ; εἰς Ἐρέτριαν ἐπ' ἄνδρας Pl. Mx. 240b ; more fully, ἐνὶ πόντῳ νηῒ θοῇ πλείοντες Od. 16.368 ; νηῒ . . πλέων ἐπὶ οἴνοπα πόντον Il. 7.88 ; πλέεν . . ποντοπορεύων Od. 5.278 ; ἐν τῇ νηΐ Pl. R. 341d ; ἐν τῇ θαλάττῃ ib. 346b ; ἐπλέομεν βορέῃ ἀνέμῳ Od. 14.253 ; αὔρᾳ A. Ag. 691 (lyr.): c. acc. cogn., πλεῖθ' ὑγρὰ κέλευθα sail the watery ways, Od. 3.71 ; πλεῖν τὴν θάλατταν And. 1.137 , Lys. 6.19 , Isoc. 8.20 , Antiph. 100 :— Pass. , τὸ πεπλευσμένον [πέλαγος] X. Cyr. 6.1.16 , cf. Babr. 71.3 ; πλεῖται ἡ θάλασσα Muson. Fr. 18 B p.104 H.; also π. στόλον τόνδε S. Ph. 1038 ; τοῦ πλοῦ τοῦ πεπλευσμένου D. 56.12 : metaph., πλεῖν ὑφειμένῃ δοκεῖ, cf. ὑφίημι 111 : prov., ὁ μὴ πεπλευκὼς οὐδὲν ἑόρακεν κακόν Posidipp. 22 ; ἐπὶ γῆς μὴ πλεῖν when on land do not be at sea, i.e. avoid the hazards of tax-farming, etc., Pythag. ap. Clem.Al. greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ ὡς ὁμοιοτάτην τῷ διαπυϊσκομένῳ σώματι θερμότητα γεννῶντα πρὸς τῷ μήτ’ ἀφαιρεῖν τι τῆς οὔσης ἐν αὐτῷ ὑγρότητος μήτε προστιθέναι, τὰ δ’ ὡς καὶ πλέονα τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἀνάπτοντα καὶ συνάγοντά τι τῆς ὑγρότητος.
english_sentence_A: For the former are so inasmuch as they generate a heat most similar to the body that is being brought to suppuration, in addition to neither removing anything of the moisture that is present in it nor adding to it; the latter inasmuch as they kindle a heat even greater than the natural one and draw together some of the moisture.
english_sentence_B: The former generate a heat most similar to that of the body being brought to suppuration, and besides neither take away any of the moisture present in it nor add any.

english_sentence_A: Now the notion of the suppurating drugs is at once clear and familiar to everyone; for suppuration is a change into pus.
english_sentence_B: The latter kindle even more heat than the natural and gather together some of the moisture.

greek_sentence: εἴ γε δὴ τὸ μὲν ἁπλῶς σκληρὸν λέγεται καθάπερ ἡ γῆ, τὸ δὲ κατ’ ἐπικράτειαν, ὡς ὄνυξ καὶ πλῆκτρον καὶ κέρας, τὸ δὲ πρὸς τὸ σύμμετρον ὁμογενὲς ἢ ὁμοειδὲς, παραβαλόντα ὡς τόδε τι ζῶον, οἷον ἐλέφας, ἢ ὅδε τις ἄνθρωπος, οἷον ὁ Ἡρακλῆς, τὸ [715] δὲ πρὸς ὁτιοῦν παραβαλλόμενον, ὡς ὁ Διογένης πρὸς τὸν Ἀριστοτέλη.

(pl.), Paul.Aeg. 3.22.23 . part of the liver, Ruf. Onom. 180 , Sch. Nic. Th. 560 . veined gem, onyx, LXX Jb. 28.16 , Aristeas 66 , J. BJ 5.5.7 ; Σαρδῷος ὄ. sardonyx, Luc. lsj_entry_text: κέρας, τό, Ep. gen. Κέραος, Att. contr. κέρως; Ep. dat. κέραϊ (elided) or κέραι or κέρᾳ Il. 11.385 , cf. Hdn.Gr. 2.75 , κέρᾳ also in Th. 2.90 , 7.6 : nom. pl. κέρα (v. infr.), gen. κεράων, κερῶν, dat. κέρασι, Ep. κεράεσσι:— Att. Inscrr. have dual [ κέρ]ατε IG 12.301.109 : pl.κέρατα ib. 237.59 ; later Ep. κεράατα () Nic. Th. 291 , κεράατος () Arat. 174 , Q.S. 6.225 :—Hdt.has gen. κέρεος 6.111 , dat. κέρεϊ 9.102 : pl. κέρεα 2.38 , κερέων ib. 132 ; but Hp. has gen. sg. κέρως, pl. κέρατα, Aër. 18 . [In nom. and acc. κέρας, α always: in the obl. cases α in Ep. , as κέρασιν Od. 3.384 (in contr. dat. κέρᾳ, nom. pl. κέρα (cf. Batr. 165 ), a is shortd. before a vowel, Il. 11.385 , Od. 19.211 ); but α in Trag.and Com., κέρατος Hermipp. 43 , κέρατα E. Ba. 921 , κεράτων [α] prob. in S. Tr. 519 (lyr.), κέρασι A. Fr. 185 . In later Ep. the quantity varies.] (κέρας is prob. related to κάρα; cf. κεραός.) the horn of an animal, in Hom. mostly of oxen, Il. 17.521 , etc.; ταῦροι . . εἰς κέρας θυμούμενοι E. Ba. 743 ; ὀφθαλμοὶ δ' ὡς εἰ κέρα ἕστασαν his eyes stood fixed and stiff like horns, Od. 19.211 ; as a symbol of strength, LXX Ps. 17(18).3 , Diogenian. 7.89 , cf. Arist. PA 662a1 ; of elephants' tusks, Aret. SD 2.13 , Opp. C. 2.494 . antennae of crustaceans, Arist. HA 526a31 , 590b27 ; of the silkworm's grub, ib. 551b10 . horn, as a material, αἱ μὲν γὰρ [πύλαι] κεράεσσι τετεύχαται Od. 19.563 ; the horn of animals' hoofs, Longus 2.28 . anything made of horn, bow, τόξον ἐνώμα . . πειρώμενος . . μὴ κέρα ἶπες ἔδοιεν Od. 21.395 , cf. Theoc. 25.206 , Call. Epigr. 38 , AP 6.75 ( Paul.Sil. ); for Il. 11.385 v. infr. v.l. of musical instruments, horn for blowing, σημῆναι τῷ κέρατι X. An. 2.2.4 , cf. Arist. Aud. 802a17 ; also, the Phrygian flute, because it was tipped with horn (cf. Poll. 4.74 ), αὐλεῖν τῷ κ. Luc. DDeor. 12.1 ; καὶ κέρατι μὲν αὐλεῖν Τυρρηνοὶ νομίζουσι Poll. 4.76 , cf. Ath. 4.184a . drinking-horn, ἐκ τοῦ κέρατος αὖ μοι δὸς πιεῖν Hermipp. 43 , cf. X. An. 7.2.23 , OGI 214.43 (Didyma, iii B.C.); ἐξ ἀργυρέων κ. πίνειν Pi. Fr. 166 , cf. IG 12.280.77 ; ἀργυρηλάτοις κέρασι χρυσᾶ στόμια προσβεβλημένοις A. Fr. 185 ; ἐκπιόντι χρύσεον κ. S. Fr. 483 ; for measuring liquids, Gal. 13.435 . Ἀμαλθείας κ. cornucopiae, v. Ἀμάλθεια . βοὸς κ. prob. a horn guard or cover attached to a fishing-line, Il. 24.81 , cf. Sch.; ἐς πόντον προΐησι βοὸς κέρας Od. 12.253 ; ψάμμῳ κ. αἰὲν ἐρείδων AP 6.230 ( Maec. ), cf. Aristarch. ap. Apollon. Lex. s.v. κέρᾳ ἀγλαέ , Arist. ap. Plu. 2.977a (also expld. as a fishing-line of ox-hair (cf. infr.v.l), ap. Plu. 2.976f , cf. Poll. 2.31 ; perh. an artificial bait). clyster-pipe, Orib. 8.32 7 . in pl., horn points with which the writing-reed was tipped, AP 6.227 ( Crin. ). of objects shaped like horns, a mode of dressing the hair, κέρᾳ ἀγλαέ Il. 11.385 (unless the meaning be bow), cf. Aristarch. ad loc., Herodorus and Apionap. Eust. ad loc.: hence κέρας is expld. as = θρίξ or κόμη, Apollon. Lex. , Hdn.Gr. ap. Eust.l.c., Poll. 2.31 , Hsch. ; cf. iv. l, and v. κεροπλάστης . arm or branch of a river, Ὠκεανοῖο κ. Hes. Th. 789 ; Νείλου Pi. Fr. 201 ; τὸ Μενδήσιον κέρας Th. 1.110 ; ἐν Ἰνδοῖς ἐν τῷ Κέρατι καλουμένῳ Arist. Mir. 835b5 , cf. Mu. 393b5 ; τὸ κ. τὸ Βυζαντίων the 'Golden Horn', Str. 7.6.2 , cf. Plb. 4.43.7 , Sch. A.R. 4.282 ; Ἑσπέρου K., name of a bay, Hanno Peripl. 14 , cf. Philostr. VS 1.21.2 . wing of an army, Hdt. 9.26 , etc.; or fleet, Id. 6.8 , Th. 2.90 , etc.; κ. δεξιόν, λαιόν, A. Pers. 399 , E. Supp. 704 ; τὸ εὐώνυμον κ. ἀναπτύσσειν X. An. 1.10.9 . κατὰ κέρας προσβάλλειν, ἐπιπεσεῖν, to attack in flank, Th. 3.78 , X. HG 6.5.16 , etc.; κατὰ κ. προσιέναι, ἕπεσθαι, Id. greek_sentence: ἐάσαντες οὖν τὰ λοιπὰ πάντα σημαινόμενα περὶ τῶν πρὸς τὸν ἄριστα κατεσκευασμένον ἄνθρωπον ἐπισκεψώμεθα μαλακῶν καὶ σκληρῶν, ὃν δὴ κανόνα καὶ μέτρον ἐποιησάμεθα τῶν οὕτω λεγομένων ἁπάντων, οὐδὲ τούτου πρὸς τὸ ἐπιτυχὸν μόριον, οἷον ὀστοῦν ἢ πιμελὴν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μέσον τῇ κράσει, τὸ δέρμα καὶ τούτου μάλιστα τὸ κατὰ τὰς χεῖρας, ἵνα περ ἡ ἁπτικὴ δύναμις ἀκριβοῦται· συμβαίνει δ’ εἰς ταὐτὸ καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἐπικράτησιν, ὡς πρὸς τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, οὕτως ὀνομάζεσθαι μαλακὸν ἢ σκληρὸν, [716] ἐπειδὴ μεσότης τίς ἐστιν ἡμῶν ἡ ἁφὴ, καθ’ ὃ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ἐδίδασκεν.
english_sentence_A: Leaving aside, then, all the remaining significations, let us examine the soft and hard things [as spoken of] in relation to the best-constituted human being, whom indeed we have made the rule and measure of all things so called—and not [in relation to] any chance part of him, such as bone or soft fat, but the part that is intermediate in mixture, the skin, and of this above all the part on the hands, where precisely the tactile faculty is at its most exact.
english_sentence_B: Leaving aside, then, all the other meanings, let us examine the things that are soft and hard relative to the best-constituted human being, whom we have made the canon and measure of all things so called. And we do not measure relative to any chance part of him, such as bone or fat, but relative to the part intermediate in its mixture, the skin, and of this especially the skin of the hands, where the tactile faculty is brought to its greatest precision.

greek_sentence: ἐάσαντες οὖν τὰ λοιπὰ πάντα σημαινόμενα περὶ τῶν πρὸς τὸν ἄριστα κατεσκευασμένον ἄνθρωπον ἐπισκεψώμεθα μαλακῶν καὶ σκληρῶν, ὃν δὴ κανόνα καὶ μέτρον ἐποιησάμεθα τῶν οὕτω λεγομένων ἁπάντων, οὐδὲ τούτου πρὸς τὸ ἐπιτυχὸν μόριον, οἷον ὀστοῦν ἢ πιμελὴν, ἀλλὰ τὸ μέσον τῇ κράσει, τὸ δέρμα καὶ τούτου μάλιστα τὸ κατὰ τὰς χεῖρας, ἵνα περ ἡ ἁπτικὴ δύναμις ἀκριβοῦται· συμβαίνει δ’ εἰς ταὐτὸ καὶ τὸ κατ’ ἐπικράτησιν, ὡς πρὸς τὴν ὅλην οὐσίαν, οὕτως ὀνομάζεσθαι μαλακὸν ἢ σκληρὸν, [716] ἐπειδὴ μεσότης τίς ἐστιν ἡμῶν ἡ ἁφὴ, καθ’ ὃ καὶ Ἀριστοτέλης ἐδίδασκεν.
english_sentence_A: Leaving aside, then, all the remaining significations, let us examine the soft and hard things [as spoken of] in relation to the best-constituted human being, whom indeed we have made the rule and measure of all things so called—and not [in relation to] any chance part of him, such as bone or soft fat, but the part that is intermediate in mixture, the skin, and of this above all the part on the hands, where precisely the tactile faculty is at its most exact.
english_sentence_B: Leaving aside, then, all the other meanings, let us examine the things that are soft and hard relative to the best-constituted human being, whom we have made the canon and measure of all things so called. And we do not measure relative to any chance part of him, such as bone or fat, but relative to the part intermediate in its mixture, the skin, and of this especially the skin of the hands, where the tactile faculty is brought to its greatest precision.

greek_sentence: Ἐπεὶ δὲ πολυειδῶς ἕκαστον γίνεται σκληρότερον ἢ ξηραινόμενον ἢ πηγνύμενον ἢ ὑπερπληρούμενον, [717] ὡς διατετάσθαι σφοδρῶς ἢ κατὰ συζυγίαν τινὰ πάσχον κατ’ αὐτὰ καὶ τὸ μαλάττεσθαι καθ’ ἕκαστον αὐτῶν ἴδιον ἔσται· διελώμεθα οὖν ὑπὲρ ἁπάντων ἑξῆς, ἀναμνήσαντες πρότερον ὡς τὸ τῶν ὀνομάτων τε καὶ ῥημάτων εὐχερὲς τὰ μὲν πολλὰ οὐκ ἀγεννὲς, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον τὸ τούτου ἐναντίον ἀνελεύθερόν ἐστιν, ὅτε μὴ ἀναγκαῖον γίγνεται διαστέλλεσθαι περὶ αὐτῶν.
english_sentence_A: But since each thing becomes harder in many ways — either being dried, or being congealed, or being overfilled [717] so as to be violently distended, or being affected according to some conjunction of these — the softening too, in the case of each of them, will be specific to it. Let us then draw distinctions concerning all of them in order, first recalling that an easy-going attitude about nouns and verbs is for the most part not ignoble, but rather its opposite is illiberal, whenever it is not necessary to make distinctions about them.
english_sentence_B: Since each thing becomes harder in many ways, being either dried, or congealed, or overfilled, [717] so as to be violently distended, or suffering these in some combination, the softening will also be specific to each of them. Let us therefore draw distinctions about all of them in order, first recalling that a free and easy use of nouns and verbs is for the most part not ignoble; rather, its opposite is illiberal, when it is not necessary to draw distinctions about them.

greek_sentence: τὸ μὲν γὰρ ὑπεῖκον εἰς ἑαυτὸ μαλακόν ἐστιν, ἐάν γε ἁπλοῦν ὑπάρχῃ σῶμα· τὸ δ’ ἐκ πλειόνων συγκείμενον ἤτοι ψαυόντων, ὡς ὁ τῶν πυρῶν σωρὸς, ἢ ἐπιπεπλεγμένων πως, ὡς ὁ πόκος ἢ τὰ πλόκαμα, δύναιτ’ ἂν ὑπείκειν τε ἅμα καὶ μὴ εἶναι μαλακόν.
english_sentence_A: For what yields into itself is soft, provided that it is a simple body; but what is composed of several things, either touching one another, like a heap of wheat-grains, or somehow interwoven, like a fleece or plaits (πλόκαμα), could yield and at the same time not be soft.
english_sentence_B: For that which yields into itself is soft, if indeed it is a simple body. But what is composed of several things, either touching one another, like the heap of wheat, or in some way interwoven, like fleece or braids, could both yield and at the same time not be soft.

greek_sentence: ἔμπαλιν δ’ ἐπὶ τῶν πεπληρωμένων ἀκριβῶς, οἷον ἀσκῶν ἢ κύστεων, οὐχ ὑπείκει μὲν εἰς αὐτὸ τὸ συναμφότερον, οὐ μὴν σκληρόν γέ ἐστι τὸ περιεχόμενον, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τὸ περιέχον, ὁπότε πεπλήρωται, σκληρότερον ἑαυτοῦ γέγονεν, ἤ τινα ἐπίκτητον ἑτέραν εἴληφε διάθεσιν, [718] ὅτι μὴ τέταται μόνον ἐκ τοῦ τέως κεχαλασμένου.
english_sentence_A: Conversely, in the case of things that have been completely filled, such as wineskins or bladders, the two together do not yield into themselves, yet neither is what is contained hard; nor, for that matter, has the container, once it has been filled, become harder than it was or taken on some other acquired condition, [718] except only that it has become stretched from having previously been slack.
english_sentence_B: Conversely, in things that are filled completely, such as wineskins or bladders, the two together do not yield into themselves; yet the contents are certainly not hard, nor has the container, when it has been filled, become harder than it was, or taken on any other acquired condition, [718] except that it has merely been stretched from its previously slack state.

english_sentence_A: For what has been hardened by dryness needs to be moistened, what by congealing to be heated, what by filling to be evacuated, what by dryness together with congealing to be both moistened and heated, and what by congealing together with filling to be both heated and evacuated.
english_sentence_B: For what has been hardened by dryness needs to be moistened; what by congelation, to be warmed; what by filling, to be emptied; what by dryness and congelation together, to be both moistened and warmed; and what by congelation and filling together, to be both warmed and emptied.

english_sentence_B: Bodies, then, are dried without congelation in immoderate exercises, in intense sun, in severe deprivations, in a causus-like fever, and by certain drugs, namely those that dry without cooling.

english_sentence_A: And of the chilling, in turn, the cause is threefold: one from the things that impinge from outside, such as air, water, or a drug, as they often bring it about in cases of erysipelas; another, the proper mixture of the affected part; and another, third, in addition to these, arising from the humour that has flowed into it. For often that humour has already become hotter than it was, either because it is putrefying or because it is altered by the parts in contact with it that are hot by nature; but the chilling which it imparted to some part of those that are colder by nature persists for a long time.

english_sentence_A: The softening drug, however, seems not to bear upon all these ways, but especially upon those that have been hardened through congelation, and still more if there is also some moisture contained in them contrary to nature, as in the case of parts that have become scirrhous.
english_sentence_B: The softening drug, however, does not seem to apply to all of these ways, but specifically to those hardened through congelation, and still more if some moisture contrary to nature is also contained in them, as in the case of things that have become scirrhous.

Sil.). stick or fix on, κεφαλὴν ἀνὰ σκολόπεσσι Il. 18.177 ; σκόλοψι δέμας E. IT 1430 ; κρᾶτα πήξασ' ἐπ' ἄκρον θύρσον Id. lsj_entry_text: περισσός, Att. περιττός, ή, όν, (from περί, as ἔπισσαι from ἐπί, μέτασσαι from μετά) beyond the regular number or size, prodigious, δῶρα Hes. Th. 399 (never in Hom. ); ῶʼμος Trag.Adesp. 458.3 ; στάθμα, dub.sens., v. ἕλκω B. 3 . out of the common, extraordinary, strange, ἔ τι περισσὸν εἰδείη if he has any signal knowledge, Thgn. 769 ; εἴ τι φρονεῖς καί τι περισσὸν ἔχεις Philisc.( PLG 2.327 ); π. λόγος S. OT 841 ; ἄγρα E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); πάθος Id. Supp. 791 (lyr.); βίος οὐδὲν ἔχων π. ἀλλὰ πάντα σμικρά Antipho Soph. 51 ; οὐ γὰρ π. οὐδὲν οὐδ' ἔξω λόγου πέπονθας E. Hipp. 437 ; περισσότερα παθήματα Antipho 3.4.5 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἔργων καὶ τερατώδη Isoc. 12.77 ; ἴδια καὶ π. Id. 15.145 ; π. καὶ θαυμαστά Arist. EN 1141b6 ; πρᾶξις π. Id. Pol. 1312a27 ; οὐθὲν δὴ λέγοντες π. φαίνονταί τι λέγειν Id. Metaph. 1053b3 ; τί π. ποιεῖτε; Ev.Matt. 5.47 ; περιττοτάτη φύσις Arist. HA 531a9 ; συνανθρωπίζον . . πάντων περισσότατον, of the dog, Ath. 13.611c , cf. Clearch. 24 ; in Literature, striking, τὸ περιττόν, as a quality of οἱ τοῦ Σωκράτους λόγοι, Arist. Pol. 1265a11 ; τὰ σοφὰ καὶ τὰ π. refinements, Epicur. Fr. 409 ; opp. κοινὸς καὶ δημώδης, Longin. 40.2 (but also, elaborate, π. καὶ πεποιημένος Id. 3.4 ; in bad sense, far-fetched, D.H. Pomp. 2 , Dem. 56 ). of persons, extraordinary, remarkable, esp. for great learning, π. ὢν ἀνήρ E. Hipp. 948 ; τοὺς . . π. καί τι πράσσοντας πλέον Id. Fr. 788 ; δυστυχεῖς εἶναι τοὺς π. Arist. Metaph. 983a2 ; π. γένος τῶν μελιττῶν Id. GA 760a4 : freq. with the manner added, π. κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν Id. Pr. 953a10 ; περὶ τὸν ἄλλον βίον περιττότερος somewhat extravagant or eccentric, Id. Pol. 1267 b24 ; τῇ φύσει π. Id. HA 622b6 ; κάλλει Plu. Demetr. 2 ; ἐν ἅπασι Id. Dem. 3 ; τὴν ὥραν Alciphr. 1.12 : c. inf., D.H. Comp. 18 . c. gen., περισσὸς ἄλλων πρός τι beyond others in . . , S. El. 155 ; θύσει τοῦδε περισσότερα greater things than this, AP 6.321 (Leon. Alex. ); περιττότερος προφήτου one greater than . . , Ev.Matt. 11.9 . more than sufficient, superfluous, αἱ π. δαπάναι X. Mem. 3.6.6 ; περιττὸν ἔχειν to have a surplus, Id. An. 7.6.31 ; οἱ μὲν . . περιττὰ ἔχουσιν, οἱ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ ἀναγκαῖα . . Id. Oec. 20.1 : c. gen., τῶν ἀρκούντων περιττά more than sufficient, Id. Cyr. 8.2.21 ; τὰ π. τῶν ἱκανῶν Id. Hier. 1.19 : freq. in military sense, οἱ π. ἱππεῖς the reserve horse, Id. Eq.Mag. 8.14 ; οἱ π. τῆς φυλακῆς ib. 7.7 ; π. σκηναί spare tents, Id. Cyr. 4.6.12 (but τοῖς περιττοῖς χρήσεσθαι their superior numbers, Id. An. 4.8.11 , cf. Cyr. 6.3.20 ); τὸ π. the surplus, residue, Inscr. ap. eund. An. 5.3.13 (but τὸ π. τοῦ Ἰουδαίου the advantage of the Jew, Ep.Rom. 3.1 ); Ἁρπυιῶν τὰ π. their leavings, AP 11.239 ( Lucill. ); τὸ π. τῆς ἡμέρας the remainder of the day, X.Eph. 1.3 ; π. γράμματα supplementary provisions in a will, BGU 326ii9 (ii A.D.). in bad sense, superfluous, useless, οὐδέ τι τοῦ παντὸς κενεὸν πέλει οὐδὲ π. Emp. 13 ; μόχθος π. A. Pr. 385 , cf. S. Ant. 780 ; π. κἀνόνητα σώματα Id. Aj. 758 ; βάρος π. γῆς ἀναστρωφώμενοι Id. Fr. 945 ; ἄχθος Id. El. 1241 (lyr.); τὰ γὰρ π. πανταχοῦ λυπήρ' ἔπη Id. Fr. 82 ; αὐδῶ σε μὴ περισσὰ κηρύσσειν A. Th. 1048 ; π. πάντες οὑν μέσῳ λόγοι E. Med. 819 ; π. φωνῶν Id. Supp. 459 . excessive, extravagant, μηχανᾶσθαι περισσά commit extravagances, Hdt. 2.32 ; περισσὰ δρᾶν, πράσσειν, to be over-busy, S. Tr. 617 , Ant. 68 ; π. φρονεῖν to be over-wise, E. Fr. 924 (anap.); ἡ π. αὕτη ἐπιμέλεια τοῦ σώματος Pl. R. 407b ; μῆκος πολὺ λόγων π. Id. Lg. 645c ; redundant, overdone, οἱ καρτεροὶ καὶ π. λόγοι Id. Ax. 365c , etc.; of dress, ἐσθὴς π. Plu. 2.615d ; περισσοτέρα λύπη 2 Ep.Cor. 2.7 ; τοῦ τὰ δέοντ' ἔχειν περιττὰ μισῶ I hate extravagance in comparison with moderation, Alex. 254 , etc. of persons, over-wise, over-curious, περισσὸς καὶ φρονῶν μέγα E. Hipp. 445 , cf. Ba. 429 (lyr.); ὁ πολυπράγμων καὶ π. Plb. 9.1.4 ; τὴν περὶ τὸ σῶμα θεραπείαν ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. Plu. Cic. 8 ; so, of speakers, π. ἐν τοῖς λόγοις Δημοσθένης Aeschin. 1.119 . as a term of praise, subtle, acute, ἀκριβὴς καὶ π. διάνοια Arist. Top. 141b13 . Arith., ἀριθμὸς π. an odd, uneven number, opp. ἄρτιος, Epich. 170.7 , Philol. 5 , Pl. Prt. 356e , etc.; π. ἡμέραι Hp. Aph. 4.61 ; τὸ π. καὶ τὸ ἄρτιον the nature of odd and even, Pl. Grg. 451c , etc.; π. χῶραι the odd places in a verse, Heph. 5.1 ; ἀρτιάκις π. ἀριθμός a number divisible by an odd number an even number of times, as 2 , 6 , 10 , Euc. 7 Def. 9 . περισσότεροι more in number, extra, Carnead. ap. S.E. M. 9.140 . περιττόν, τό, = στρύχνος μανικός, θρύον 11 , Thphr. HP 9.11.6 ; περισσόν Dsc. 4.73 ; περίσκον Orib. 12.8.56 . Adv. περισσῶς extraordinarily, exceedingly, θεοσεβέεες π. ἐόντες Hdt. 2.37 ; ἐπαινέσεται π. E. Ba. 1197 (lyr.); π. παῖδας ἐκδιδάσκεσθαι to have them educated overmuch, Id. Med. 295 ; περιττοτέρως τῶν ἄλλων far above all others, Isoc. 3.44 ; περισσότερον τοῦ ἑνός Luc. Pr.Im. 14 ; also περισσά Pi. N. 7.43 , E. Hec. 579 , etc. remarkably, περισσότερον τῶν ἄλλων θάψαι τινά more sumptuously, Hdt. 2.129 ; οἴκησις π. ἐσκευασμένη Plb. 1.29.7 ; περιττότατα ἔχειν to be most remarkable, Arist. HA 589a31 ; κοσμουμένη π. καὶ σεμνῶς Plu. 2.145e ; περισσότατα ἀνθρώπων θρησκεύειν in the most singular way, D.C. 37.17 ; ἡδέως καὶ π. in an uncommon manner, D.H. Comp. 3 ; εἰπεῖν στρογγύλως καὶ π. Id. Is. 20 ; ἰδίως καὶ π. Plu. Thes. 19 ; τὰ καινῶς ἱστορούμενα καὶ π. Id. 2.30d . abundantly, ἐχέτω π. τῆς κρόκης Alciphr. 3.41 . with a neg., οὐδὲν περισσὸν τούτων nothing more than or beyond these, Antipho 3.4.6 ; οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιττότερον πραγματεύεσθαι Pl. Ap. 20c ; οὐδὲν π. ἢ εἰ . . no otherwise than if . . , Id. Smp. 219c ; περισσόν alone, furthermore, LXX Ec. 12.12 ,al. τὰ περισσά in vain, AP 12.182 ( Strat. ). ἐκ περιττοῦ superfluously, uselessly, Pl. Prt. 338c , Sph. 265e ; but ὑπερέχειν ἐκ π. to be far superior, Id. Lg. 734d , cf. 802d ; ἡ κάμινος ἐκαύθη ἐκ π. Thd. Da. 3.22 ; ἐκ π. χρησάμενος τῇ παρρησίᾳ Luc. Pro Merc.Cond. 13 ; cf. ὑπερεκπερισσοῦ.

greek_sentence: ἐκκενοῖ γὰρ τὴν περιττὴν ὑγρότητα ταῦτα σύμπαντα, κατ’ ἴδιον ἕκαστον λόγον.
english_sentence_A: For all of these evacuate the surplus moisture, each according to its own principle.
english_sentence_B: For all of these evacuate the superfluous wetness, each by its own principle.

lsj_entry_text: νοτ-ίς, ίδος, ἡ, moisture, A. Fr. 481 , E. Ph. 646 (lyr.), Pl. Ti. 60d , Thphr. CP 5.6.1 , etc. ; ποντία ν. E. Hec. 1259 ; of perspiration, Arist. Pr. 866a21 , Gal. 10.541 .
greek_sentence: ὅσα μὲν ψύχει κατὰ διττὸν τρόπον, ἀποκρουόμενά τε ἅμα καὶ συνεξάγοντα τῷ θερμῷ νοτίδα πολλὴν, ὡς Ἀριστοτέλης ἐδίδασκεν.
english_sentence_A: Those that cool do so in a twofold manner, at once repelling and at the same time drawing out, together with the heat, much moisture, as Aristotle taught.
english_sentence_B: Those that cool do so in two ways, at once repelling and also drawing out, together with the heat, much moisture, as Aristotle taught.

lsj_entry_text: ἀτμός, ὁ, steam, vapour, A. Eu. 138 ; ὅταν ἐκ γῆς ἀ. ἀνίῃ . . ὑπὸ τοῦ ἡλίου Arist. Pr. 862a4 ; Ἄραψ ἀ., of incense, Pae.Delph.II: in pl., vapours, A. Fr. 205 ; clouds of steam, Jul. Mis. 341d ; esp. of odours, A. Ag. 1311 , Arist. Pr. 908a21 , Ph. 1.96 ,al., Lib. Or. 12.79 (pl.), etc.; distd. from ἀτμίς, as dry from moist, by Olymp. in Mete. 165.25 . [ατμ A. Fr. 205 .]
greek_sentence: ὅσα δὲ θερμαίνει, τῷ λύειν εἰς ἀτμοὺς μὲν τὸ περιεχόμενον ὑγρὸν ἐν τοῖς θερμαινομένοις σώμασιν, ὅσα δὲ ξηραίνει, καθάπερ τὰ διαφορητικὰ προσαγορευόμενα, κατὰ διττὸν καὶ ταῦτα τρόπον, ἢ ἀναπίνοντα τὰς ὑγρότητας, ὅταν ἐν πόροις τισὶν ὑπάρχωσιν, ἢ ὅλον ἀλλοιοῦντα τὸ μόριον.
english_sentence_A: Those that heat, by dissolving into vapours the moisture contained in the bodies that are being heated; and those that dry, like those called dispersing, these too in a twofold manner, either drinking up the moistures when they are present in certain pores, or altering the whole part.
english_sentence_B: Those that heat do so by dissolving into vapours the moist matter contained in the bodies being heated. Those that dry, such as the so-called dispersing drugs, these too act in two ways, either by drinking up the wetnesses, when they are present in certain pores, or by altering the whole part.

greek_sentence: ὅσα δὲ θερμαίνει, τῷ λύειν εἰς ἀτμοὺς μὲν τὸ περιεχόμενον ὑγρὸν ἐν τοῖς θερμαινομένοις σώμασιν, ὅσα δὲ ξηραίνει, καθάπερ τὰ διαφορητικὰ προσαγορευόμενα, κατὰ διττὸν καὶ ταῦτα τρόπον, ἢ ἀναπίνοντα τὰς ὑγρότητας, ὅταν ἐν πόροις τισὶν ὑπάρχωσιν, ἢ ὅλον ἀλλοιοῦντα τὸ μόριον.
english_sentence_A: Those that heat, by dissolving into vapours the moisture contained in the bodies that are being heated; and those that dry, like those called dispersing, these too in a twofold manner, either drinking up the moistures when they are present in certain pores, or altering the whole part.
english_sentence_B: Those that heat do so by dissolving into vapours the moist matter contained in the bodies being heated. Those that dry, such as the so-called dispersing drugs, these too act in two ways, either by drinking up the wetnesses, when they are present in certain pores, or by altering the whole part.

english_sentence_A: But what the right moment for the use of each is belongs not to the present treatise but to the therapeutic method.
english_sentence_B: But what the right time for the use of each is belongs not to the present treatise but to the therapeutic method.

greek_sentence: ὅσα δ’ [721] ὑπὸ ψύξεώς τε ἅμα καὶ ξηρότητος ἐσκλήρυνται, θερμαίνειν ὁμοῦ ταῦτα καὶ ὑγραίνειν προσῆκεν, οὐχ οἷάπερ τὰ διαπυήσαντα, θερμότητι ἅμα καὶ ὑγρότητι συμμέτρῳ κατὰ φύσιν, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον μὲν εἶναι χρὴ τὸ φάρμακον θερμότερον, ἐφ’ ὅσον ἡ ψύξις ἐκράτησεν, ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον δ’ ὑγρότερον, ἐφ’ ὅσον ἡ ξηρότης· ἔστι δὲ καὶ τούτων μέτρον ὁρίσαι τῆς θεραπευτικῆς μεθόδου.
english_sentence_A: But those [721] that have been hardened by cooling together with dryness, it is fitting to heat and at the same time to moisten, not in the way that suppurating parts are treated, with heat and moisture that are moderate according to nature; rather, the drug must be hotter to the extent that the cooling has prevailed, and moister to the extent that the dryness has; and to define the measure of these too belongs to the therapeutic method.
english_sentence_B: But those parts that [721] have been hardened by cold and dryness together ought to be warmed and moistened at the same time; not in the way that parts that have suppurated are treated, with heat and moisture together that are moderate and in accordance with nature, but the drug must be warmer by as much as the cold has prevailed, and moister by as much as the dryness has; and defining the measure of these too belongs to the therapeutic method.

greek_sentence: εἰ δὲ καὶ μιχθεῖεν εἰς ταὐτὸ ἀμφότερα, πολὺ δὴ μᾶλλον ὑγραῖνον ἅμα καὶ θερμαῖνον ἔσται τὸ μικτὸν ἐξ αὐτῶν, ὥσπερ καὶ λουτρὰ τῶν ποτίμων ὑδάτων σὺν ἐλαίῳ δαψιλεῖ.

english_sentence_B: And if both are mixed together into one, the mixture made from them will be much more moistening and warming at once, just as baths of potable waters with abundant oil are.

english_sentence_A: The one contrary to nature, by contrast, has its change brought about by an alien heat, and to nothing useful; while the one intermediate between them, the one that follows in suppurations, is brought about by the innate heat, though not by one that masters completely; for neither is it accomplished out of matter that is completely useful, just as not out of matter that is altogether alien either.
english_sentence_B: The one intermediate between them, which accompanies suppurations (empyēseis), comes about through the innate heat, but a heat that does not exactly master it. For it is not accomplished out of material that is exactly useful, just as it is not accomplished out of material that is wholly foreign either.

greek_sentence: τοιοῦτον οὖν εἶναι χρὴ καὶ τὸ τῇ διαπυήσει [725] συλληψόμενον φάρμακον, οἷόν περ καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἔμφυτον ὑπάρχει θερμὸν ἐν ταῖς εὐκράτοις φύσεσιν· εἰ δὲ θερμοτέρα τοῦ δέοντος ἡ φύσις ὑπάρχει, τὸ διαπυΐσκον φάρμακον ἐν ἐκείνῳ τῷ σώματι θερμότερον εἶναι δεήσει, καὶ τοσούτῳ γε τοῦ συμμέτρου θερμότερον, ὅσῳ καὶ ἡ φύσις ἐστὶ τῆς εὐκράτου θερμοτέρα, ὥστε καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ἤδη πρόδηλον ἐκ τῆς θεραπευτικῆς ὑπάρχει μεθόδου, τὸ καθ’ ἕκαστον ἄνθρωπον ἴδιον εἶναι τὸ διαπυΐσκον φάρμακον.
english_sentence_A: Such, then, must also be the drug that is going to assist [725] suppuration, of the very same kind as the innate heat itself is in well-tempered natures; but if the nature is hotter than it ought to be, the suppurating drug in that body will need to be hotter, and hotter than the moderate one by just so much as the nature too is hotter than the well-tempered one, so that this, for its part, is already evident from the therapeutic method, namely that the suppurating drug is peculiar to each individual human being.

english_sentence_A: Such, then, must also be the drug that is going to assist [725] suppuration, of the very same kind as the innate heat itself is in well-tempered natures; but if the nature is hotter than it ought to be, the suppurating drug in that body will need to be hotter, and hotter than the moderate one by just so much as the nature too is hotter than the well-tempered one, so that this, for its part, is already evident from the therapeutic method, namely that the suppurating drug is peculiar to each individual human being.
english_sentence_B: Such, then, must also be the drug that is to assist suppuration [725], namely of the same kind as the innate heat itself is in well-tempered natures. But if the nature is hotter than it should be, the suppurating drug will have to be hotter in that body, and hotter than the moderate one by just as much as the nature too is hotter than the well-tempered one.

greek_sentence: οὐχ ἥκιστα δὲ καὶ τὸ πολλάκις ἡμῖν ἀποδεδειγμένον ὑπὸ τούτων μαρτυρεῖται, τὸ χρῆναι πάσας τῶν φαρμάκων τὰς δυνάμεις πρὸς τὸν ἄριστα κεκραμένον ἄνθρωπον ἐξετάζεσθαι· μηδὲ γὰρ συστῆναι δύνασθαι τέχνην μηδεμίαν, εἰ μὴ πρότερον οἷον κανόνα τινὰ καὶ σκοπὸν τῷ γένει τῆς ὕλης, ἐν ᾗ καταγίνεται, θέμενος πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ἤδη τὰ κατὰ μέρος ἀπευθύνοι πάντα.
english_sentence_A: And not least is what has often been demonstrated by us also attested by these considerations, namely that all the powers of drugs must be examined with reference to the best-mixed human being; for no art whatsoever can be constituted, unless one first sets up, as it were, a certain rule and target for the kind of material in which it is engaged, and then directs all the particulars toward that.
english_sentence_B: And these things bear witness, not least, to what we have often demonstrated, that all the powers of drugs must be examined with reference to the best-tempered human being. For no art can be established at all unless one first sets up a kind of canon and target for the class of material with which it is occupied, and then directs all the particulars by reference to that.

greek_sentence: πάλιν οὖν ὑποθέμενοι τῷ λόγῳ τὸν ἄριστα κεκραμένον ἄνθρωπον οἷον σκοπόν τινα, πρὸς ἐκεῖνον ἀναφέροντες, ἐκπυΐσκον τι λέγομεν εἶναι φάρμακον ἕτερον τοῦ μαλάττοντος τὰ σκιῤῥούμενα, τάς τε κράσεις αὐτῶν ὑπάρχειν οἵας ἔμπροσθεν ἔφαμεν [726] εἶναι, τοῦ μὲν εἰς πύου γένεσιν συντελοῦντος τῇ φύσει, σύμμετρόν τε καὶ ὁμοίαν ᾧ προσάγεται σώματι;
english_sentence_A: Again, then, positing in our account the best-mixed human being as a kind of target, and referring to him, we say that a suppurative drug is something different from the one that softens parts that are becoming scirrhous, and that their mixtures are such as we said earlier [726] they were: that of the one which assists nature toward the generation of pus being well-proportioned and similar to the body to which it is applied; and, because our nature is moist and warm, such drugs are often called moist and warm; whereas that of the one which softens the scirrhous part is much warmer than the well-mixed nature, yet certainly not already strongly warm.
english_sentence_B: Once more, then, positing in our account the best-mixed human being as a kind of target, and referring to him, we say that a suppurative drug is something different from one that softens indurated parts, and that their mixtures are such as we said [726] earlier: that of the drug which contributes to the generation of pus is moderate and similar to the body to which it is applied by nature; and because our nature is moist and hot, such drugs are often called moist and hot.

english_sentence_A: Again, then, positing in our account the best-mixed human being as a kind of target, and referring to him, we say that a suppurative drug is something different from the one that softens parts that are becoming scirrhous, and that their mixtures are such as we said earlier [726] they were: that of the one which assists nature toward the generation of pus being well-proportioned and similar to the body to which it is applied; and, because our nature is moist and warm, such drugs are often called moist and warm; whereas that of the one which softens the scirrhous part is much warmer than the well-mixed nature, yet certainly not already strongly warm.
english_sentence_B: The mixture of the drug that softens what is indurated, on the other hand, is much hotter than the well-mixed nature, yet not already strongly hot.

greek_sentence: ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ μετὰ ψύξεως ἦν ὑγρότης περιττὴ, σύνθετον ἔσται καὶ τὸ ἴαμα, διὰ μὲν τὴν ψύξιν τῶν θερμαινόντων δεομένης τῆς διαθέσεως, διὰ δὲ τὴν ἀλλοτρίαν τε καὶ περιττὴν ὑγρότητα τῶν ἐκκενούντων.
english_sentence_A: But since the surplus moisture was present together with the cooling, the remedy too will be composite: because of the cooling the condition needs warming agents, and because of the alien and surplus moisture, evacuating agents.
english_sentence_B: But since there was superfluous moisture together with the chilling, the remedy too will be compound: the condition requires warming agents because of the chilling, and evacuating agents because of the foreign and superfluous moisture.

greek_sentence: ὅθεν οὐδὲ θεραπεύεται τῶν σκιῤῥουμένων οὐδὲν οὔθ’ ὑπὸ τῶν σφοδρῶς ξηραινόντων οὔθ’ ὑπὸ τῶν ἰσχυρῶς θερμαινόντων [727] οὔθ’ ὑπὸ τῶν ταῦτ’ ἄμφω δυναμένων.
english_sentence_A: Hence none of the scirrhous conditions is cured either by agents that dry vehemently, or by those that heat strongly, [727] or by those that are capable of both of these.
english_sentence_B: Hence none of the parts undergoing scirrhous hardening is cured either by the drugs that dry vehemently, or by those that heat strongly, [727] or by those capable of both.

lsj_entry_text: ἀνίατος [ι], Ion. ἀνθωρο-ίητος, ον, incurable, Hp. Aph. 7.87 ; ἕλκος, τραῦμα, Pl. Lg. 877a , 878c : also in moral sense, πράγματα ib. 660c ; ἀ. καὶ ἀνήκεστα κακά Aeschin. 3.156 ; ἀνελευθερία ἀ. ἐστιν Arist. EN 1121b13 . of persons, incurable, incorrigible, Pl. R. 410a , Grg. 526b ; ἀ. κατὰ τὴν μοχθηρίαν Arist. EN 1165b18 , al. Adv. ἀνιάτως, ἔχειν to be incurable, Pl. Phd. 113e , D. 18.324 ; οἱ ἀ. κακοί Arist. EN 1137a29 . Act. , ἀ. μετάνοια unavailing repentance, Antipho 2.4.12 .
greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ σφοδρῶς θερμαίνοντα διαφορήσαντα βιαίως τὸ παρακείμενον καὶ περιεχόμενον ἐν τοῖς μορίοις ὑγρὸν, ἀποξηραίνει τὸ ὑπόλοιπον, ὡς ἀνίατον γενέσθαι· τὰ δὲ σφοδρῶς ξηραίνοντα, κᾂν μὴ θερμαίνῃ ταῦτα, οὐδὲ διὰ μέσου τοῦ κενοῦντος τὸ λεπτομερὲς, ἀλλ’ ἄντικρύς τε καὶ κατὰ τὴν ἑαυτῶν φύσιν εἰς ἄκρον ξηρότητος προσάγει τὸ ἐσφηνωμένον ἐν τοῖς σκιῤῥουμένοις ῥεῦμα.
english_sentence_A: For those that heat vehemently, having dispersed by force the moisture lying beside and contained within the parts, dry out the remainder, so that it becomes incurable; while those that dry vehemently, even if they do not heat, bring the flux wedged in the scirrhous parts to the extreme of dryness, not through the intermediate step of evacuating the fine-particled portion, but directly and in accordance with their own nature.
english_sentence_B: For the drugs that heat vehemently, having violently dispersed the moisture lying alongside and contained in the parts, dry out what remains, so that it becomes incurable. The drugs that dry vehemently, even if they do not heat, and not through the intermediate step of evacuating the fine-particled part, nevertheless bring the flux wedged in the scirrhous parts to the extreme of dryness, directly and in accordance with their own nature.

greek_sentence: μόνα τοίνυν ὅσα θερμαίνει μὲν, οὐ μὴν σφοδρῶς, ἅμα τῷ μηδὲ ξηραίνειν ἰσχυρῶς ἰᾶται τὰς τοιαύτας διαθέσεις, καὶ καλεῖται τὰ τοιαῦτα φάρμακα μαλακτικὰ, καθ’ ἕνα καιρὸν ἄμφω δρῶντα καὶ χέοντα τὸ πεπηγὸς καὶ κατὰ βραχὺ διαφοροῦντα.
english_sentence_A: Therefore only those which heat, yet not vehemently, together with not drying strongly, cure such conditions; and such drugs are called softening, since at one and the same time they do both things, melting what is congealed and little by little dispersing it.
english_sentence_B: Only those drugs, then, which heat, but not vehemently, and at the same time do not dry strongly either, cure such conditions. Such drugs are called softening, since they do both things at one and the same time: they liquefy what has been congealed and disperse it little by little.

lsj_entry_text: ὅμοιος or (as in Hom. , Ion. , and old Att. ) ὁμοῖος, α, ον (cf. ἐρῆμος, ἑτοῖμος) : later Ep. also ὁμοίιος (B, q.v.) ; Aeol. ὔμοιος Theoc. 29.20 (Adv. -ως IG 12(2).69a6 ) ; Arc. ὑμοῖος Schwyzer 665 A 15 (Orchom., iv B.C.) : (ὁμός) :—like, resembling, ὡς αἰεὶ τὸν ὁ. ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὁ. 'birds of a feather flock together', Od. 17.218 ; ὁ ὅ. τῷ ὁ. Pl. Grg. 510b ; ὁ ὅ. ὡς τὸν ὅ. Arist. EN 1155a34 ; τὸ ὅ. τῷ ὁ. φίλον ib. 1165b17 , v. infr. 6 ; ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν ὁ. as in similar cases (of persons), BGU 79.18 (ii A.D.), etc. : Comp. -ότερος more like, Pl. Phd. 79b : Sup. -ότατος most like, Hdt. 2.92 , S. Ant. 833 (lyr.), etc. the same, ἄμφω γὰρ πέπρωται ὁμοίην γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι Il. 18.329 ; χρὼς οὐκέθ' ὁ. Od. 16.182 ; hence (sc. ἑαυτῷ), always the same, unchanging, αἰεὶ πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὁμοῖοι Hes. Op. 114 ; ὅ. τὴν γνώμην the same as ever, Antipho 5.76 ; γνῶμαι πρὸς τοὺς αὐτοὺς κινδύνους ὁμοῖαι Th. 2.89 ; ἀεὶ ὅ. εἶ, ὦ Ἀπολλόδωρε Pl. Smp. 173d ; ἓν καὶ ὅ. one and the same, Id. Phdr. 271a . equal in force, a match for one, Il. 23.632 , Hdt. 9.96 . of things, suiting, according with, πολλά τε καὶ ὅ. ἑαυταῖς Id. R. 549e ; ὅ. τῇ φύσει Ar. Th. 167 . ὁμοῖον ἡμῖν ἔσται it will be all the same, all one to us, Hdt. 8.80 ; σὺ δ' αἰνεῖν εἴτε με ψέγειν θέλεις, ὁμοῖον A. Ag. 1404 , cf. 1239 , E. Supp. 1069 ; ἐν τῷ ὁ. καθειστήκει Th. 2.49 . τὸ ὅ. ἀνταποδιδόναι give 'tit for tat', Hdt. 1.18 ; so τὴν ὁμοίην (sc. δίκην, χάριν) ἀποδιδόναι τινί Id. 4.119 , 6.21 , 62 ; τὴν ὁ. φέρεσθαι παρά τινος to have a like return made one, ibid. ; ἐπ' ἴσῃ καὶ ὁμοίᾳ, v. ἴσος 11.2 . ἐν ὁμοίῳ ποιεῖσθαί τι hold a thing in like esteem, Id. 7.138 , 8.109 . ἐκ τοῦ ὁ. in like fashion, likewise, Th. 6.78 , 87 ; ἐκ τῶν ὁ. ceteris paribus, Pl. Phdr. 243d ; on equal terms, in fair fight, A. Ag. 1423 ; so ἐν τῷ ὁ. στρατεύεσθαι καὶ ὅτε . . as when . . , Th. 6.21 , etc. of the same rank or station, Hdt. 1.134 ; γαμεῖν ἐκ τῶν ὁ. Cleobul. ap. Stob. 3.1.172 , POxy. 124.2 (iii A.D.), PSI 2.120.33 (iv A.D.?) : hence οἱ ὅμοιοι, in aristocratic states, peers, all citizens who had equal right to hold state-offices, esp. at Sparta, X. HG 3.3.5 , Lac. 13.1 , 7 , Arist. Pol. 1306b30 ; Περσέων ὁμοίους τοῖσι πρώτοισι δυώδεκα Hdt. 3.35 . Geom., of figures, similar, Euc. 6 Def. 1 , 3 Def. 11 , al. ; of angles, similar, i.e. equal, Arist. Cael. 296b20 , 297b19 , 311b34 , cf. Thalesap. Procl. in Euc. 1p.251F. of Numbers, square, the product of two equal factors, Plot. 6.2.21 ; cf. ἀνόμοιος 2 . Construction : abs., freq. in Hom. , etc. (v. supr.). c. dat. of the person or thing which another resembles : so always in Hom. , Hes. , and usu. in Hdt. and Att. (v. supr.) : but sts. c. gen., τοῖσι τούτων ὁμοίοις χύμασι v.l. in Hp. Art. 12 (DielsZtschr.f.vergl. Sprachf. 47.200 ), v. l. in Hdt. 3.37 and Pl. R. 472d ; τουτέων οὐκ ἔστιν ἄλλο ἔθνος ὁμοίας τὰς κεφαλὰς ἔχον οὐδέν (ellipt. as in b. infr.) Hp. Aër. 14 ; ὁ λεκτικὸς πῇ μὲν ὅμοιος Ἡροδότου, πῇ δὲ ἐνδεέστερος D.H. Pomp. 4 ; ὁμοία ἀνδριάντος Dion.Byz. 53 ; ὅμοιον ἱέρακος Cyran. 22 , cf. 12 . ellipt. phrases, κόμαι Χαρίτεσσιν ὁμοῖαι, for κόμαι ταῖς τῶν Χαρίτων ὁμοῖαι, Il. 17.51 ; οὔ τις ὁμοῖα νοήματα Πηνελοπείῃ ᾔδη, for τοῖς τῆς Πηνελοπείης, Od. 2.121 : also in Prose, ἅρματα ὅ. ἐκείνῳ, for τοῖς ἐκείνου, X. Cyr. 6.1.50 ; ὁμοίαν ταῖς δούλαις ἐσθῆτα, for τῇ τῶν δουλῶν, ib. 5.1.4 ; cf. ἴσος 1.1 , συγγενής 111.2 . c. acc. of that in which a person or thing resembles another, ἀθανάτῃσι φυὴν καὶ εἶδος ὁμοίη Od. 6.16 , cf. 3.468 , Il. 5.778 ; ὀργὴν ὁ. τῷ κάκιστ' αὐδωμένῳ A. Th. 678 , cf. S. Aj. 1153 , etc. : also with Preps., ὁμοῖοι ἐν πολέμῳ Il. 12.270 ; ἐς φύσιν οὐδὲν ὁ. Batr. 32 ; ὅ. τινὶ πρός τι X. Cyn. 5.29 ; but οὐδὲν ὁμοῖον ἦν μοι πρὸς τοῦτον I had nothing in common with him, Is. 8.26 . c. inf., θείειν ἀνέμοισιν ὁμοῖοι like the winds in running, Il. 10.437 ; τῷ οὔ πώ τις ὁμοῖος κοσμῆσαι ἵππους like him to marshal or in marshalling horses, 2.553 , cf. 14.521 ; ὅμοιοι ἦσαν θαυμάζειν (s. v.l., θαυμάζοντες codd. dett.) X. An. 3.5.13 . ὅμοιον εἰπεῖν approximately, Men. Epit. 548 . folld. by a Relat., ὁμοίη, οἵην με τὸ πρῶτον ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσι νόησας like as when thou saw'st me first, h.Ven. 178 ; ὅμοιον . . , οἷόνπερ τὸ τῶν ποταμῶν X. HG 4.2.11 , cf. greek_sentence: τὰ μὲν γὰρ σύμφυλόν τε καὶ ὁμοιοτάτην ἔχει τοῖς σώμασιν ἡμῶν τὴν θερμότητα, τὰ δὲ μαλάττοντα σφοδρότερα μὲν, οὐ [728] μὴν ὥστε τῷ βιαίῳ τῆς ὁλκῆς καταξηραίνειν τὸ ὑπόλοιπον.
english_sentence_A: For the former have a heat that is akin and most similar to that of our bodies, whereas the softening ones are more vehement, yet not [728] so much so as to dry up the remainder by the violence of their attraction.
english_sentence_B: For the former possess a heat that is akin and most similar to our bodies, whereas the softening ones are more intense, though not [728] so much as to dry out the remainder by the violence of their drawing.

lsj_entry_text: μαλακ-τικός, ή, όν, emollient, χρίσματα Hp. Vict. 2.66 ; δύναμις Plu. 2.659c ; μ. οἶκος, of the outer chamber in a bath, Alex. Trall. Febr. 5 .
greek_sentence: ἔτι δὲ τὰ μὲν ἐκπυΐσκσντα τὴν προϋπάρχουσαν ἐν τοῖς σκιῤῥουμένοις μορίοις ὑγρότητα φυλάττει, τὰ δὲ μαλακτικὰ βραχύ τι μέρος αὐτῆς ἀναλίσκει.
english_sentence_A: Further, the suppurative ones preserve the moisture already present in the parts affected by scirrhus, whereas the softening ones consume some small portion of it.
english_sentence_B: Further, the suppurating ones preserve the moisture already present in the parts undergoing skirrhos, whereas the softening ones consume some small part of it.

lsj_entry_text: βδέλλιον, τό, the aromatic gum obtained from Balsamodendrum africanum and B. Mukul, Dsc. 1.67 , Damocr. ap. Gal. 14.118 , Plin. HN 12.35 , Aq. , Sm. , Thd. Ge. 2.12 . (Semitic word.)
greek_sentence: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο μυρίων ὄντων τῶν θερμαινόντων καὶ ξηραινόντων φαρμάκων, ὅσα συμμέτρου τε ἅμα θερμότητος μετέχει ἀνάλογόν τε ταύτῃ ξηρότητος εὐτύχησε, ταῦτα μόνα μαλακτικὰ τῶν σκιῤῥουμένων ἐστὶν, οἷον βδέλλιον καὶ στύραξ καὶ χαλβάνη καὶ ἀμμωνιακὸν θυμίαμα καὶ μυελὸς ἐλάφειός τε καὶ μόσχειος, καὶ στέαρ αἴγειόν τε καὶ ταύρειον, ὅσα τ’ ἄλλα τοιαῦτα.
english_sentence_A: And for this reason, though the heating and drying drugs are countless, those which partake at once of a moderate heat and have had the good fortune to possess a dryness proportionate to it—these alone are softening of parts affected by scirrhus, such as bdellium, storax, galbanum, ammoniac incense, deer's and calf's marrow, goat's and bull's fat, and whatever others are of this kind.
english_sentence_B: And for this reason, though heating and drying drugs are countless, only those which share in a moderate heat and have also happened to have a dryness proportionate to it are softening of parts undergoing skirrhos: for example bdellium, storax, galbanum, ammoniac incense, the marrow of deer and of calf, the fat of goat and of bull, and all other such things.

greek_sentence: νῦν γὰρ οὐ πρόκειται τὴν ὕλην ἐπεξιέναι πᾶσαν, ἀλλὰ καθόλου μίαν ὑπὲρ ἁπασῶν τῶν τοιούτων δυνάμεων ποιήσασθαι διδασκαλίαν, τί δὴ τὸ καθόλου, ὃ περί τε τῶν ἐκπυϊσκόντων καὶ μαλαττόντων ἐστὶ γνῶναι βέλτιον, ὡς τὰ μὲν ἴσην ἀνάπτει θερμότητα τῇ τοῦ ζώου κατὰ φύσιν, ὅσα δὲ μαλάττει, πολὺ πλέονα, καὶ ὡς τὰ μὲν οὐ τῷ ποιῷ τῆς θερμότητος, ἀλλὰ τῷ ποσῷ μᾶλλον ἐνεργεῖν πέφυκεν, ὅσα δὲ τῶν σκιῤῥουμένων ﻿ [729] ἐστὶ μαλακτικὰ, τῷ ποιῷ μᾶλλον.
english_sentence_A: For at present it is not my purpose to go through all the material, but to produce one general teaching concerning all such powers—namely, what the general point is which it is better to know about both the suppurating and the softening agents: that the former kindle a heat equal to that of the animal according to nature, whereas those that soften kindle much more; and that the former by nature act not by the quality of the heat but rather by its quantity, whereas those that are softening of indurated parts [729] act rather by the quality.
english_sentence_B: For it is not our present purpose to go through all the material, but to give a single general instruction covering all such powers. And what is the general point that it is better to know about those that bring to suppuration and those that soften?

english_sentence_A: And nothing prevents one from understanding by 'innate heat' also the blood-like and airy substance together with the pneuma.
english_sentence_B: Nothing, however, prevents us from also understanding by innate heat the sanguineous and airy substance together with the pneuma.

lsj_entry_text: ἀερώδης, ες, like air, of the soul, Epicur. Fr. 314 ; Astrol., of signs, connected with the air, Vett.Val. 7.26 ; light of texture, Sch. E. Or. 1431 . = ἀέρινος 2 , τὴν χρόαν Dsc. 5.152 (dub.). τὸ ἀ. the airy nature, Placit. 2.11.2 , al., cf. Arist. Mu. 395a20 . full of air, Id. PA 669b2 .
